guides.intro:
Remote roles draw applicants from everywhere, so each opening can receive a very large pile. Being qualified is often not enough to be noticed.

This guide helps you diagnose where your search is stalling, tailor what screeners see first, and reach someone on the team directly, so your remote application has a real chance to be read.

free.title: Step 1: Run a 15-minute silence diagnosis
free.body:
Before you send one more application, find out where the leak is. Open a sheet and list your last 20 applications. For each one, write three things: the job title, how closely your last job matches it (strong, partial, stretch), and whether you contacted any person at the company (yes or no).

Now look at the pattern. If most are stretch roles, the problem is targeting. If most are strong matches but you still hear nothing, the problem is how your resume reads in the first few seconds. If almost every row says no person contacted, the problem is that you are relying only on a pile that may never be read in order.

Most people find more than one leak. That is fine. Fix the biggest one first.
free.prompt:
I have applied to a lot of jobs and I am not hearing back. Act as a blunt career diagnostician. Here is my list of recent applications, with job title, how closely my experience matches (strong, partial, stretch), and whether I contacted anyone at the company:

[paste your list]

Here is my current resume:

[paste resume]

Tell me: 1) which of these three problems is my biggest leak: targeting, how my resume reads in the first few seconds, or no human contact. 2) The evidence from my list that points to it. 3) The three most specific changes I should make this week, in order. Be direct. No encouragement filler.

free.title: Step 2: Fix the first six seconds of your resume
free.body:
A screener skims the top third of your resume and decides fast. If that section does not say plainly who you are and what you deliver for this kind of role, the rest rarely gets read.

Rewrite the top for each job family you target. Use a one-line headline that matches the job title they posted, not a vague label. Under it, write two or three lines that name the problems you solve and the kind of results you produce, using real numbers only if they are true. Then make sure your most relevant recent job sits right under that, with its strongest bullet first.

Test it: hand the top third to a friend for six seconds, take it away, and ask what job you do. If they cannot say it, rewrite.
free.prompt:
Here is a job posting:

[paste job posting]

Here is the top third of my resume (headline, summary, and my most recent role):

[paste]

Rewrite only the top third so a screener who skims for six seconds knows I fit this job. Rules: the headline should mirror the posted job title if my experience honestly supports it. Keep the summary to three lines. Lead my most recent role with the bullet most relevant to this posting. Use the posting's own words where they truthfully describe my work. Do not invent numbers or skills I did not list. Then list any requirement in the posting my resume does not show yet, so I can decide whether to add real evidence or skip this job.

free.title: Step 3: After every application, reach one human
free.body:
An application alone sits in a pile. A short note to a real person gives you a second way in. After you apply, find one person connected to the role: the likely hiring manager, someone who leads that team, or a peer on it.

To find them yourself, search LinkedIn for the company name plus the team (for example, "Netflix marketing" or "product design lead"), check the company team or about page, and read recent press releases, which often name leaders. Pick the person closest to the work.

Send a note that is short, specific, and easy to answer. Template:

"Hi [Name], I just applied for the [Role] on your team. I have spent [X years] doing [the core work], most recently [one specific result or project]. I would love to be considered, and I am happy to share more if useful. Thanks, [Your name]"

One note per application. Polite, then leave it.
free.prompt: Write a short LinkedIn message (under 300 characters) and a short email version (under 90 words) to [Name], who is [their title] at [Company]. I just applied for the [Role]. My most relevant experience: [2-3 lines about your background and one specific result]. Something about their team or company I genuinely noticed: [detail]. Tone: confident, plain, not needy. No flattery, no "I know you are busy". End with an easy, low-pressure ask. Give me two versions of each.

locked.title: Step 4: Swap volume for a weekly shortlist
locked.body:
Applying to everything feels productive, but it spreads your effort thin. Try a different week: pick a small shortlist of roles where you are a strong match, and give each one the full treatment from Steps 2 and 3.

A simple weekly rhythm: Monday, pick your shortlist and write down why each one fits. Tuesday and Wednesday, tailor your top third and apply. Thursday, send your human notes. Friday, update your tracker and decide what to change.

To pick the shortlist, score each job on three things from one to three: how closely your recent work matches, whether you meet the must-have requirements, and whether you can find a real person on the team. Keep the highest scores. Let the rest go without guilt.
locked.prompt:
Here are the jobs I am considering this week:

[paste titles, companies, and the key requirements of each]

Here is a short summary of my experience:

[paste]

Score each job from 1 to 3 on: match to my recent work, whether I meet the must-have requirements, and how easy it will be to identify a real person on the team. Total the scores, rank the list, and recommend the top ones to focus on this week. For each top pick, give me one sentence on my strongest angle for that specific job.

locked.title: Step 5: Show them, instead of telling them
locked.body:
A resume tells. A short page built for one company shows. When a person clicks your note, give them something that answers the question "why you, for us" in under a minute.

You can build this yourself as a one-page document or simple personal page. Include a two-line opener addressed to that company, three short proof points that map to what the posting asks for, one example of your work or a short story of a problem you solved, and a clear way to reach you.

Link it in your human note: "I put together a one-page summary of how I would help your team, here." This gives the reader something more interesting than another PDF.
locked.prompt:
Help me build a one-page "why me for [Company]" summary for the [Role] position. Here is the posting:

[paste posting]

Here is my background:

[paste resume or summary]

Create: 1) a two-line opener written to this company, 2) three proof points, each tied to a specific requirement in the posting and backed by something real from my background, 3) one short story (problem, what I did, result) that fits this role, 4) a closing line inviting a conversation. Plain language. Do not invent results. Flag anything where I need to add a real number or example.

locked.body:
If you would rather not do every step by hand, Scout can do much of it with you. Scout builds your Career ID and a career diagnosis that shows where your search is getting stuck. It builds Showcases, which are personal web pages built for one job or one company, with many designs to choose from.

You, or someone you authorize, approve the sends. It follows up, tells you when someone views your Showcase, and sends you a weekly report of everything it did.

locked.prompt: Scout, why am I not hearing back?

locked.title: Step 7: Track it for two weeks, then change one thing
locked.body:
Guessing is how searches stall. Keep a simple tracker with these columns: date, company, role, match score, top third tailored (yes or no), person contacted (name and title), note sent date, any reply, next step.

After two weeks, look at it honestly. Which applications got any response at all? What did they have in common: a stronger match, a tailored top third, a human note? Do more of that. If nothing has moved, go back to Step 1 and re-run the diagnosis with the new data.

Change one thing at a time so you can tell what helped. That is how you turn silence into information.
locked.prompt:
Here is my job search tracker for the last two weeks:

[paste your tracker rows]

Analyze it like a coach. Tell me: 1) any patterns in which applications got a reply, 2) what the ones with no reply have in common, 3) the single change I should test next week, and how I will know if it worked. Keep it short and specific.

guides.tip: Put your time zone and remote work setup in one line near your contact info, for example "Remote, Eastern Time, experienced with async teams." It answers a question remote screeners often have.

guides.intro:
Remote roles often get large applicant pools, so many companies lean on automated screening. Location rules and time zone questions are common filters.

This guide walks through the screening checks that trip people up on remote roles, how to make your resume easy to read, and how to build a one-job Showcase a hiring team can review on their own time.

free.title: Step 1: Know what the robot is actually checking
free.body:
A rejection at 2am usually means a rule fired, not that someone read your resume and said no. Many application systems let employers set filters. The common ones: knockout questions (work authorization, willingness to relocate, minimum years, a required license or degree), location, and how closely your resume's wording matches the posting.

So before you blame your experience, check the rules. Reread the posting and write down every hard requirement: anything with words like "required", "must", or "minimum". Then write your honest answer next to each one.

If you truly miss a hard requirement, skip that job and save your energy. If you meet them all and still got auto-rejected, the problem is likely how your answers or resume were read, and the next two steps fix that.
free.prompt:
Here is a job posting:

[paste posting]

List every hard requirement or likely screening filter in it: work authorization, location or on-site expectations, minimum years of experience, required degrees, licenses, certifications, tools, and anything marked required or must. Then, using my resume below, mark each one as Clearly met, Met but not obvious on my resume, or Not met.

[paste resume]

For anything marked Met but not obvious, tell me exactly where and how to make it visible in plain words.

free.title: Step 2: Run the knockout question checklist before you submit
free.body:
Portal questions can reject you faster than your resume. Go slow on them. Use this checklist every time:

1. Work authorization and sponsorship: answer exactly and truthfully. Read the question twice, they are often worded differently.
2. Years of experience: count all relevant years honestly, including related roles, not only jobs with the exact title.
3. Location and relocation: if the role is hybrid or on-site, answer what you will actually do.
4. Salary expectation: if a number is required, use a range based on research for that role and city, not a guess.
5. Yes or no skill questions: if you have used the tool or done the work, the honest answer is yes. Then make sure your resume shows it.
6. Free text boxes: never leave them blank. Two clear sentences beat nothing.

Screenshot your answers before you submit, so you can learn from them later.
free.prompt:
I am filling out an application for [Role] at [Company]. Here are the screening questions in the portal:

[paste questions]

Here is my background:

[paste resume or summary]

For each question, tell me: what the employer is most likely checking for, how to answer truthfully in a way that does not undersell me, and any wording trap to watch for. For free text questions, draft a clear two to three sentence answer from my real experience. Do not suggest answering anything untruthfully.

free.title: Step 3: Make your resume easy for software to read
free.body:
Some systems struggle with fancy layouts. Columns, text boxes, tables, icons, and graphics can scramble your information when parsed, which can make you look like a weaker match than you are.

Use a plain version for portals: one column, standard section headings (Summary, Experience, Skills, Education), regular fonts, dates in a consistent format, and your job title and company on their own lines. Save as the file type the portal asks for. Keep your designed version for humans.

Then build a keyword map. Pull the key skills and phrases from the posting and make sure each one you truly have appears in your resume in the same words, inside a real bullet that shows how you used it. A skills list alone is weaker than a bullet that proves it.
free.prompt:
Here is a job posting:

[paste posting]

Here is my resume as plain text:

[paste resume]

Build a keyword map. 1) List the most important skills, tools, and phrases in the posting. 2) For each one, show whether my resume uses the same wording, a different wording, or does not mention it. 3) For the ones I truly have but describe differently, rewrite the relevant bullet so it uses the posting's wording naturally and shows how I used it. 4) List any I do not have, so I do not fake them. Keep my real facts unchanged.

locked.title: Step 4: Build a one-job Showcase page
locked.body:
A Showcase is a personal page built for one job or one company. It gives a human something to see that a filter cannot flatten. You can make one yourself with any simple page builder or a well-designed one-page document.

Use this blueprint:

1. Headline: "[Your name] for [Role] at [Company]".
2. Why this team: two or three sentences on what you noticed about their work and why it fits you.
3. Three proof blocks: each one maps to a top requirement in the posting, with a real example and a result.
4. One deeper story: a problem you solved, how, and what changed.
5. Your first 90 days: three sensible things you would focus on, framed as ideas, not promises.
6. Contact: email and LinkedIn, and a resume download.

Keep it scannable. One screen per section.
locked.prompt:
Write the copy for a one-page Showcase built for one job. Role: [Role] at [Company]. Posting:

[paste posting]

My background:

[paste resume]

What I know about the company or team: [notes]

Produce these sections: Headline, Why this team (2-3 sentences), three Proof blocks (each tied to a named requirement in the posting, with a real example from my background), one Deeper story (problem, action, result), My first 90 days (three focus areas framed as ideas, not promises), and a short Contact line. Plain language, no hype. Do not invent results. Mark anywhere I should add a real number or link.

locked.title: Step 6: The 48 hours after an auto-reject
locked.body:
An automated rejection closes one door, not every door. If you are a genuine match, you have options.

First, check your Step 2 screenshots. If you mis-answered a knockout question, some companies let you apply again to a different, related opening. Look for one.

Second, go to a person. Find the hiring manager or a team lead on LinkedIn or the company team page and send a short note with your Showcase. Do not complain about the rejection. Just show fit. Example:

"Hi [Name], I am interested in the [Role] on your team and built a short page on how my experience in [area] could help with [something specific to their work]. Happy to share more if it is useful. [Your name]"

Third, check the company careers page for similar roles you can apply to with the same Showcase.
locked.prompt:
I was auto-rejected for [Role] at [Company] shortly after applying, but I believe I am a strong match. Here is the posting:

[paste]

Here is my background:

[paste]

Help me plan the next 48 hours: 1) likely reasons the screen rejected me, based on the posting and my resume, 2) what to fix before I apply anywhere similar, 3) a short, gracious note to a hiring manager or team lead that shows fit without mentioning the rejection, 4) what kinds of related roles at this company I should look for.

locked.title: Step 7: Your pre-submit checklist
locked.body:
Use this before every application from now on. It takes a few minutes and catches most avoidable screen-outs.

1. I meet every hard requirement, or I am skipping this one.
2. I am using my plain, single-column resume for this portal.
3. My keyword map is done and the key terms appear in real bullets.
4. I have read every knockout question twice and answered truthfully.
5. No free text box is blank.
6. My resume file name includes my name and the role.
7. I have a Showcase or one-page summary ready for a human.
8. I know who I will contact on the team after I apply.

Save this list somewhere you will see it. Over time, note which items you skip most, because that is usually where rejections come from.

guides.tip: Read the location fine print on remote postings. Many say remote within a specific country or set of time zones. Answer location questions to match what you can actually do.

guides.intro:
Remote job searches often mean many portals across many companies and time zones. Retyping the same details into each one adds up fast.

This guide helps you build a reusable kit and answer bank, set up a simple weekly rhythm, and spend your time on the roles and people most worth it.

free.title: Step 1: Audit one week of job search time
free.body:
You cannot get your nights back until you know where they went. For one week, log every job search session in a simple note: date, minutes, and what you were doing. Use four buckets:

1. Data entry: retyping your resume, filling portal fields, creating accounts.
2. Searching: scrolling boards and reading postings.
3. Tailoring: adjusting your resume or writing for a specific job.
4. Human contact: messaging people, networking, interviews.

At the end of the week, add up each bucket. Most people find that data entry and scrolling eat the biggest share, while human contact, the part that tends to move a search forward, gets the least.

Your goal for the rest of this guide: shrink buckets 1 and 2, and move that time into 3 and 4.
free.prompt:
Here is my job search time log for the past week, with minutes and activity for each session:

[paste log]

Sort each entry into four buckets: data entry, searching, tailoring, and human contact. Total the minutes per bucket and show the percentages. Then give me three specific ways to cut time from data entry and searching next week, and a plan to move that time into tailoring and human contact. Be practical.

free.title: Step 2: Build a copy-paste application kit
free.body:
Most portals ask for the same information in slightly different boxes. Build it once, then paste. Create a single document called Application Kit with these sections, each formatted as plain text:

1. Contact block: full name, email, phone, city, LinkedIn.
2. Each job: title, company, city, start and end month and year, and three to five bullets, written so each bullet can be pasted alone.
3. Education and certifications with dates.
4. A skills list in one line, comma separated.
5. Short and long versions of your summary: one sentence, and three sentences.
6. References, if you have permission to share them.

Keep it in plain text so formatting does not break when you paste. Pin it somewhere you can open in one click. Many browsers can also save your basic contact details for autofill, which helps with the first page of most forms.
free.prompt:
Turn my resume into an Application Kit made for copying and pasting into job portals. Here is my resume:

[paste resume]

Format everything as plain text, no bullet symbols or special characters that might break in a form. Create: a contact block, each job as a separate block (title, company, location, start month and year, end month and year, then three to five standalone bullets), education, certifications, a one-line comma-separated skills list, a one-sentence summary, and a three-sentence summary. Also give each job a short description under 500 characters, since many portals limit that field.

free.title: Step 3: Write your answer bank once
free.body:
Portals keep asking the same open questions. Write strong answers once and reuse them, adjusting one line for each company.

Common ones to prepare:

1. Why are you interested in this role?
2. Why do you want to work here?
3. Tell us about yourself.
4. Why are you leaving, or why did you leave, your last job?
5. Describe a challenge you overcame.
6. What are your salary expectations?
7. When can you start?
8. Is there anything else you would like us to know?

For each one, write a reusable core answer, then leave a clearly marked slot like [company-specific line] that you fill in each time. That one line is where you show you actually read about them. The rest stays the same.
free.prompt:
Write an answer bank for common job application questions. My background:

[paste resume or summary]

The kind of roles I am targeting: [role type and level]

Write a core answer, under 120 words each, for: Why this role, Why this company, Tell us about yourself, Why I am leaving or left my last job (my honest reason: [reason]), A challenge I overcame (use this real situation: [describe]), Salary expectations (my researched range: [range]), Start date (my availability: [availability]), and Anything else you would like us to know. In each answer, include a clearly marked [company-specific line] slot where I add one sentence about that employer. Keep the tone plain and confident.

locked.title: Step 4: Decide which portals are worth it
locked.body:
Not every portal deserves an hour. Before you start a long form, run a quick worth-it test:

1. Am I a strong match for the hard requirements?
2. Was this posted recently?
3. Can I identify at least one person on the team to contact after I apply?
4. Do I actually want this job?

If you answer yes to all four, give it the full effort. If you get two or fewer, skip it or save it for a low-energy moment.

Also, check the company careers page before applying through a board. Applying directly is often cleaner, and sometimes you find a better fitting role there. If a portal asks you to create an account, use a consistent username and save it in your password manager so you are not resetting passwords at midnight.
locked.prompt:
Here are the jobs in my queue this week, with title, company, posting date, and key requirements:

[paste list]

My background in brief:

[paste]

Run a worth-it test on each one: match to hard requirements, how recent the posting is, how likely I can find a person on the team, and a fit score based on my stated goals: [what you want in your next job]. Sort them into Full effort, Quick apply, and Skip, with one line of reasoning each.

locked.body:
Once you see how much time goes to data entry and searching, you can decide what to hand off. Scout is built for this. It builds Showcases, which are personal pages made for one job or one company, with many designs to choose from.

Scout can also find people at a target company, like hiring managers or team leads, and reach out with a short note and your Showcase in small paced waves, with you or someone you authorize approving the sends. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, and gives you a weekly report of everything it did. That leaves your time for interviews and conversations.

locked.title: Step 6: Protect your evenings with a time-boxed week
locked.body:
A search with no edges takes over every night. Give it a container. Pick a set number of focused sessions per week and stop when the time is up.

A sample week:

Monday, 45 minutes: search and run the worth-it test. Save your shortlist.
Tuesday, 60 minutes: tailor and apply to your Full effort jobs, pasting from your kit and answer bank.
Wednesday, 30 minutes: contact one person per application.
Thursday, off.
Friday, 30 minutes: follow-ups and tracker update.
Weekend: one optional session, or rest.

Set a timer. When it goes off, write the very next action at the top of your tracker so tomorrow starts fast. Rest is part of the plan, not a reward for finishing.
locked.prompt: Help me design a time-boxed weekly job search schedule. My constraints: [work hours, family time, energy levels, days I am free]. Total time I am willing to spend per week: [hours]. My current biggest time sinks: [from your audit]. Build a weekly calendar with specific sessions, what to do in each, and a hard stop time. Include at least one full night off. Add a short end-of-session routine so I can pick up quickly next time.

locked.title: Step 7: Re-audit and reclaim more time
locked.body:
After two weeks on the new system, repeat the Step 1 audit. Compare the bucket totals. Has data entry shrunk? Has human contact grown?

Then look at results alongside time: replies, conversations, interviews. Note which activity tends to come before each good outcome. If messages to people come before most replies, give that bucket more time. If a type of portal keeps eating your evening with nothing to show, drop it.

Update your Application Kit and answer bank with anything you found yourself typing more than once. Every repeat you capture is time you never spend again.
locked.prompt:
Here are two time logs: my first week and my most recent week of job searching.

Week 1: [paste]
Recent week: [paste]

And here are the results from the recent period: [replies, conversations, interviews, with dates]

Compare how my time shifted across data entry, searching, tailoring, and human contact. Point out which activities seem connected to the results I got. Recommend what to cut, what to keep, and what to add next week. Also list anything I seem to be retyping that should go into my Application Kit.

guides.intro:
With remote interviews, there is no office visit and no hallway chat, so it can be harder to read how things went. Teams may also be spread across time zones, which can slow decisions.

This guide gives you a steady follow-up rhythm with clear templates, so you stay visible to a distributed team without overdoing it.

free.title: Step 1: Set up the follow-up before you leave the interview
free.body:
The best follow-up starts in the room. In the last few minutes of every interview, ask two questions:

"What are the next steps, and when do you expect to make a decision?"
"Who is the best person for me to stay in touch with?"

Write the answers down right after. Now you have a date and a name, so your follow-up is not a guess. Also note one or two specific things that came up: a project they mentioned, a problem the team has, something you connected on. You will use these in every message.

If you already finished the interview and did not ask, that is fine. Your Day 4 check-in can ask for the timeline instead.
free.prompt:
I just finished an interview for [Role] at [Company] with [Name, title]. Here are my rough notes on what we discussed:

[paste notes]

Pull out: 1) the two or three specific topics I should reference in follow-ups, 2) any problem or priority the team mentioned that I could help with, 3) any timeline or next step they gave. Then list anything I should have asked but did not, so I can work it into my follow-up naturally.

free.title: Step 2: Day 1, send a specific thank you
free.body:
Send it within a day, to each person you met if you have their contact, otherwise to your main contact or the recruiter. Keep it short and specific. A generic thank you is easy to forget, but one that mentions your conversation shows you were paying attention.

Template:

"Hi [Name], thank you for the time today. I enjoyed talking about [specific topic], especially [one detail]. It made me even more interested in the role, because [one reason tied to your experience]. I am looking forward to next steps. Best, [Your name]"

If you met several people, change the specific detail for each person. They may compare notes.
free.prompt: Write a short thank you email (under 100 words) to [Name, title] after my interview for [Role] at [Company]. Specific things we talked about: [topics]. One reason I am a strong fit that connects to our conversation: [reason]. Tone: warm, professional, not gushing. Subject line included. If I met more than one person, I will tell you who, and you will write a separate version for each with a different specific detail: [other names and what you discussed with each].

free.title: Step 3: Day 4, a short check-in
free.body:
If you have heard nothing a few business days after the interview, or the day after the date they gave you, send a brief check-in. Its only job is to stay visible and get a timeline.

Template:

"Hi [Name], I hope your week is going well. I wanted to check in on the [Role] position. I am still very interested and would be glad to provide anything else that helps. Is there an updated timeline for next steps? Thanks, [Your name]"

Do not apologize for following up. Do not ask if they have made a decision. Ask for the timeline, which is easier to answer. If they reply with a date, put it on your calendar and wait until the day after it before you send anything else.
free.prompt: Write a short check-in email (under 70 words) to [Name] about the [Role] at [Company]. I interviewed on [date]. They said they would decide by [date, or "they did not give a date"]. Tone: friendly, confident, not anxious. Ask for an updated timeline rather than a decision. Give me two versions, one slightly warmer and one more direct, and a subject line for each.

locked.title: Step 4: Day 9, add value instead of asking again
locked.body:
If the check-in did not get an answer, do not send the same message twice. Send something useful instead. This keeps you top of mind and shows how you think.

Ideas for a value-add follow-up:

1. A short written idea on a problem they mentioned in the interview.
2. A relevant article or example, with one line on why it made you think of them.
3. A brief summary of a past project similar to their challenge.
4. A one-page outline of how you would approach your first month, framed as ideas.

Template:

"Hi [Name], after our conversation about [problem], I kept thinking about it and put a few quick ideas together, attached. No reply needed. I just wanted to share. I am still very interested in the role. [Your name]"
locked.prompt:
I interviewed for [Role] at [Company] and have not heard back after a check-in. In the interview they mentioned this challenge or priority: [describe]. My relevant experience: [describe].

Help me write a value-add follow-up. 1) Suggest three possible value-adds I could realistically create in under an hour. 2) For the one you think is strongest, draft a short outline (five to eight bullet points) of the content. 3) Draft the email to go with it, under 80 words, that does not pressure them for an answer.

locked.title: Step 5: Let Scout run your follow-ups
locked.body:
Keeping track of who to follow up with, and when, gets hard once you have several applications moving. Scout follows up on your applications for you, and when you reach out to people at a target company through Scout, it sends short notes with your Showcase in small paced waves, with you or someone you authorize approving the sends.

Scout also alerts you when someone views your Showcase, which tells you when interest is active. When a company replies, you get a prep brief on that company so you can show up ready. A weekly report shows you everything Scout did. Scout also builds your Career ID, Showcases for specific jobs, and finds and applies to matching jobs with your Showcase link included.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=the-follow-up-playbook-that-scout-runs-for-you&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, follow up on my applications

locked.title: Step 6: Follow up on applications that never got a reply
locked.body:
Interviews are not the only thing to follow up on. Applications that went quiet deserve a light touch too, aimed at a person, not the portal.

A simple sequence:

Day 1 after applying: a short note to the hiring manager or a team lead (find them on LinkedIn or the company team page) saying you applied and why you fit.
About a week later: one brief follow-up with a new detail, like a relevant project or a short page about how you would help.
About two weeks later: a final, friendly note, then move on.

Three touches, spaced out, each with something new. Never the same message twice. If anyone asks you to stop, stop.
locked.prompt: Write a three-message follow-up sequence for a job I applied to with no reply. Role: [Role] at [Company]. Person I am writing to: [Name, title]. My strongest fit points: [list]. Something new I can share in message two: [project, idea, or page]. Message 1: under 80 words, says I applied and why I fit. Message 2: under 70 words, adds the new detail. Message 3: under 50 words, friendly final note that leaves the door open. No guilt, no pressure, no repeated wording.

locked.title: Step 7: Close the loop and keep the door open
locked.body:
If you still hear nothing after the value-add, send one final close-the-loop message, then move your energy to other opportunities. This often gets a reply because it is easy to answer.

Template:

"Hi [Name], I have not heard back, so I will assume the team has moved in another direction for now. Thank you again for the conversations. I enjoyed learning about [team or project]. If anything changes or another role opens up, I would love to stay in touch. [Your name]"

If the answer is a no, reply graciously and ask one question: "Is there any feedback you are able to share?" Then connect on LinkedIn. People who were finalists are sometimes remembered when a new role opens. Log the person, the date, and what you learned in your tracker so you can reach out again later if it makes sense.
locked.prompt: Write two short messages for [Role] at [Company], contact [Name]. 1) A close-the-loop email for when I have heard nothing after my thank you, check-in, and value-add. Under 70 words. Gracious, no guilt, leaves the door open. 2) A reply to a rejection, under 60 words, that thanks them, asks if they can share any feedback, and says I would like to be considered for future roles. Things I enjoyed about the process: [details].

guides.tip: If the team works across time zones, ask in the interview which channel and timing they prefer for updates, then follow up that way.

guides.intro:
Remote hiring teams often get to know you only through what you send them. A single PDF gives them very little to go on, especially when many applicants have similar experience.

This guide helps you build a clear pitch and a Showcase that tells your story, shows your work, and helps a distributed team see why you would be a strong remote colleague.

free.title: Step 1: Build a proof inventory
free.body:
A resume lists what you did. It rarely shows how you think, what you fixed, or what changed because you were there. Before you can pitch yourself, you need the raw material.

Open a blank document and spend 20 minutes answering these for your last two or three roles:

1. What was broken, slow, or messy when I arrived, and what did I do about it?
2. What did people come to me for, even if it was not my job?
3. What am I proud of that never made it onto my resume?
4. What did I build, launch, start, or improve?
5. What did a manager, client, or coworker thank me for?
6. What numbers do I actually know: time saved, money, volume, people, growth?

Do not edit as you go. Messy is fine. You will shape it in the next steps.
free.prompt:
Interview me to build a proof inventory for my career. I will paste my resume below. Ask me questions one at a time, for my last two or three roles, to uncover: problems I solved, things people relied on me for, projects I am proud of that are not on my resume, things I built or improved, praise I received, and any real numbers I know. After each answer, ask one follow-up that digs for specifics. When we finish, organize everything into a list of proof points grouped by theme.

[paste resume]

free.title: Step 2: Pick your angle
free.body:
The same career can be pitched many ways. Your angle is the one sentence that makes a hiring manager think, "That is exactly what we need." Look at your proof inventory and see which of these angles your evidence supports best:

1. The Fixer: you walk into messes and make them work.
2. The Builder: you start things from nothing.
3. The Scaler: you take something working and grow it.
4. The Translator: you connect two groups who do not speak the same language, like tech and sales.
5. The Operator: you make teams run smoothly and on time.
6. The Specialist: you are deep in one skill others struggle with.
7. The Customer Champion: you know the customer better than anyone.
8. The Career Changer: your past field gives you a view others in this field do not have.

Pick one main angle, and maybe a second. Your angle can change by role, which is why a pitch beats a fixed list.
free.prompt:
Here is my proof inventory:

[paste inventory]

Here is the kind of role I am targeting: [role or paste a posting]

From these angles, The Fixer, The Builder, The Scaler, The Translator, The Operator, The Specialist, The Customer Champion, The Career Changer, tell me which two my evidence supports most strongly for this target role. For each, give the three strongest proof points that back it up, and one weakness or gap a hiring manager might see. Then recommend one as my main angle and explain why in two sentences.

free.title: Step 3: Write your positioning statement
free.body:
Now turn your angle into one clear line you can use at the top of a resume, a LinkedIn headline, an intro email, or a Showcase. Use this formula:

"I help [type of team or company] [achieve a result or solve a problem] by [how you do it, using your strengths]."

Examples of the shape:

"I help growing software teams turn messy support queues into calm, fast customer experiences by building simple processes people actually follow."
"I help retail brands launch new products on time by keeping design, supply, and marketing teams moving together."

Read it out loud. If it sounds like anyone could say it, make it more specific. If it sounds like a slogan, make it plainer. Write three versions, then pick one.
free.prompt:
Write five versions of a one-sentence positioning statement for me using this formula: I help [type of team or company] [achieve a result or solve a problem] by [how I do it].

My main angle: [angle]
My strongest proof points: [paste three to five]
The roles I am targeting: [roles]

Make each version specific to my real experience. No buzzwords like passionate, results-driven, or dynamic. Then give me a shorter version of the best one, under 12 words, for a LinkedIn headline.

locked.title: Step 4: Turn bullets into short case stories
locked.body:
A bullet like "Managed vendor relationships" tells a reader nothing about you. A short story does. Take your three strongest proof points and turn each into a mini case story with four parts:

1. The situation: what was going on, in one or two sentences.
2. The problem: what was at stake or not working.
3. What you did: your specific actions and choices.
4. What changed: the result, with a real number if you have one, or a clear before and after if you do not.

Keep each story under 120 words. These become the heart of your Showcase, and they double as interview answers. When someone asks "Tell me about a time when," you will already have it ready.
locked.prompt:
Turn these three proof points into short case stories, each under 120 words, with four labeled parts: Situation, Problem, What I did, What changed.

Proof point 1: [describe in your own words, as much detail as you remember]
Proof point 2: [describe]
Proof point 3: [describe]

Use plain, specific language. Only use numbers I gave you. If a story is missing a clear result, ask me a question to find one instead of inventing it. Then give each story a short title, five words or fewer.

locked.title: Step 5: Build your main Showcase
locked.body:
Your main Showcase is a personal web page that pitches you, not just lists you. Later you can make versions for specific jobs, but start with one strong main page. Structure:

1. Top: your name, your positioning statement, and a professional photo if you like.
2. What I do best: three short lines, each a strength backed by your angle.
3. Case stories: your three stories from Step 4.
4. How I work: a few lines on your approach, values, or the kind of team you thrive in.
5. What people say: real quotes from past reviews or recommendations, only with permission.
6. Contact: email, LinkedIn, and a resume download.

You can build this with any simple website builder. Keep it short enough to read in a couple of minutes.
locked.prompt:
Write the full copy for my main Showcase page. Sections: Top (name and positioning statement), What I do best (three one-line strengths), Case stories (use the three below, lightly edited for the web), How I work (three to four sentences), What people say (format the real quotes below, if any), and a Contact line.

Name: [name]
Positioning statement: [statement]
Angle: [angle]
Case stories: [paste]
Real quotes I have permission to use: [paste or write none]

Plain language, warm and confident, no hype. Do not add anything I did not provide.

locked.title: Step 6: Let Scout find your best angle and build your Showcase
locked.body:
If you want help with this, Scout builds your Career ID and a career diagnosis from your background, which helps surface your strongest angle for the role you want. Then it builds Showcases for you: a main page, plus versions made for one job or one company, with many designs to choose from.

Scout can also find matching jobs and apply for you with your Showcase link included, and find people at target companies, like hiring managers and team leads, then reach out with a short note and your Showcase in small paced waves, with you or someone you authorize approving the sends. You get an alert when someone views your Showcase, and a weekly report of everything Scout did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=what-a-showcase-is-and-why-resumes-aren-t-enough&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, what's my best angle for this role?

locked.title: Step 7: Test your pitch and sharpen it
locked.body:
A pitch gets better when real people react to it. Show your Showcase to three people: one who knows your work, one who works in the field you are targeting, and one who knows neither.

Ask each of them three questions after they look for one minute:

1. What do you think I do?
2. What kind of team would want me?
3. What part was most convincing, and what part did you skip?

If their answers match your positioning statement, it is working. If not, tighten the top section first, since that is what most people read. Swap weak stories for stronger ones as your proof inventory grows. Revisit your Showcase whenever you finish a big project, so it always reflects your best recent work.
locked.prompt:
I showed my Showcase to three people and asked: what do you think I do, what kind of team would want me, and what was most convincing versus skipped. Here are their answers:

[paste feedback]

Here is my current positioning statement and top section:

[paste]

Compare their answers to my intended positioning. Tell me where the message is landing and where it is not. Suggest a revised top section and say which case story to strengthen or replace.

guides.tip: Add a How I work section that covers your communication style and how you stay organized remotely. Remote teams often weigh this heavily.

guides.intro:
Remote job boards can be very crowded, and some listings are not as remote as they sound. Using only boards also means missing roles posted on company sites and openings filled through people.

This guide helps you filter boards for real remote roles, track remote-friendly companies directly, and connect with people on distributed teams.

free.title: Step 1: Door 1, use job boards smarter
free.body:
Job boards are useful. The mistake is using only them, and using them by scrolling. Turn boards into a system that brings jobs to you.

1. Set saved searches with alerts for your exact titles, plus two or three related titles people use for the same work.
2. Filter by date posted, and focus on recent postings, since early applicants are more likely to be seen.
3. Use the filters that matter to you: location, remote, level, salary range if shown.
4. Use search operators where the board allows, like quotes for exact phrases and a minus sign to exclude words you do not want.
5. Set a limit: check alerts once a day, for a set time, then close the tab.

The goal is less time scrolling, more time on the other two doors.
free.prompt:
I am searching for [target role] in [location or remote]. My background: [two to three lines].

Give me: 1) eight to ten alternative job titles companies use for this kind of work, 2) keywords to include and keywords to exclude in my searches, 3) three ready-to-use search strings using quotes and minus signs, 4) which filters I should set for my situation. Keep it practical.

free.title: Step 2: Door 2, go straight to company career pages
free.body:
Many companies post roles on their own careers page, and some roles show up there before they appear widely on boards, or never appear on boards at all. To use this door, you need a target list.

Build a list of 25 companies you would genuinely like to work for. Mix three types:

1. Dream companies: well-known names you admire. For example, say you want to work at Netflix.
2. Lookalikes: smaller or less famous companies in the same space.
3. Local or niche: employers near you, or in a specific industry you know well.

For each one, save the link to its careers page in a sheet. Once a week, check every page and note any new roles. Many careers pages also let you sign up for job alerts or join a talent community. Do that for your top companies.
free.prompt:
Help me build a target list of 25 companies for my job search. My target role: [role]. Industry I know or want: [industry]. Location or remote: [preference]. Companies I already admire: [list a few].

Give me: eight dream companies, ten lookalikes (similar work, possibly smaller or less known), and seven local or niche employers that fit. For each, one line on why it fits. Then suggest the columns for a simple sheet to track their careers pages weekly.

free.title: Step 3: Door 3, map the people you already know
free.body:
The third door is people. Many jobs are filled through someone who knew someone. You probably have more connections than you think.

Make a list of everyone you could reasonably message: former coworkers and managers, classmates, friends in your field, people from groups, clubs or events, past clients or vendors. Do not filter yet.

Now match them to your target list. On LinkedIn, search each target company and look at who works there, then check if you share any connections. Mark anyone who works at a target company, or used to, or knows someone who does.

Your first move is simple: reach out to three people you already know, tell them what you are looking for in one clear sentence, and ask a small, easy question.
free.prompt:
Write three short, friendly messages to people I already know, letting them know I am job searching. Each under 80 words.

1) To a former coworker I have not talked to in a while: [name, how we worked together].
2) To a friend who works at a company on my target list: [name, company].
3) To a past manager who could know people in my field: [name, context].

What I am looking for, in one sentence: [your one-line goal]. Each message should have a small, specific ask, like a name, a quick opinion, or a 15-minute chat. Not a request for a job. Warm and natural, not formal.

locked.title: Step 4: Open Door 3 with people you have not met yet
locked.body:
Your network does not stop at people you know. You can reach people at target companies directly, before a role is even posted. The key is to ask for a conversation, not a job.

Find them yourself: on LinkedIn, search the company and the team you want to join. Check the company team page, recent press releases, and talks or articles people from the team have published. Pick someone close to the work, like a team lead or a peer.

Script:

"Hi [Name], I have been following [Company]'s work on [specific thing], and I am exploring roles in [area]. I would love to hear how your team approaches [topic]. Would you be open to a 15-minute chat sometime in the next couple of weeks? Totally fine if not. [Your name]"

In the chat, ask about their work, their team's challenges, and what they look for in people. At the end, ask, "Is there anyone else you think I should talk to?"
locked.prompt:
I want to request a short conversation with [Name], [title] at [Company]. What I noticed about their work or team: [specific detail]. The area I am exploring: [area]. My background in one line: [line].

Write: 1) a LinkedIn connection note under 300 characters, 2) an email version under 100 words. Then give me eight thoughtful questions to ask during a 15-minute conversation, ending with a polite ask for anyone else I should talk to. Do not ask for a job in the messages.

locked.body:
Running three doors at once takes time. Scout can help on each one. It builds your Career ID and a career diagnosis, then finds matching jobs and applies for you, adding your Showcase link to each application. A Showcase is a personal web page built for one job or one company, with many designs to choose from.

For the people door, Scout finds people at a target company, like hiring managers and team leads, and reaches out with a short note and your Showcase in small paced waves, with you or someone you authorize approving the sends. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief when a company replies, and sends a weekly report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=the-3-doors-to-every-job&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, where should I be looking?

locked.title: Step 6: Split your week across all three doors
locked.body:
If boards are all you know, they will eat all your time. Give each door a slot. A balanced week might look like:

Door 1, boards: check alerts for a short, fixed time each weekday. Apply only to strong matches.
Door 2, career pages: one session a week to check your target list and apply directly to new roles.
Door 3, people: two sessions a week, one to message people you know, one to request conversations with people at target companies. Plus any calls you book.

As your search goes on, shift time toward whichever door is producing conversations. For many people, Door 3 needs more time than it feels like it should, because it builds slowly and then opens up.
locked.prompt:
Help me plan a weekly job search schedule using three doors: job boards, company career pages, and people. Time I have per week: [hours]. Days and times I am available: [details]. Current state: I have [number] companies on my target list and [number] people I could reach out to.

Build a weekly schedule with specific sessions for each door, what to do in each, and a small weekly goal per door that I control, like messages sent or pages checked. Do not set goals based on outcomes I cannot control.

locked.title: Step 7: Score your doors every two weeks
locked.body:
Track where every opportunity comes from. In your tracker, add a Door column (1, 2, or 3) for every application and conversation. Then, every two weeks, count for each door:

1. How many actions you took: applications, page checks, messages.
2. How many replies you got.
3. How many real conversations or interviews came from it.

Compare. Do not judge a door by one week, especially Door 3, which builds slowly. But after a few cycles, you will see which door gives you the most conversations for your time. Lean into it, and keep the others running at a lower level.

And when someone from Door 3 helps you, thank them and tell them how it turned out. People like knowing they helped.
locked.prompt:
Here is my job search tracker with a Door column (1 = job boards, 2 = career pages, 3 = people) for the last few weeks:

[paste tracker]

For each door, count actions taken, replies, and conversations or interviews. Show the reply rate per door from my own data. Tell me which door is giving me the best return on time so far, what might be holding back the weaker doors, and how to rebalance my next two weeks. Keep in mind that the people door can take longer to build.

guides.tip: Build part of your target list from companies that describe themselves as remote-first or distributed. Their careers pages often list roles open across many locations.

guides.intro:
Remote roles often draw applicants from many places at once, which makes it easy for a strong candidate to blend in. Being qualified matters, and so does being visible to the people deciding.

This guide helps you find where you disappear, reach the right person on a distributed team, and show your work in a way that's easy to review from anywhere.

free.title: Step 1: Separate the two problems
free.body:
Being qualified means you can do the job. Being seen means a person at the company knows you exist. Most job seekers work hard on the first and almost nothing on the second, then read silence as a verdict on their skills. It usually is not.

Take your last 20 applications and sort each into one bucket: 1) Never heard anything. 2) Got an automated rejection. 3) Talked to a human. If almost everything sits in bucket 1, your problem is visibility, not qualification. If you reach humans but stall there, the problem is later in the process and needs a different fix.

Write one sentence at the top of a note: 'My main problem right now is ____.' Naming it correctly stops you from rewriting a resume that was never read.
free.prompt:
I'm job hunting and want an honest diagnosis. Here are my last [number] applications with what happened to each:

[paste a simple list: company, role, date applied, how I applied (job board, company site, referral), result (silence, rejection, call, interview)]

My target role is [role] and my background is [2-3 sentence summary].

Sort these into: never heard back, automated rejection, spoke to a human. Then tell me plainly whether my main problem looks like visibility (no human sees me), screening (I'm filtered out), or conversion (I talk to people but stall). Give me the 3 most likely causes based only on this data, and one concrete thing to change this week for each. Don't guess beyond the data. If you need more info, ask me.

free.title: Step 2: Find the 4 places you go invisible
free.body:
Qualified people usually disappear in one of four places.

1) The pile: you apply through a big job board where the role already has a long list of applicants, and nothing makes you stand out in the first few seconds. 2) The keyword gap: your resume describes your work in your old company's language, not the language in the posting. 3) The no-human route: every application goes into a system and none goes to a person. 4) The quiet profile: someone does look you up, and your LinkedIn headline says 'Seeking new opportunities' with nothing about what you do.

Check yourself against each one. For the pile, apply in the first few days a role is posted when you can, and favor company career pages. For the keyword gap, mirror the posting's exact phrases where they are true for you. For the no-human route, see Step 3. For the quiet profile, rewrite your headline as 'Role who does X for Y.'
free.prompt:
Act as a blunt recruiter doing a 6-second scan. Here is a job posting:

[paste posting]

Here is my resume:

[paste resume]

Here is my LinkedIn headline and About section:

[paste]

1) List the 8 most important words or phrases in the posting. Mark which ones appear in my resume, which are missing, and which I describe in different words.
2) Tell me what you'd conclude about me in the first 6 seconds of reading the resume.
3) Rewrite my LinkedIn headline 3 ways in the format 'Role who does X for Y', using only things true in my resume.
4) Point out anything that would make you skip me. Be direct.

free.title: Step 3: Put one human in front of every application
free.body:
The fastest visibility fix is simple: for every role you really want, find one person connected to it and send a short, specific note. That person is usually the hiring manager, the team lead, or someone on the team.

How to find them yourself: search LinkedIn for the company name plus the team (for example 'Netflix marketing'), check the company's team or leadership page, and look at who posted the job or shared it. Pick the person closest to the role, not the CEO.

Use this message, under 60 words: 'Hi [Name], I just applied for the [Role] on your team. I've spent [X years] doing [the core thing the role needs], most recently [one specific result or project]. If it's useful, I'd be glad to share how I'd approach [one priority from the posting]. Either way, thanks for reading.' Send it as a LinkedIn connection note or message. One note per role. No attachments, no long story.
free.prompt:
Help me write a short note to a person at a company where I just applied.

Role: [role title]
Company: [company]
Person: [name and their title]
What the posting says matters most: [paste 3-5 lines from the posting]
My most relevant experience: [2-3 bullets with specifics]

Write 3 versions, each under 60 words: one that leads with a result, one that leads with a question about their priorities, one that leads with why this company. No flattery, no 'I hope this finds you well', no asking for a job directly. End with a low-pressure line. Then tell me which version you'd send and why.

locked.title: Step 4: Run a 'seen this week' plan instead of an 'applied this week' plan
locked.body:
Counting applications rewards volume. Counting moments where a real person saw your name rewards visibility. Switch your weekly goal.

Each week, aim for these: pick 5 roles you actually want, not 50 you could do. For each, apply on the company site, send one note to a person (Step 3), and engage once with something that person or team posted, a thoughtful comment, not 'Great post!'. Add one visibility move for yourself: a short LinkedIn post about a problem you solved, or an updated Featured section.

Track it in four columns: Role, Person contacted, Date, Reply or view. On Friday, look at which roles produced any human signal and ask why. Was it the note, the timing, the fit? Do more of that next week. This turns a guessing game into a loop you can improve.
locked.prompt:
Build me a weekly job search plan focused on being seen, not on volume.

My target role: [role]
Target industries or companies: [list]
Hours I can give per week: [number]
Where I am now: [e.g. 'applying a lot, almost no replies']

Give me: 1) a day-by-day plan for one week with specific tasks and time per task, 2) a simple tracking table I can copy into a spreadsheet, 3) 5 ideas for short LinkedIn posts I could write from my own experience in [field], each with a first line that would make someone keep reading. Keep it realistic for my hours.

locked.title: Step 5: Give people something to see when they look
locked.body:
When your note works, the person clicks your name. What they find decides what happens next. A generic resume PDF and a blank profile are where many good candidates lose the moment.

Build one page of proof for each target role. It can be a simple doc or a free one-page site. Include: a one-line summary written for that role, 3 short results with numbers you can honestly stand behind, one short case story (problem, what you did, what changed), and a line on what you'd focus on first in this role. Keep it to what someone can read in under two minutes.

Then point to it. Add it to your LinkedIn Featured section and mention it in your note: 'I put together a short page on how I'd approach [priority].' That one line gives a busy person a reason to look.
locked.prompt:
Help me build a one-page proof page for a specific role.

Role and company: [role at company]
Posting highlights: [paste key lines]
My experience: [paste resume or key bullets]

Write: 1) a one-line summary of me written for this exact role, 2) three result statements in the format 'Did X, which led to Y', using only facts from my experience (flag any place where I need to add a real number), 3) one short case story under 120 words: the problem, what I did, what changed, 4) a 'What I'd focus on first' section with 3 bullets tied to the posting. Plain language, no buzzwords.

locked.body:
Everything above works by hand. It also takes hours each week. If you'd rather have it done for you, Scout runs the same visibility playbook.

Scout builds your Career ID and gives you a career diagnosis, so you know whether you have a visibility, screening or conversion problem. It builds Showcases, a personal web page made for one job or one company. It finds matching jobs and applies for you, adding your Showcase link. It finds people at your target companies, like hiring managers and team leads, and reaches out with a short note and your Showcase in small paced waves, with you approving the sends. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief when a company replies, and sends you a weekly report.

locked.title: Step 7: Review in two weeks and choose your next move
locked.body:
After two weeks of seen-first work, look at your tracker and answer three questions. Did more humans respond than before? Which kind of note or role got a reply? Where did things stop?

If you're now getting replies and calls, your visibility problem is shrinking. Move your effort to interview prep and telling your story well. If you're getting views but no replies, your note or your proof page needs work, so test a different opening line. If you're still getting nothing, narrow your target: fewer roles, closer to your actual experience, with a person contacted for each.

Write down one change for the next two weeks and stick to it. Changing everything at once makes it impossible to see what worked.

[paste table: role, company, person contacted, note version used, result]

guides.intro:
Remote teams often review candidates without ever meeting them in person early on. That makes a clear, easy-to-open page especially useful: it shows how you think and communicate in writing.

This guide walks you through the six sections, a free way to publish, and how to tailor it so a distributed team can see you're a fit.

free.title: Step 1: Understand what a Showcase is (and isn't)
free.body:
A Showcase is a short personal web page built for a specific job or company. A resume lists everything you've done. A Showcase answers one question for one reader: 'Why this person, for this role, right now?'

The difference matters. A resume gets scanned against a checklist. A Showcase gets read like a short pitch, with a headline, a few results, and a clear idea of what you'd do first. It's something a hiring manager can open in a browser in one click and finish in about two minutes.

What it is not: a portfolio of everything, a long life story, or a fancy design project. If it takes longer than two minutes to read, cut it. Your resume still exists for the formal application. The Showcase is what you send to a human.

free.title: Step 2: Fill in the 6-section blueprint
free.body:
Every Showcase needs six parts, in this order.

1) Headline: who you are for this role. Example: 'Operations manager who cuts fulfillment delays for growing e-commerce teams.' 2) Three results: short lines in the form 'Did X, which led to Y.' Example: 'Rebuilt the returns process, which cut handling time by [X].' Only use numbers you can defend. 3) One short story: a problem you faced, what you did, what changed. Under 120 words. 4) How I'd approach this role: three bullets tied to the posting. 5) How I work: two or three lines on your style, like 'I write things down and share updates before anyone asks.' 6) Next step: one line, like 'I'd welcome a short call to talk about [team priority].'

Draft each section in a plain doc first. Don't worry about design yet. Words first, looks later.
free.prompt:
Turn my resume into a Showcase: a short, one-page personal pitch for one job.

Target role: [role]
Company: [company]
Posting: [paste the job posting]
My resume: [paste resume]

Write these 6 sections:
1) Headline (one line: who I am for this role)
2) Three results in the format 'Did X, which led to Y'. Use only facts from my resume. Where a number would help but I didn't give one, write [add number] instead of inventing it.
3) One short story under 120 words: problem, what I did, what changed
4) 'How I'd approach this role': 3 bullets tied to the posting's priorities
5) 'How I work': 2-3 short lines
6) A one-line next step

Keep it readable in under 2 minutes. Plain words, no buzzwords, no 'passionate' or 'results-driven'.

free.title: Step 3: Publish it free in minutes
free.body:
You don't need a website builder account or a designer. Pick the simplest option you already have.

Option A: a shared document. Paste your six sections into a Google Doc or similar, add a clean title like 'Jordan Lee for [Company] Operations', set sharing to 'anyone with the link can view', and you have a link. Option B: a free page tool like Notion, which lets you publish a page to the web from its share menu. Option C: a free one-page site builder if you already use one.

Whatever you pick, check four things before sharing: it opens on a phone, it opens in a private browser window (so you know it isn't locked), your name and the role are at the top, and there are no typos. Then open it once more as if you were a busy manager reading between meetings.
free.prompt:
Proofread my Showcase like a busy hiring manager reading it on a phone between meetings.

[paste your Showcase text]

Tell me: 1) what you understood about me in the first 10 seconds, 2) any line that's vague, long, or sounds like a template, with a sharper rewrite, 3) any spelling or grammar issues, 4) whether the headline would make you keep reading, with 2 alternatives. Keep my facts unchanged.

locked.title: Step 4: Make a version for one specific company
locked.body:
A general Showcase is good. One made for a single company is better, because the reader sees their own world in it.

Spend 15 minutes on research: read the company's About page, recent press releases or news, and the team's job posts. Note three things: what they're trying to grow or fix, words they use often, and any recent change like a new product or a new market.

Then adjust three parts of your Showcase. Change the headline to name their world: 'Operations manager for fast-growing subscription brands.' Rewrite 'How I'd approach this role' so each bullet points at something you found. Add a short line near the top: 'Made for the [Company] [Team] team.' Keep your results and story the same unless a different one fits better. Save each version with the company name so you don't mix them up.
locked.prompt:
Help me tailor my Showcase to one company.

Company: [company]
Role: [role]
What I learned about them: [paste notes from their About page, recent news, and job posts]
My current Showcase: [paste]

1) Summarize in 3 bullets what this company seems to be focused on right now, based only on my notes.
2) Rewrite my headline 3 ways for this company.
3) Rewrite my 'How I'd approach this role' section so each bullet connects to something in my notes.
4) Suggest which of my results to move to the top for this reader, and why.
Don't invent facts about the company or me.

locked.title: Step 5: Put the link where people will see it
locked.body:
A Showcase nobody opens doesn't help. Place it in the spots where a person is already looking at you.

1) Your note to the hiring manager or team lead: one line, 'I made a short page for the [Team] role: [link].' 2) Your LinkedIn Featured section, with a clear title. 3) The application itself: many forms have a 'website' or 'portfolio' field, or room in a cover letter. 4) Your email signature while you're searching. 5) A follow-up after an interview: 'Here's the page I mentioned, with the plan I described.'

Never paste a long, messy link. If your tool lets you rename the page or shorten the address, do it. And only send it to people tied to the role. A Showcase works because it's personal, so it shouldn't feel like a mass mailing.
locked.prompt:
Write the short lines I'll use to share my Showcase in different places.

Role: [role] at [company]
What my Showcase focuses on: [one sentence]

Write: 1) a one-line mention for a LinkedIn note to the hiring manager, 2) a title and one-line description for my LinkedIn Featured section, 3) a sentence for a cover letter, 4) a post-interview follow-up email under 80 words that includes the Showcase, 5) an email signature line. Natural tone, no hype.

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, show me my Showcase

locked.title: Step 7: Keep your Showcase sharp with a monthly check
locked.body:
A Showcase is a living page. Once a month, or whenever you change your target role, run this quick check.

Is the headline still the role you want? Are your three results still your strongest? Did you finish a project, course or win you could add? Does every 'How I'd approach' bullet still match the kinds of postings you're seeing? Is there anything you'd be embarrassed to be asked about in an interview? If so, cut it or make sure you can talk about it.

Keep a simple log: which version you sent, to whom, and what happened. Over time you'll see which headline or story gets the best response, and you can make that your default.
locked.prompt:
Here's my current Showcase and the last few job postings I'm targeting.

Showcase: [paste]
Postings: [paste 2-3 postings]

Audit it: 1) Is my headline still a match for these postings? Suggest an update if not. 2) Which of my results is weakest for these roles? 3) What skills or themes appear in the postings that my Showcase doesn't mention but my experience might cover? Ask me about each one. 4) Give me a one-line summary of what to change this month.

guides.intro:
Remote roles can attract applicants from many places, and a vague resume is easy to pass over. A clear angle helps a busy reviewer place you quickly.

This guide shows you how to decode the posting, choose the right angle, and rewrite the top of your resume, with a note on how remote-specific strengths fit in.

free.title: Step 1: Read the posting for the problem behind it
free.body:
Every job posting exists because something needs doing. A team is growing, something is broken, a new product is launching, or someone left. Your angle should answer that problem, not the generic list of duties.

Read the posting three times. First, highlight anything repeated or listed first, which usually signals priority. Second, look for change words: 'new', 'build', 'scale', 'improve', 'launch', 'turnaround'. Third, read the 'About us' and any line about the team. Then finish this sentence: 'They are hiring because ____.'

Two postings with the same title can have different answers. One 'Marketing Manager' role is about growing a new channel. Another is about running a busy calendar of campaigns without dropping anything. Same title, different problem, different angle.
free.prompt:
Decode this job posting for me.

[paste posting]

1) In one sentence, why is this company most likely hiring for this role right now? Base it only on the text.
2) List the top 3 priorities, in order, with the exact phrases that point to each.
3) What would success look like in the first 6 months, based on the posting?
4) What kind of person would the hiring manager be most relieved to find: a builder, a fixer, a scaler, an operator, or something else? Explain using the text.
5) Which words should I mirror in my resume and outreach?

free.title: Step 2: Pick from the angle menu
free.body:
An angle is the one idea you want the reader to remember about you. Here are ten that cover most roles:

1) Growth: you make numbers go up. 2) Operator: you make things run smoothly and on time. 3) Fixer: you turn around what's broken. 4) Builder: you start things from zero. 5) Scaler: you take something working and make it bigger. 6) Cost saver: you do more with less. 7) Customer champion: you understand and keep customers. 8) Translator: you connect technical and non-technical people. 9) Specialist: deep skill in one area. 10) Steady hand: reliable through change.

Most people can honestly claim three or four of these. Match your best fit to the problem you found in Step 1. Write your angle as one line: 'I'm the [angle] who [does what] for [whom].' Example: 'I'm the operator who keeps multi-team launches on schedule.'
free.prompt:
Here's my resume:

[paste resume]

And here's the job I'm targeting:

[paste posting]

From this list of angles: growth, operator, fixer, builder, scaler, cost saver, customer champion, translator, specialist, steady hand.

1) Which 3 angles can I honestly claim based on my resume? For each, list the 2 strongest pieces of proof from my experience.
2) Which ONE angle best fits this job's main problem, and why?
3) Write my positioning line 3 ways in the format 'I'm the [angle] who [does what] for [whom].'
4) Tell me which angle would be a stretch for me and why I should avoid it here.

free.title: Step 3: Rewrite the top third of your resume for the angle
free.body:
Most readers decide in the top third of the page. That's the only part you need to change for each angle.

Change three things. 1) The headline under your name: swap a generic title for your angle line. 2) The summary: two or three sentences that lead with your angle and one result that proves it. 3) The order of bullets in your most recent role: move the bullets that prove this angle to the top.

Example with the same person. For a growth role: 'Marketing lead who grows new channels from zero. Built paid social into the team's second-largest source of signups.' For an ops role: 'Marketing lead who keeps a busy campaign calendar running on time. Ran 40+ launches a year across four teams with a shared process.' Same career, different first impression. Keep a master resume and save each version with the angle in the file name.
free.prompt:
Rewrite the top third of my resume for a specific angle.

My angle for this job: [angle line from Step 2]
The job: [paste posting or key lines]
My current resume: [paste]

1) Write a new headline under my name (one line).
2) Write a 2-3 sentence summary that leads with this angle and includes one result from my resume as proof.
3) Reorder the bullets in my most recent role so the ones that prove this angle come first. Lightly rewrite each to start with a strong verb and end with the result.
Don't add anything I didn't do. Mark any spot where a real number would help with [add number].

locked.title: Step 4: Build your proof inventory once, use it for every angle
locked.body:
Re-thinking your whole career for each application is tiring. Instead, build a proof inventory: a single list of every result and story you have, tagged by angle.

Make a table with four columns: What happened, Result (with a number if you can honestly give one), Angle tags, and Story ready (yes or no). Aim for 15 to 25 entries. Include small wins too: a process you cleaned up, a customer you saved, a new hire you trained.

Tag each one with every angle it supports. 'Rebuilt onboarding for new clients' might be operator, customer champion and fixer at once. When a new job comes in, filter by angle and pull your top three. Mark 'Story ready' only when you can tell it out loud in under a minute: the situation, what you did, what changed.
locked.prompt:
Help me build a proof inventory from my career.

Here's my resume: [paste]
Here are extra wins not on my resume: [list anything you remember: projects, saves, process fixes, people you trained]

Create a table with columns: What happened | Result | Angle tags (from: growth, operator, fixer, builder, scaler, cost saver, customer champion, translator, specialist, steady hand) | Story ready?

Then ask me 5 follow-up questions to uncover wins I might have forgotten, focusing on angles where I have the least proof. Don't invent results. Where a number is missing, write [ask me].

locked.title: Step 5: Position a career change or a mixed background
locked.body:
If your background doesn't line up neatly with the role, the angle matters even more. Don't hide the mix. Frame it.

Use a bridge angle: 'I bring [skill from old field] to [new field].' Examples: a teacher moving into training: 'Trainer who designs learning people actually finish.' A sales rep moving into customer success: 'Customer success lead who already knows how buyers think.' A military veteran moving into operations: 'Operations manager with experience running teams under pressure.'

Then pick results that transfer. Skip industry jargon from your old field and describe what you did in the new field's words. In your summary, name the move directly in one line so the reader doesn't have to guess: 'After eight years in classrooms, I now design training for adult learners.' Clear beats clever here.
locked.prompt:
I'm changing careers and need a bridge angle.

My past field and roles: [describe]
The field and role I'm targeting: [describe]
A posting I like: [paste]
My resume: [paste]

1) List the skills from my past that transfer most directly to this role, translated into the new field's language.
2) Write 3 bridge angle lines in the format 'I bring [X] to [Y].'
3) Write a 2-sentence summary that names the change plainly and leads with what transfers.
4) Pick 3 results from my resume that will read as relevant to this new field and rewrite them in its language.
5) Name the biggest question a hiring manager will have about my change, and give me a short honest answer to it.
