Running the angle work for every job takes time. Scout can do it for you.

Scout builds your Career ID from your resume and gives you a career diagnosis. From there it can suggest angles for a specific job and build a Showcase, a personal web page made for one job or one company, around the angle you choose, with many designs to pick from. Same career, different Showcase for each role. Scout can also find matching jobs and apply for you with your Showcase link, reach out to people at the company with a short note and your Showcase in small paced waves (you approve the sends), follow up, and send you a weekly report.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=positioning-101-pick-the-angle-that-gets-the-cal&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, give me 3 angles for this job

locked.title: Step 7: Keep an angle log and learn what works
locked.body:
Positioning gets better with feedback. Keep a simple angle log: Date, Company, Role, Angle used, Result (silence, reply, screen, interview).

After 10 to 15 applications, look for patterns. Does one angle get more replies? Does a certain kind of company respond to the operator angle but not the growth one? Are you choosing a stretch angle too often?

Also notice what interviewers ask about. If every first call asks about the same project, that's a clue to your strongest story. Move it higher in your resume and Showcase. If people keep asking about something you barely mention, that topic might deserve its own angle.
locked.prompt:
Here's my angle log so far:

[paste: date, company, role, angle used, result]

Analyze it: 1) Which angles got the best results, and for which kinds of companies or roles? 2) Where might I be using the wrong angle for the job? 3) Based on this, which angle should be my default, and when should I switch? 4) Suggest one test for my next 10 applications. Be clear when the data is too small to draw conclusions.

guides.tip: For remote roles, the operator and translator angles often pair well with proof of written communication. Mention a doc, process or update you created that others relied on.

guides.intro:
Remote teams often meet you through a screen first. A page that's easy to read on any device and clear in tone helps you come across well before the first call.

This guide covers four styles, simple design rules and a phone test, so your page works wherever it's opened.

free.title: Step 1: Match the design style to the role
free.body:
You don't need to design anything from scratch. You need to pick a style that feels right for the reader. Think of it like choosing what to wear to an interview.

Four styles cover most roles. 1) Classic: white background, dark text, one accent color, serif or simple fonts. Fits finance, law, healthcare, government, senior leadership. 2) Clean modern: lots of white space, a sans serif font, simple sections. Fits tech, product, operations, analytics. 3) Bold: strong color blocks, big headlines, visuals up front. Fits marketing, creative, media, consumer brands. 4) Warm: soft colors, a friendly photo, a more personal tone. Fits teaching, healthcare support, HR, customer roles, nonprofits.

Look at the target company's own website for a hint. A company with a quiet, formal site will likely feel at home with Classic. A colorful consumer brand may welcome Bold. When unsure, pick Clean modern. It rarely feels wrong.
free.prompt:
Help me choose a design style for my personal job page (a Showcase).

Target role: [role]
Company: [company]
How the company's own website looks: [describe: colors, tone, formal or playful, lots of images or mostly text]
My personality at work in 3 words: [words]

From these styles: Classic, Clean modern, Bold, Warm.
1) Which style fits best and why?
2) Suggest one accent color and one font pairing (heading and body) that would suit it, using common free fonts.
3) What should I avoid so the page doesn't feel off for this company?
4) Describe in 3 sentences what the top of the page should look like.

free.title: Step 2: Follow 7 rules that make any page look good
free.body:
Good design for a job page is mostly about restraint. Follow these seven rules and your page will look clean even if you've never designed anything.

1) One accent color, used only for headings, links or one button. 2) Two fonts at most, one for headings and one for body text. 3) Body text big enough to read on a phone without zooming. 4) Lots of space between sections. Crowded pages feel stressful. 5) Short lines and short paragraphs, three lines max on a phone. 6) Your name and the role at the very top, before anything else. 7) No more than one image per section.

Before you change anything, print or screenshot your page and squint at it. You should see clear blocks with space between them, not a wall of gray. If it looks like a wall, add space and cut words.
free.prompt:
Review my Showcase layout against these design rules: one accent color, max two fonts, readable on a phone, generous spacing, short paragraphs, name and role at the top, max one image per section.

Here's a description of my page, section by section: [describe each section: what's in it, colors, fonts, images, length]
Here's the text: [paste]

For each rule, tell me if I pass or fail and give a specific fix. Then suggest which 20% of the text I could cut without losing anything important.

free.title: Step 3: Borrow the company's feel, not its brand
free.body:
A small nod to the company's look can make your page feel made for them. Just don't copy their logo or make it look like an official company page. That can confuse people.

Do this instead. Look at the company's site and note its main color, whether it uses lots of photos or mostly text, and its tone of voice. Then pick an accent color in the same family, not the exact shade. Match the mood: if their site is spacious and calm, keep yours calm. Mirror a couple of words they use for their mission or customers in your headline.

Add a small, honest line near the top like 'Made for the [Company] [Team] team.' That tells the reader it's personal without pretending to be anything official. Keep your own name as the biggest text on the page.
free.prompt:
I'm making a personal job page for a role at [company]. I want it to feel made for them without copying their brand.

What their website looks like: [describe main colors, imagery, tone, key phrases they use]
My current page style: [describe]

1) Suggest an accent color in the same family as theirs but clearly different, described in plain words (I'll find the exact shade myself).
2) Suggest 2-3 of their own words or ideas I could naturally reflect in my headline or 'How I'd approach this role' section.
3) Write a short 'Made for the [Company] [Team] team' line in 3 styles.
4) List anything I should avoid so it doesn't look like an official company page.

locked.title: Step 4: Add visuals that prove, not decorate
locked.body:
Images should do a job. Every visual on your page should either help the reader trust you or help them understand your work faster.

Useful visuals: a clear, friendly headshot with a plain background (optional, but it makes the page feel human). A simple before and after, such as two short lines or a small chart you made yourself showing a process time or a metric going in the right direction. A screenshot of work you're allowed to share, with anything confidential removed. A short list of tools you use, as plain text or simple icons.

Skip: stock photos of handshakes, logos of past employers you don't have permission to use, busy backgrounds and anything that only looks nice. If you're not sure, ask: 'If I removed this, would the reader lose anything?' If not, remove it.
locked.prompt:
Help me pick visuals for my Showcase.

Role: [role]
My top 3 results: [paste]
Work I could show (screenshots, documents, projects): [list, noting what's confidential]

1) For each result, suggest one simple visual I could make myself (like a basic before and after or a short list), and describe exactly what it should show.
2) Tell me which of my possible screenshots would help and what to blur or remove first.
3) Give me headshot tips for a clean, friendly photo taken at home with a phone.
4) List visuals I should NOT include for this role.

locked.title: Step 5: Run the phone and readability test
locked.body:
Many hiring managers will open your link on a phone, often between other things. Test like they will.

Open your page on your phone and check: Does your name and role show without scrolling? Can you read every line without zooming? Do images load quickly and fit the screen? Are links easy to tap? Does any section feel too long when you scroll through it?

Then test readability. Is the contrast strong, with dark text on a light background or the reverse, not gray on gray? Do your images have a short description in case they don't load? Is your most important result readable in the first screen? Finally, send the link to one friend and ask: 'In 30 seconds, what do I do and what job is this for?' If they can't answer, simplify the top of the page.
locked.prompt:
I'm going to describe what I see when I open my Showcase on my phone. Act as a usability reviewer.

First screen shows: [describe]
Scrolling down, I see: [describe each section and how long it feels]
Anything hard to read or tap: [describe]

1) List the top 3 problems a busy hiring manager would hit on a phone.
2) Suggest exactly what should appear on the first screen.
3) Give me a short checklist I can reuse before sending any version of my page.

locked.title: Step 6: Let Scout try designs for you
locked.body:
If you'd rather see options than build them, Scout does this part for you.

Scout builds Showcases, personal web pages made for one job or one company, with many designs to choose from. If one doesn't feel like you, ask for a different design and compare. It starts from your Career ID, so the content stays yours while the look changes. Scout can also find matching jobs and apply for you with your Showcase link, reach out to people at your target companies with a short note and your Showcase in small paced waves with you approving the sends, and alert you when someone views your Showcase.

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, try a different design

locked.title: Step 7: Get feedback from three people and pick a winner
locked.body:
You're too close to your own page to judge it well. Get three quick outside opinions.

Pick three people: one who works in your target field, one who doesn't, and one who'll be blunt. Send them two versions of your page, for example Classic and Clean modern. Ask the same three questions: 'Which one would you keep reading?', 'What do you remember about me after 30 seconds?', and 'Anything that felt off?'

Keep the design that wins two of three votes, then fix anything all three mentioned. Save your winning design as your default and only change it when you move into a very different kind of role or company. A consistent look you're confident in is better than a new style every week.
locked.prompt:
Write a short, friendly message I can send to 3 people asking for quick feedback on two versions of my personal job page.

Who they are: [e.g. a friend in my field, a family member, a former manager]
What I need: which version they'd keep reading, what they remember after 30 seconds, anything that feels off.

Keep it under 70 words, easy to answer from a phone, and make it clear 2 minutes is enough. Then give me a simple table to record their answers and decide on a winner.

guides.tip: Keep contrast strong and text large enough to read without zooming. Your reader might be on a laptop, a phone or a small tablet.

guides.title: Find your story: 5 questions that turn your resume into a pitch
guides.blurb: A calm guide to finding your story and telling it clearly on video calls and in writing.
inside: 5 questions that pull your real story out of your resume
A simple story structure that works in writing and out loud
Your 30-second and 2-minute versions, ready to use
Word swaps that stop you from underselling yourself
A story bank mapped to common interview questions
guides.intro:
In remote hiring, much of your first impression happens in writing and on short video calls. A clear, simple story helps you come across well in both.

This guide walks you through five questions, a story structure that works in text and out loud, and a practice routine you can do from home.

free.title: Step 1: Answer the 5 story questions
free.body:
Most people can't describe their work well because they've never been asked the right questions. Set a timer for 20 minutes and answer these in writing. Don't edit. Just get it down.

1) What do people come to you for, even when it's not your job? 2) What's a problem you fixed that others had given up on, or didn't notice? 3) What part of your work do you lose track of time doing? 4) What would fall apart, or get worse, if you left tomorrow? 5) What's the result you're proudest of, and what did you personally do to make it happen?

The answers to questions 1 and 4 often reveal your real value better than your job title. Question 5 is your first story. Write at least three sentences for each. If you get stuck, think of a specific week or project instead of your job in general.
free.prompt:
Interview me to find my career story. Ask me these 5 questions one at a time, and after each answer, ask one follow-up question to get a more specific example:

1) What do people come to you for, even when it's not your job?
2) What's a problem you fixed that others had given up on or didn't notice?
3) What part of your work do you lose track of time doing?
4) What would fall apart or get worse if you left tomorrow?
5) What's the result you're proudest of, and what did you personally do?

For context, here's my resume: [paste resume]

After all 5, summarize in 3 bullets the themes you see in my answers that my resume doesn't show clearly.

free.title: Step 2: Shape it with a simple story structure
free.body:
A story isn't your whole history. It's one thread that explains who you are at work. Use this four-part shape: 1) Where things were: the problem or situation. 2) What you noticed: the thing others missed or the reason you stepped in. 3) What you did: specific actions, using 'I', not 'we'. 4) What changed: the result, and what it meant for the team or customer.

Example: 'Our support team was buried in repeat tickets. I noticed most of them were the same five questions. I wrote clear help articles for each one and added links to our replies. Repeat tickets dropped and the team had time for harder cases.'

Then pull out your through-line, the pattern across your best stories. It sounds like: 'I'm the person who spots the repeat problem and builds the fix.' That one line becomes the spine of your resume summary, your LinkedIn About and your interview answers.
free.prompt:
Here are my answers to 5 career story questions:

[paste your answers from Step 1]

1) Pick my 2 strongest stories and rewrite each in this shape: where things were, what I noticed, what I did (using 'I'), what changed. Keep each under 90 words. Use only what I wrote. Mark any spot where a specific detail or number would help with [add detail].
2) Find the through-line across my answers and write it 3 ways in the format 'I'm the person who...'
3) Tell me which version sounds most like a real person and least like a template.

free.title: Step 3: Build your 30-second and 2-minute versions
free.body:
You need your story in two lengths. The 30-second version is for 'Tell me about yourself,' networking chats and the top of your LinkedIn. The 2-minute version is for interviews and longer calls.

30 seconds: your through-line, one proof point, what you want next. Example: 'I'm an operations lead who spots the repeat problem and builds the fix. Most recently I cut our support backlog by turning our top questions into self-serve help. Now I'm looking for a team that's growing fast and needs that kind of structure.'

2 minutes: the same opening, then one full story using the four-part shape, then a line on why this role. Say both out loud three times. Record yourself on your phone once. You'll hear where it drags or sounds memorized. Aim for natural, not perfect.
free.prompt:
Write my 'Tell me about yourself' answer in two lengths.

My through-line: [your 'I'm the person who...' line]
My strongest story: [paste the shaped story]
The kind of role I want next: [describe]
A specific job I'm targeting (optional): [paste key lines]

1) A 30-second version (about 75 words): through-line, one proof point, what I want next.
2) A 2-minute version (about 280 words): opening, one full story, why this role.
Write it the way a person talks: short sentences, no jargon, no 'I'm passionate about'. Then point out the one sentence most likely to sound rehearsed and give a more natural version.

locked.title: Step 4: Stop underselling with word swaps
locked.body:
People undersell themselves in predictable ways. Fix these and your story gets stronger without exaggerating anything.

1) 'We' when you mean 'I': if you led it, say 'I led'. Credit the team separately. 2) 'Helped with' or 'assisted': say what you actually did, like 'built', 'wrote', 'ran', 'negotiated'. 3) 'Responsible for': that's a duty, not a result. Say what happened because of you. 4) Missing scale: add size where it's true, like how many customers, people, locations or dollars. 5) 'Just': 'I just set up a spreadsheet' becomes 'I set up the tracker the team used to run every launch.' 6) Leaving out the before: a result only means something next to where things started.

Read your resume and LinkedIn with a highlighter and mark every 'helped', 'assisted', 'responsible for', 'just' and 'we'. Rewrite each one honestly.
locked.prompt:
Find where I'm underselling myself.

Here's my resume and LinkedIn About section:
[paste]

1) List every instance of: 'helped', 'assisted', 'supported', 'responsible for', 'just', 'involved in', and 'we' where it may hide my own role.
2) For each one, ask me a short question to find out what I actually did, then wait for my answers.
3) After I answer, rewrite each line with a strong, honest verb and a result.
Don't make anything sound bigger than what I tell you.

locked.title: Step 5: Build a story bank for interviews
locked.body:
Most interview questions are asking for one of a handful of stories. Prepare six and you can answer almost anything.

Build these six: 1) A win you're proud of. 2) A time you fixed something broken. 3) A conflict or disagreement you handled well. 4) A mistake and what you learned. 5) A time you led without being the boss. 6) A time you learned something fast.

Write each one in the four-part shape from Step 2, under 90 words. Then map them to common questions: 'Tell me about a challenge' uses story 2. 'Tell me about a time you failed' uses story 4. 'How do you handle disagreement' uses story 3. One story can cover several questions. Keep the bank in one doc and reread it before every interview.
locked.prompt:
Help me build an interview story bank.

Here's my resume: [paste]
Stories I already have: [paste any you shaped]

I need 6 stories: a proud win, fixing something broken, handling a conflict, a mistake and lesson, leading without authority, learning fast.

1) Tell me which of these I already have material for, based on my resume and stories.
2) For the missing ones, ask me 2 specific questions each to help me remember a real example.
3) Once I answer, write each story in this shape: where things were, what I noticed, what I did, what changed. Under 90 words each.
4) Map each story to 3 common interview questions it can answer.

locked.title: Step 6: Let Scout find your story with you
locked.body:
If digging through your own career feels hard, Scout can do the heavy lifting.

Scout builds your Career ID from your resume and gives you a career diagnosis, so you can see your strengths, your story and where your search is getting stuck. That story then flows into your Showcases, personal web pages made for one job or one company. Scout can also find matching jobs and apply for you with your Showcase link, reach out to people at your target companies with a short note in small paced waves that you approve, and give you a prep brief on a company when it replies, so your story fits the room.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=find-your-story-the-5-questions-scout-asks&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, what's my story?

locked.title: Step 7: Test your story and tune it
locked.body:
A story gets better each time you tell it to a real person. Over the next two weeks, use your 30-second version at least five times: in a networking message, on a call, at the top of your LinkedIn, in an interview.

After each one, jot down three things: what made them lean in, what question they asked next, and where you felt yourself rambling. The follow-up question is gold. It shows what was interesting or unclear.

If people keep asking about the same detail, move it earlier. If no one reacts to a line, cut it. Update your resume summary and LinkedIn About to match the version that's working. Your story should sound the same everywhere, so the person who reads your page and the person who meets you hear the same through-line.
locked.prompt:
I've told my career story to a few people. Here's what happened:

[for each: who it was, which version I used, what they asked next, where I felt I rambled]

My current 30-second version: [paste]

1) What patterns do you see in what people respond to?
2) Rewrite my 30-second version based on this feedback.
3) Suggest one line to update in my LinkedIn About so it matches.
Keep it in my voice.

guides.tip: Practice your intro on a video call with a friend. Look at the camera, not the screen, and keep it to 30 seconds.

guides.title: How to write a 2-line note that makes your link worth opening
guides.blurb: A calm guide to writing short, trustworthy notes to remote hiring teams.
inside: Why links from strangers get ignored, and the 5 signals that earn a click
The 2-line formula plus 6 fill-in templates
Subject lines and how to present a link so it feels safe
A 10-minute research routine for the personal hook
A polite follow-up schedule with ready-to-send messages
guides.intro:
On remote teams, a lot of hiring happens in writing, often across time zones. A short, clear note is easy to read whenever the person gets to it, and a page made for their team gives them something to review on their own schedule.

This guide covers the 2-line formula, the right channel and a gentle follow-up schedule.

free.title: Step 1: Know why links get ignored, and what earns a click
free.body:
People are taught to be careful with links from strangers, and they should be. A busy manager deciding whether to click is asking: 'Is this safe, is this real, and is it about me?'

Five signals help. 1) Their name and their company, spelled right. 2) A specific reason you're writing, tied to their team or a role. 3) A clear description of what the link is: 'a one-page summary of how I'd approach your onboarding project,' not 'check this out.' 4) A clean, readable link, not a long string of random characters. 5) A real person behind it: your full name and a profile they can check.

What hurts: generic greetings, vague teasers, all-caps, multiple links, attachments from strangers, and anything that sounds like a sales pitch. If your note would make sense sent to anyone, it will feel like it was sent to everyone.
free.prompt:
Review this outreach note as a cautious hiring manager who gets a lot of messages from strangers.

[paste your draft note]

Score it 1 to 5 on each: feels safe to click, clearly personal, clear about what the link is, short enough to read in 10 seconds, sounds like a real person. For anything below 4, tell me exactly what to change. Then rewrite it in 2 sentences that keep my facts.

free.title: Step 2: Use the 2-line formula
free.body:
Line 1 says why them. Line 2 says what the link is and why it's worth a look. That's it.

Formula: '[Name], [specific reason I'm writing to you]. I put together [what the link is] for [their team or goal]: [link].'

Six templates to adapt. 1) Role: 'Hi Maya, I applied for the Customer Success Lead role on your team. I made a one-page summary of how I'd approach your first 90 days: [link].' 2) Company news: 'Hi Sam, saw [Company] is expanding into Canada. I built a short page on how I ran a similar launch: [link].' 3) Their post: 'Hi Priya, your post on reducing churn stuck with me. Here's a short page with what worked for me on that exact problem: [link].' 4) Shared ground: 'Hi Leo, fellow [school or past company] alum here. I made a page for the analyst role on your team: [link].' 5) Team growth: 'Hi Ana, looks like your team is hiring across ops. Here's a quick page on the systems I've built for teams at this stage: [link].' 6) Referral: 'Hi Ben, [Name] suggested I reach out. Here's a one-page overview made for your team: [link].' Only use a template when the reason is true.
free.prompt:
Write a 2-line outreach note to send with my personal job page.

Person: [name, title]
Company: [company]
Why I'm writing to them specifically: [role I applied for, a post of theirs, company news, shared background, or a referral]
What my page shows: [one sentence]

Write 4 versions. Each must be 2 sentences: line 1 is why them, line 2 says what the link is and why it's relevant to their team, ending with [link]. Under 45 words each. No flattery, no 'I hope you're well', no asking for a job. Then tell me which one feels most natural and least like a template.

free.title: Step 3: Pick the channel, subject line and link format
free.body:
Where you send matters. A LinkedIn connection note has a short character limit, so the 2-line note fits well. A LinkedIn message after connecting gives a little more room. Email works if you found a public work address on their company site or in a press release, and gives you a subject line.

Subject lines that feel personal, not salesy: '[Role] on your team', 'For the [Team] team at [Company]', '[Mutual name] suggested I reach out', 'Re: your post on [topic]'. Skip anything like 'Opportunity!' or 'Quick question' with no context.

Present the link cleanly. If your page tool lets you set a readable address with your name in it, use it. Put the link on its own at the end of line 2 so it's easy to see and tap. One link only. Before sending, click it yourself from a private browser window and from your phone to be sure it opens without a login.
free.prompt:
Help me adapt my 2-line note for different channels.

My note: [paste]
Person and company: [name, title, company]

1) A LinkedIn connection note version that fits in about 200 characters.
2) A LinkedIn message version (after we connect), up to 3 sentences.
3) An email version with 5 subject line options that sound personal, not salesy.
Keep the same core message in each and only one link.

locked.title: Step 4: Find the personal hook in 10 minutes
locked.body:
Line 1 only works if it's real and specific. Here's a 10-minute routine to find a hook for any person.

Minutes 1 to 3: their LinkedIn. Look at their recent posts, comments, headline and how long they've been in the role. A new leader may be building a team. Minutes 4 to 6: the company. Check the newsroom or press page, the careers page for how many similar roles are open, and any recent product or market news. Minutes 7 to 9: the team. Look at who else is on the team and what they post about. Minute 10: pick one hook and write it down.

Good hooks, best to okay: they posted about a problem you've solved, a referral from someone they know, company news tied to the role, shared background, the role itself. Never mention personal details about their life outside work. Stick to what they've shared professionally.
locked.prompt:
Help me find a personal hook for outreach. Here's what I found in 10 minutes of research:

Person: [name, title, time in role]
Their recent posts or comments: [summarize]
Company news: [summarize]
Open roles on the team: [list]
Anything we have in common professionally: [list]
My relevant experience: [2-3 bullets]

1) Rank the possible hooks from strongest to weakest and explain why.
2) Write line 1 of my note using the strongest hook, 3 ways.
3) Flag anything I should NOT mention because it could feel too personal or off-topic.

locked.title: Step 5: Follow up politely with a set schedule
locked.body:
Busy people miss messages. A short, polite follow-up is normal and often welcome. A pile of them is not. Use a simple schedule and then stop.

Day 0: send your 2-line note. Day 5 to 7: follow-up 1, adding one new useful thing. 'Hi Maya, one more thought: I added a short section on how I'd handle your support backlog. Same page: [link].' Day 12 to 14: follow-up 2, short and gracious. 'Hi Maya, I know your inbox is full. If the timing's not right, no problem at all. I'm still interested in the role and happy to talk whenever it's useful.' Then stop with that person. If there's another relevant person on the team, you can reach out to them separately.

Track every send: name, company, date, which note, follow-ups sent, reply. Never send the same note twice to the same person.
locked.prompt:
Write my follow-up messages for a hiring manager who hasn't replied.

My original note: [paste]
Person: [name, title, company]
Something new I could add: [a new section on my page, a relevant result, a thought on recent company news]

1) Follow-up 1 (for day 5 to 7): under 40 words, adds one new useful thing.
2) Follow-up 2 (for day 12 to 14): under 40 words, gracious, makes it easy to say not now.
No guilt, no 'just checking in', no 'bumping this'. Then give me a simple tracking table with columns I should use.

locked.title: Step 6: Have Scout write the note and handle the sends
locked.body:
Writing a personal note, finding the right person and following up for every company takes real time. Scout can take this on.

Scout builds a Showcase made for one job or one company, finds people at that company such as hiring managers and team leads, and writes a short note to go with your Showcase. It reaches out in small paced waves, and nothing goes out until you, or someone you authorize, approve the sends. Scout follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief on the company if they reply, and sends you a weekly report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=how-to-write-a-2-line-note-that-gets-opened&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, write the note that goes with my Showcase

locked.title: Step 7: Review your notes and sharpen what works
locked.body:
After you've sent 15 to 20 notes, look at your tracker. You're not looking for a magic formula. You're looking for what fits you and your field.

Compare: which hooks got replies, and which got silence? Did LinkedIn or email work better for your target companies? Did the first note or a follow-up get the reply? Were replies more likely when the person was close to the role, like a team lead, versus far from it, like an executive?

Pick one thing to change for your next batch, such as a different hook type or writing to team leads first, and keep everything else the same. When someone does reply, answer within a day, thank them, and suggest one or two specific times for a short call by email. Then prepare: reread the company's recent news and your own Showcase before you talk.
locked.prompt:
Here's my outreach tracker:

[paste: person title, company, channel, hook type, note version, follow-ups sent, result]

1) What patterns do you see in which notes got replies?
2) Which hook type, channel and kind of person seems to work best for me so far? Say clearly if the sample is too small to tell.
3) Recommend one change to test in my next 15 notes.
4) Write a short reply I can send when someone responds, offering 2 specific times for a 15-minute call: [my available times].

guides.tip: For remote teams, leave a few extra days before following up. People in other time zones may simply not have reached your message yet.

guides.intro:
Remote roles draw applicants from everywhere, so it's easy to feel invisible. Without any signal back, you can't tell if your work was ever opened.

This guide shows you a calm, simple way to track views and follow up at the right time, in writing, the way remote teams prefer to communicate.

free.title: Step 1: Set yourself up to actually see a signal
free.body:
You can't act on a view you never hear about. Before you send anything, make your work trackable. Put your portfolio, one-page case study or personal page behind a link that counts clicks. Many free link tools show you how many times a link was opened and roughly when. Make a separate link for each company, so a click tells you which application or message it came from.

Then add that company-specific link to the places people actually look: the top of your resume, the first line of your application answers, your email signature and your outreach note. One link per company. Name each one so you know where it went, for example 'acme-ops-manager'.

Last, write down the date you sent each link. A view is only useful if you know what it's responding to.
free.prompt: I am applying to [number] companies this week. For each one I want a short, clean label for a trackable link to my work. Here is the list: [Company, role, where I'm sending it: application, email or LinkedIn]. For each row, give me: 1) a short link label using the company and role, 2) the best single place to put the link so a hiring manager sees it in the first 5 seconds, 3) one line of text to sit next to the link that tells them why to click, written for that specific role. Keep it plain, no hype.

free.title: Step 2: Read the view correctly before you react
free.body:
A view is a door opening a crack, not a yes. It can mean one of a few things: a recruiter is screening a stack, a hiring manager got your application forwarded, a teammate is checking you out before a call, or someone clicked by accident. Several views from the same company over a day or two may mean your link is being passed around. That's the moment that matters most.

Use this quick read. These are educated guesses, not facts. One view, soon after you sent it: probably screening. Act in 1 to 2 business days. A view several days later: something may have moved internally, maybe a shortlist. Act the same or next day. Repeat views: you may be being discussed. Act today, briefly. No view after a week: the link wasn't seen. Change the channel, not the volume.

The rule: never mention that you saw them look. You simply show up at the right moment with something useful.

free.title: Step 3: Send the right follow-up for the moment
free.body:
Here are three short follow-ups. Pick the one that matches what you saw. Keep each under 90 words.

After a first view (screening): 'Hi [Name], I applied for the [Role] role last week and wanted to add one thing that didn't fit in the form: [one specific result or idea tied to their team]. Happy to walk through it in 15 minutes if useful.'

After repeat views (being discussed): 'Hi [Name], quick note in case it helps your decision on the [Role] role. I put together a short plan for my first 30 days on [their stated priority]. Want me to send it over?'

After a late view (shortlist): 'Hi [Name], still very interested in [Role]. Since applying, I [did something relevant: finished a project, learned a tool, read their latest announcement]. Glad to answer anything before next steps.'

Each one adds new value. None of them says 'just checking in.'
free.prompt: I think someone at [Company] just looked at my application for [Role]. Here is the job post: [paste]. Here is what I sent: [paste resume summary or cover note]. Write me three follow-up messages under 90 words each: 1) one for a first view during screening, 2) one for repeat views where I'm likely being discussed, 3) one for a late view after a week or more. Each must add one new, specific piece of value tied to the job post. Never mention that I know they viewed anything. No 'just checking in' or 'circling back'. Plain and friendly.

locked.title: Step 4: Tune the page so a view turns into a reply
locked.body:
A view only helps if what they land on makes them want to talk. Open your page or portfolio and look at it for 10 seconds, the way a busy hiring manager would. Can they tell what role you want, what you've done that matters to them, and how to reach you? If not, fix the top first.

The top of the page should hold: a one-line headline for their role, two or three results that match the job post, and one clear next step ('Reply to set up 15 minutes'). Put long case studies lower down. Cut anything that's about a different kind of job.

If you track views and get clicks but no replies over a couple of weeks, that's a page problem, not a reach problem. Change the headline and the first result, then send to the next few companies and compare.
locked.prompt: Act as a hiring manager for [Role] at a company like [Company]. Here is the text of my portfolio or personal page: [paste]. Give me: 1) what you understood in the first 10 seconds, 2) the three things that would make you reply, 3) the three things that would make you close the tab, 4) a rewritten top section: a one-line headline, three result bullets that match this job post [paste], and one clear next step. Be blunt and specific.

locked.title: Step 5: Let Scout watch for views and handle the follow-up
locked.body:
If you'd rather not build trackable links and watch them yourself, Scout does this part for you. It builds a Showcase, a personal web page made for one job or one company, with many designs to pick from. It adds your Showcase link to the applications it sends and to the short notes it writes to people at your target companies. You approve the sends.

When someone views your Showcase, Scout alerts you, so you know the moment a company is looking. It follows up for you, and if a company replies, it gives you a prep brief so you walk in knowing what they do and what they care about. Each week you get a report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=what-to-do-when-someone-views-your-showcase&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, who's looked at my Showcases?

locked.title: Step 6: Turn a hot company into a real conversation
locked.body:
When a company shows repeat interest and your follow-up gets no answer, widen the circle, gently. Find one more person tied to the role: the likely hiring manager, a team lead, or someone who'd be your peer. Look at the company's LinkedIn page under People, the team or about page on their website, and recent posts or press releases that name who runs the team.

Send that person a different, shorter note. Don't forward your application. Ask one smart question about the work, and offer your page as context. For example: 'Hi [Name], I applied for [Role] on your team. I'm curious how you're thinking about [specific challenge from the job post]. Here's a short page on how I've handled it before, if useful.'

One extra person per company is plenty. The goal is a conversation, not coverage.
locked.prompt: I've seen repeat interest from [Company] for [Role] but no reply to my follow-up. Here is the job post: [paste]. Help me: 1) list the 3 roles or titles most likely to be the hiring manager or team lead for this job, 2) tell me where on LinkedIn or their website I'd most likely find them, 3) write a 60-word note to that person that asks one specific question about the work and offers my page as context, without forwarding my application or sounding pushy.

locked.title: Step 7: Keep a simple view log and review it weekly
locked.body:
Make a small sheet with these columns: Company, Role, Link label, Date sent, Date of first view, Number of views, Follow-up sent (date and which script), Reply (yes or no), Next move.

Once a week, spend 10 minutes on it. Sort by number of views. The companies at the top are warming up, so they get your best effort: a tailored follow-up, a second person, a sharper page. Companies with zero views after a week need a new channel, such as a direct note to a team lead instead of another application. Companies that viewed and went quiet for two weeks get one last value-add note, then you move on.

Over a few weeks, the log shows you patterns: which headlines get clicks, which roles respond, which follow-ups get answers. Do more of what works.
locked.prompt: Here is my job search view log: [paste rows: company, role, date sent, first view date, number of views, follow-up sent, reply]. Sort these into four groups: 1) warming up, act today, 2) viewed but quiet, send one final value-add note, 3) never viewed, switch channel, 4) closed, move on. For each company give me the single next action and the day to do it. Then tell me any pattern you see in which roles or companies are engaging.

guides.tip: Remote hiring teams are often spread across time zones. If you see a view late in your day, send your follow-up the next morning in their time zone, not yours.

guides.intro:
Remote roles often get applications from many places at once, and reviewers move quickly. A long cover letter is easy to pass over.

This guide shows you how to replace it with a calm, clear note and a page that proves you can do the work and communicate well in writing, which remote teams care about.

free.title: Step 1: Build a one-page proof page
free.body:
A cover letter tells. A proof page shows. Make one simple page that a hiring manager can scan in under a minute. You can use any free website builder, a public document, or a portfolio tool. The format matters less than the structure.

Use this structure, top to bottom. 1) Headline: the role you want and who you help, in one line. 2) Three results: each one a short sentence with what you did and what changed. 3) One mini case study: the problem, what you did, the result, in about 100 words. 4) How you'd approach their work: three bullets. 5) A clear next step: how to reach you.

Keep it to one screen on a laptop if you can. No life story, no list of every job. If a line doesn't help someone decide to talk to you, cut it.
free.prompt: Help me build a one-page proof page for [target role]. Here is my resume: [paste]. Here are 2 or 3 things I'm proudest of at work: [describe]. Write: 1) a one-line headline that says the role and who I help, 2) three result statements, each one sentence, specific and honest (use only facts I gave you, and mark any spot where I should add a real number with [add number]), 3) a 100-word case study in problem, action, result format, 4) three bullets on how I'd approach this kind of work, 5) a one-line call to action. Plain language, no buzzwords.

free.title: Step 2: Put the link where screeners actually look
free.body:
Your link only works if someone sees it. Put it in several places on every application, not just one.

Resume: in the header, right under your name, labeled with words, for example 'Portfolio: see my work for [Role]'. Cover letter field: if it's optional, paste the short note from Step 3 instead of a full letter. If it's a required upload, make a one-page document with that same note and the link at the top. 'Website' or 'Portfolio' field: always fill it in with your page. 'Additional information' box: one sentence plus the link. LinkedIn: add the page to your Featured section and your contact info.

Some forms strip formatting, so the full link should also appear as plain text somewhere in your resume. Test this by pasting your resume into a plain text editor and checking the link survives.

free.title: Step 3: Swap the cover letter for a 4-line note
free.body:
This note replaces a long cover letter. It's short enough to actually get read, and it points to proof.

Line 1: Why this role, in one specific sentence. 'I'm applying for [Role] because [specific thing about their product, team or goal].'

Line 2: Your strongest matching result. 'Most recently I [result that maps to their top requirement].'

Line 3: The link with a reason to click. 'I put together a short page showing how I'd approach [their challenge]: [link].'

Line 4: An easy next step. 'Happy to talk through it whenever works for you.'

That's it. Four lines, one link. The note does the job of a cover letter (why you, why them) in a fraction of the time to read, and the page carries the detail.
free.prompt: Write a 4-line application note to replace my cover letter. Job post: [paste]. My proof page covers: [list what's on it]. My strongest result for this role: [describe]. Format: line 1, why this role, mentioning one specific thing about the company or team from the post; line 2, my strongest matching result; line 3, a reason to click my link, naming the challenge my page addresses, then [LINK]; line 4, an easy next step. Under 75 words total. No 'I am writing to express my interest'. No hype.

locked.title: Step 4: Tailor the page to each job in 15 minutes
locked.body:
One generic page is good. One page per job is better, and it doesn't have to take long. Copy your base page and change only three things.

Worksheet for each job. A) Top requirement: read the post and write down the one thing they care about most (often the first bullet or the thing repeated twice). B) Headline swap: rewrite your headline to name that requirement. C) Result order: move your most relevant result to the top, and swap out the least relevant one. D) Approach bullets: rewrite the three bullets to match their stated goals, using their words. E) Name check: put the company name and role title on the page once, near the top.

Set a 15-minute timer. If you go over, you're rewriting too much. The base page stays the same, the top third does the tailoring.
locked.prompt: Here is my base proof page: [paste]. Here is the job post: [paste]. Using only facts already on my page, give me: A) the single top requirement in this post and why you chose it, B) a new one-line headline that names that requirement, C) which of my results should go first and which to drop, D) three rewritten 'how I'd approach this' bullets using the post's own language, E) one sentence near the top that names the company and role. Do not invent any experience or numbers.

locked.title: Step 5: Have Scout build Showcases and add them to your applications
locked.body:
If building and tailoring a page for every job sounds like a lot, Scout does it for you. It builds a Showcase, a personal web page made for one job or one company, and you choose from many designs. Then it finds jobs that match you and applies for you, adding your Showcase link to each application.

Scout also alerts you when someone views your Showcase, follows up for you, and gives you a prep brief on any company that replies. You get a weekly report of everything it did, so you can see every application and every link.

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, add my Showcase to my applications

locked.title: Step 6: Run the pre-send link checklist
locked.body:
A broken or confusing link is worse than no link. Before every application, run this checklist. It takes two minutes.

1) Open the link in a private browser window, so you see what a stranger sees. 2) Open it on your phone. Many hiring managers check links on mobile between meetings. 3) Make sure it doesn't ask for a login or permission to view. 4) Check that the company name and role are right. Sending a page that names a different company is the most common mistake. 5) Read the top section out loud. If it sounds like a different job, retailor it. 6) Make sure your contact details are on the page. 7) Confirm the link appears in both your resume and the application form.

If any check fails, fix it before you hit submit.
locked.prompt: I'm about to submit an application for [Role] at [Company]. Here is the text of my proof page: [paste] and my 4-line note: [paste]. Check them for: 1) any mention of a different company or role, 2) anything that doesn't match this job post [paste], 3) missing contact details, 4) typos, 5) any sentence that sounds generic or could be cut. List each issue and the exact fix.

locked.title: Step 7: Track which version gets responses and improve it
locked.body:
Keep a simple record: Company, Role, Date applied, Page version (which headline you used), Note version, Response (none, rejection, screen, interview).

Every two weeks, look at it. Which headlines led to a reply? Which roles responded at all? If one style of headline keeps getting replies, use it as your new base. If nothing is landing for a certain kind of role, that's a signal to adjust your target or your top result, not to send more of the same.

Also watch what people mention in interviews. If a hiring manager says 'I liked the case study on your page,' that part is working. Make it bigger. If nobody mentions the page at all, move the link higher in your resume and make your note's line 3 more specific.
locked.prompt: Here is my application tracker: [paste rows: company, role, page headline used, note version, response]. Tell me: 1) which headline and note versions are linked to replies, 2) which roles or industries are not responding, 3) one change to test on my next 5 applications, 4) whether my target roles look right based on where I'm getting traction. Be specific and practical.

guides.tip: Add a short line on your page about how you work remotely: your time zone, your overlap hours and how you keep people updated.

guides.intro:
Remote teams can be harder to map. People are in different places, and the job post may not say which team or region the role sits in.

This guide gives you a calm, step-by-step way to find the likely hiring manager and confirm it, using public profiles, team pages and the clues in the post.

free.title: Step 1: Learn the five people in every hire
free.body:
A job post feels like one door. Behind it are usually several people, each with a different role.

1) The hiring manager: the person you'd report to. They usually decide who gets hired and they feel the pain of the empty seat most. 2) The skip-level: the hiring manager's boss. Often approves the hire and sometimes set the goal the role exists for. 3) The recruiter or talent partner: runs the process, screens applicants and schedules. A real ally, but usually not the final decider. 4) Team peers: people who'd work beside you. They often interview you and give input. 5) HR or people ops: handles offers, policy and paperwork.

A general careers inbox or application portal feeds the process, so still apply. But the person who feels the need for you is the hiring manager. That's who you want to know exists, and who you want to know you exist.

free.title: Step 2: Use the cheat sheet to guess the hiring manager's title
free.body:
Hiring managers are usually one or two levels above the role. Use this as a starting point, then adjust for company size.

Individual contributor roles (analyst, specialist, coordinator, engineer): look for Manager or Senior Manager of that function, or a Team Lead. Manager roles: look for Senior Manager, Director, or Head of that area. Director roles: look for VP, Senior Director, or Head of. VP roles: look for SVP, Chief (CMO, CTO, COO), or the CEO at smaller companies.

Company size matters. At a small startup, a 'Head of' or a founder may be the hiring manager for almost every role. At a big company, the same title might exist in several regions or product lines, so match the team, not just the title.

The job post often gives clues: 'reports to the Director of Growth', 'join our payments team', or a location. Write those down before you search.
free.prompt: Here is a job post: [paste]. Based on the post, the company's size [startup, mid-size, large, or unknown], and the role level, tell me: 1) the 3 most likely job titles of the hiring manager, ranked, 2) the likely title of their boss, 3) any clues in the post about the team, product line, region or reporting line I should use when searching, 4) 2 or 3 titles of peers who might interview me. Explain your reasoning briefly.

free.title: Step 3: Find the person yourself
free.body:
Now go find them. Try these in order.

LinkedIn: go to the company page, click People, and search for the title from Step 2 plus a keyword from the team, for example 'Director Growth' or 'Manager Payments'. Filter by location if the role has one. Company website: check About, Team, Leadership and Blog pages. Blog authors are often team leads. News and press releases: search the company name plus the team area, for example 'Netflix data platform lead'. People quoted in announcements often run the team. Talks and podcasts: team leads often speak at industry events. Job posts: sometimes the recruiter or the manager shares the post on LinkedIn themselves. Look at who posted or reposted it.

Write down two or three candidates. You'll confirm the right one in Step 4.
free.prompt: I'm trying to find the hiring manager for [Role] on the [team or area] team at [Company]. Give me: 1) five LinkedIn people-search keyword combinations to try on the company's People tab, 2) which pages on a company website usually list team leads, 3) five web search phrases that might surface someone who runs this team in news, blog posts or talks, 4) what to look for in a LinkedIn profile that suggests this person manages the team I'd join. Do not guess any real names.

locked.title: Step 4: Confirm you found the decider
locked.body:
Similar titles can fool you. Before you reach out, check for at least two of these signals.

Their profile mentions the same team, product or region as the job post. They've posted or shared the job, or posted about growing their team. People with titles one level below them sit on the same team, which you can spot on LinkedIn. Their tenure fits: someone who joined last week is less likely to be hiring than someone who's built the team. Their recent posts or talks touch the problems in the job post.

If you find two equally likely people, that's fine. Reach the more likely one first, and keep the other for later. If you can't confirm anyone, aim one level higher. A director can forward you to the right manager, and a forward from above carries weight.
locked.prompt: Here are 2 or 3 people I think might be the hiring manager for [Role] at [Company]. For each, here's what's on their public profile: [paste title, team, tenure, recent posts or summary]. And here's the job post: [paste]. Rank them from most to least likely to be the hiring manager, explain which signals point to each, and tell me who to reach first and why.

locked.body:
Mapping every target company by hand takes time. Scout can do it for you. Tell it the company, and it finds people there who matter for your role, like hiring managers and team leads.

Then it reaches out with a short note and your Showcase, a personal web page built for that company. It sends in small, paced waves, and you (or someone you authorize) approve the sends. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, and gives you a prep brief if a company replies. You get a weekly report of everything it did.

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, who should I reach at [Company]?

locked.title: Step 6: Build a one-company target map
locked.body:
For each company you care about, fill out a simple map with three people. This keeps you from putting all your hope on one inbox.

The Decider: the likely hiring manager. What they care about: hitting the team's goals and filling the seat with someone who won't need hand-holding. The Influencer: a peer or senior team member who'd work with you. What they care about: whether you'd be good to work with and could carry real work. The Connector: the recruiter for that function, or someone you share a school, past company or group with. What they care about: moving good candidates forward and making a smooth process.

For each person, write: name, title, why you think they're the right one, one thing they've posted or worked on, and the one question you'd ask them. That last part is what makes your note feel personal.
locked.prompt: Help me build a target map for [Company], role: [Role]. Here's what I found: Decider candidate: [title, team, any public posts]. Influencer candidate: [same]. Connector candidate: [same]. Here's my background: [2 or 3 lines]. For each person, write: 1) what they most likely care about in this hire, 2) the strongest thing in my background for them specifically, 3) one smart question I could ask them, based on their public work. Keep it short and practical.

locked.title: Step 7: Say the right thing to each person
locked.body:
Each person needs a different message. Keep every note under 80 words.

To the Decider: lead with their problem. 'Hi [Name], I saw you're hiring for [Role]. I've spent [time] solving [problem from the post], most recently [one result]. Would a short call be useful?'

To the Influencer: lead with curiosity, not a job ask. 'Hi [Name], I'm applying for [Role] on your team. I liked your post on [topic]. How are you thinking about [related challenge]?'

To the Connector: lead with fit and make their job easy. 'Hi [Name], I've applied for [Role]. Quick summary: [two-line fit]. Happy to share anything that helps your review.'

Send to the Decider first. Wait about a week before reaching the next person, and never send the same text to two people at one company. Track who you've contacted so you don't double up.
locked.prompt: Write three short messages, each under 80 words, for [Role] at [Company]. Job post: [paste]. My strongest result: [describe]. 1) To the likely hiring manager: lead with the problem in the post and my result, end with a low-pressure ask. 2) To a team peer: mention their public work on [topic], ask one curious question, no job ask. 3) To the recruiter: a two-line fit summary, offer to help their review. Each must sound different and none should repeat the others' wording.

guides.tip: For remote roles, filter LinkedIn people search by the team keyword, not location. Remote hiring managers can be anywhere.

guides.intro:
Remote teams run on written communication, so a clear, short note is exactly the kind of thing they're used to reading. Reaching out isn't intrusive. It shows how you'd communicate on the team.

This guide helps you write calm, specific notes and follow up at a respectful pace, without feeling pushy.

free.title: Step 1: Reset what 'pushy' really means
free.body:
Pushy is about how you ask, not whether you ask. Hiring managers have open roles they need to fill. A short note from someone who could help them is not a bother. What feels pushy is length, pressure and entitlement: long life stories, demands for a call, 'I'd be perfect for this', or messaging every day.

Here's the test. A note is not pushy if it is short (under 100 words), specific to them, offers something useful, makes one small ask, and gives them an easy out. If your draft passes all five, send it.

Also remember the other side of the math. If you send nothing, nobody knows you exist. A polite note that gets no reply costs you nothing. A note never sent can't open anything.

free.title: Step 2: Write with the 4-part anatomy
free.body:
Every not-pushy note has four parts, in this order.

1) Context: why you're writing to them specifically. One line. 'I saw your team is hiring for [Role].' 2) Value: one specific thing you bring or noticed. One or two lines. A result, an idea, or an observation about their work. 3) Small ask: something easy to say yes to. 'Would a 15-minute call next week be useful?' or 'Would it help if I sent a short page on how I'd approach this?' 4) Easy out: a line that removes pressure. 'If the timing's off, no worries at all.'

That's it. No apologizing for writing ('Sorry to bother you'). No over-explaining. The easy out is the part most people skip, and it's what makes the note feel respectful instead of pushy.
free.prompt: Write a not-pushy outreach note to a hiring manager. Their name and role: [Name, title]. Company: [Company]. The role I want: [Role]. One specific thing about them or their team: [their post, product, news, goal from the job post]. My strongest relevant result: [describe]. Use exactly four parts: 1) one line of context on why I'm writing to them, 2) one or two lines of specific value, 3) one small ask that's easy to say yes to, 4) one easy-out line that removes pressure. Under 90 words. No apologies, no 'I'd be perfect', no 'just following up'.

free.title: Step 3: Pick an opening angle that fits
free.body:
Using the same opener for everyone makes notes feel like a template. Rotate through these six angles and pick the one that fits the person.

1) The result: 'I helped [type of team] cut [problem] by [real result].' Best when your experience maps directly. 2) The question: 'How are you thinking about [challenge from the post]?' Best for peers and curious leaders. 3) The idea: 'One thing I'd try on [their product]: [idea].' Best when you've studied their work. 4) The shared link: 'We both worked at [company] / studied at [school].' Best when it's real. 5) The content reply: 'Your post on [topic] stuck with me because [reason].' Best for people who post publicly. 6) The referral: '[Name] suggested I reach out.' Only if they actually did.

Never fake an angle. A real, smaller one beats an invented big one.
free.prompt: I want to reach [Name, title] at [Company] about [Role]. Here's what I know about them: [their public posts, team, product, background]. Here's my background: [3 lines]. Write 3 different opening lines for my note, each using a different angle from this list: result, question, idea, shared link, content reply. Only use a shared link or content reply angle if I gave you real details for it. Tell me which opener you'd pick and why.

locked.title: Step 4: Warm up before you write
locked.body:
A cold note from a total stranger is fine. A note from someone they've seen before is easier to answer. Spend a week or two warming up, lightly.

Warm-up routine: follow the person and the company page on LinkedIn. When they post, leave one thoughtful comment that adds something, not just 'Great post'. Two comments over a week or two is plenty. If they wrote an article, gave a talk or launched something, take note, because it's perfect for your opener. Send a connection request with a short note only after you've commented once or twice.

Connection note template (keep it short, LinkedIn limits the length): 'Hi [Name], enjoyed your post on [topic]. I work in [field] and I'm interested in what your team is building. Would love to connect.' Save the job conversation for after they accept.
locked.prompt: Here is a recent post by [Name], [title] at [Company]: [paste post]. I work in [field] with experience in [area]. Write me: 1) two thoughtful comments I could leave, each adding a real point or question, under 40 words, 2) a short LinkedIn connection note under 250 characters that references the post and doesn't mention a job. Sound like a real professional, not a fan.

locked.title: Step 5: Let Scout draft and pace your outreach, with your approval
locked.body:
If you'd rather have help with this part, Scout can do it for you. It finds people at your target company, like hiring managers and team leads, and drafts a short note that includes your Showcase, a personal web page built for that company.

Nothing goes out without approval. You, or someone you authorize, approve every send, and Scout sends in small, paced waves so it does not read like a mass blast. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, and gives you a prep brief on the company if they reply. Each week you get a report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=the-not-pushy-outreach-guide&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, draft my outreach to [Company]

locked.title: Step 6: Follow up politely, then close the loop
locked.body:
No reply usually means busy, not no. A good follow-up rhythm is two follow-ups, spaced out, each adding something new.

Follow-up 1, about 5 to 7 business days later: 'Hi [Name], one more thought on [their challenge]: [new idea, result or resource]. Still happy to chat if useful.' Follow-up 2, about 10 business days after that: 'Hi [Name], I know things get busy. I'll leave it here, but if [Role] is still open or something similar comes up, I'd love to talk. Thanks either way.'

Then stop. That last note is the graceful close. It leaves a good impression and keeps the door open for later. If they say no, reply with one line: 'Thanks for letting me know. If anything changes, I'd be glad to hear from you.' Never argue a no.
locked.prompt: I sent this note to [Name] at [Company] on [date]: [paste]. No reply yet. Write two follow-ups: 1) one to send 5 to 7 business days later that adds one new, specific piece of value, under 60 words, 2) a graceful closing note to send about 10 business days after that, under 50 words, that leaves the door open with no guilt or pressure. Also write a one-line reply in case they say no.

locked.title: Step 7: Run the pushy check and track every send
locked.body:
Before any note goes out, scan it for pushy signals and cut them. Words and phrases to remove: 'I'd be perfect for this', 'You need someone like me', 'I know you're busy, but', 'Just following up', 'Circling back', 'As per my last message', 'ASAP', 'I'm sure you'll agree'. Also cut: more than one ask, more than 100 words, more than one link, any guilt.

Then log the send: Name, Title, Company, Channel (LinkedIn or email), Date sent, Angle used, Follow-up 1 date, Follow-up 2 date, Reply. Never message the same person twice with the same note, and never contact more than one person at a company in the same week.

Every couple of weeks, check which angles got replies. Use those more.
locked.prompt: Review this outreach note for anything that could feel pushy, needy or generic: [paste note]. Flag: 1) any phrase that pressures, guilts or assumes, 2) more than one ask, 3) anything over 100 words, 4) any line that could be sent to anyone. Then give me a cleaned-up version that keeps my meaning, stays under 90 words and ends with an easy out.

guides.tip: Treat your outreach note as a sample of your remote writing. Clear, short and easy to act on. That's what remote managers want from teammates.

Remote-first companies often hire from wide, global pools, so getting noticed early matters. Waiting for a posting can mean competing with a very large field.

This guide shows you a calm, steady way to research the company, show proof of your work and build a relationship over time, all in writing.

free.title: Step 1: Build an insider dossier on the company
free.body:
No posting doesn't mean no way in. It means you get there by knowing the company better than other candidates do. Say you want to work at Netflix. Spend an afternoon building a one-page dossier.

Collect: 1) What they sell and to whom, in one sentence. 2) Their stated priorities: read the most recent annual report, shareholder letter or CEO interview if public, or the founder's posts if private. 3) Recent news: launches, expansions, new leaders, partnerships. 4) Their current job posts, even for other roles. These show which teams are growing and the language they use. 5) The teams that match your skills. 6) Two or three problems they seem to be working on.

Write each item in your own words. This dossier powers everything else in this playbook.
free.prompt: I want to work at [Company]. I do [your field and level]. Help me build a one-page insider dossier. Organize it as: 1) what they sell and to whom, in one sentence, 2) where I should look for their stated priorities (types of documents, interviews or posts), 3) what kinds of recent news to search for and the search phrases to use, 4) how to read their current job posts for clues about which teams are growing, 5) a list of questions I should be able to answer before reaching out. Then, based on this public information I gathered: [paste notes], summarize the 3 biggest problems they seem to be working on that relate to my field.

free.title: Step 2: Pick your door: the team and the problem
free.body:
'I want to work at [Company]' is a wish. 'I want to help [team] with [problem]' is a pitch. Turn the wish into a pitch.

From your dossier, choose one team where your skills fit best. Then pick one problem that team likely has. Write a single sentence: 'I help [type of team] do [outcome] by [how], and I think [Company]'s [team] could use that for [specific problem].'

Then sketch the role that should exist, even if it isn't posted. Give it a plain title, three things that person would do in the first six months, and who they'd report to. You aren't inventing a job for them. You're making it easy for someone inside to picture you on the team.

If you can't pick a door, your dossier needs more detail. Go back and look harder at their job posts and news.
free.prompt: Here is my dossier on [Company]: [paste]. Here is my background: [paste resume summary]. Help me: 1) pick the one team where I'd add the most value and explain why, 2) name the most likely problem that team is facing based on the dossier, 3) write a one-sentence pitch in this format: 'I help [type of team] do [outcome] by [how], and I think [Company]'s [team] could use that for [problem]', 4) sketch the role that should exist: a plain title, three six-month priorities, and the likely title of the person it would report to. Use only facts I gave you.

free.title: Step 3: Make a small proof project
free.body:
When there's no posting, proof beats a resume. Make one small thing that shows how you'd think on the job. Keep it to a few hours of work.

Pick one format. A teardown: what's working and what you'd test on one of their products, pages or processes. A 30-60-90 plan for the role you sketched in Step 2. A mini analysis: public data or reviews about their space, and what it suggests. A sample: a short piece of work in your field, like a campaign idea, a design, a process map, or a code sketch, aimed at their problem.

Rules: use only public information, be respectful (curious, not critical), keep it to one or two pages, and end with 'Here's what I'd want to learn from your team.' That humility matters. You're showing how you think, not telling them they're doing it wrong.
free.prompt: Help me create a small proof project for [Company]'s [team]. The problem I'm focused on: [problem]. My skills: [list]. Pick the best format for me from: teardown, 30-60-90 plan, mini analysis, or work sample, and explain why. Then outline it: a title, 3 to 5 sections with what goes in each, and a closing section called 'What I'd want to learn from your team' with 3 good questions. Keep the tone curious and respectful, never critical. Use only public information.

locked.title: Step 4: Find your people and write the 'no posting' note
locked.body:
Now find two or three people on the team you picked: the likely team lead, a senior person on the team, and someone who'd be a peer. Use the company's LinkedIn People tab with team keywords, their blog, and recent talks or news.

Your note is different from a job application note. You're not asking for a job that doesn't exist. You're sharing proof and asking to learn.

Template: 'Hi [Name], I've followed [Company]'s work on [specific thing] and put together a short [teardown, plan, analysis] on [problem] from the outside. I'm not replying to a posting, I just think I could help your team here someday. Would you be open to a 15-minute call so I can learn how you see it? If not, no worries.' Attach or link the proof.

Start with the team lead. Wait a week before reaching the next person.
locked.prompt: Write a 'no posting' outreach note to [Name, title] at [Company]. I've made a proof project: [describe it in 1 to 2 lines]. The problem it addresses: [problem]. My background in one line: [line]. The note should: mention one specific thing about their team's work, say plainly that I'm not responding to a posting, offer the proof, ask for a 15-minute call to learn how they see it, and give an easy out. Under 100 words. Curious and respectful, never presumptuous.

It builds a Showcase, a personal web page made for that one company, with many designs to choose from. It finds people there who matter for your work, like hiring managers and team leads, and reaches out with a short note and your Showcase.

locked.title: Step 6: Watch for trigger signals
locked.body:
Roles open when something changes. If you watch for change, you can reach out at the right moment, often before anything is posted.

Set up these signals. Job alerts on the company's careers page and on LinkedIn for your target team, even if roles are slightly off. A news alert for the company name. Follow the company page and your two or three team contacts.

Triggers that often lead to hiring: a new leader joins the team (new leaders often build their own teams), a funding round or strong results, a product launch or new market, a team lead posting about growth or 'building the team', a job posted on an adjacent team, or someone in your target role leaving.

When a trigger hits, send one short note within a few days: 'Congrats on [news]. I imagine [team] has a lot ahead. My [proof] is still relevant, happy to help if useful.'
locked.prompt: I'm tracking [Company] as a dream employer. My target team: [team]. Here is the latest news or change I've seen: [paste]. Tell me: 1) whether this change is likely to lead to hiring on my target team and why, 2) the best person to contact about it, 3) a short note under 70 words that congratulates them on the news, connects it to my proof project [describe], and offers help without asking for a job directly.

locked.title: Step 7: Run a 90-day stay-in-touch plan
locked.body:
Dream companies are often a longer game. The goal is to be the person they think of when a role opens. Here's a light, respectful 90-day plan.

Weeks 1 to 2: dossier, door and proof project done. First notes sent. Weeks 3 to 4: follow up once with something new, like an update to your proof. Weeks 5 to 8: engage publicly. Comment thoughtfully on two or three of their team's posts. Share something useful related to their work. Weeks 9 to 12: send one value-only note, like an article or idea relevant to their problem, with no ask at all. Then check in roughly once a quarter.

Meanwhile, keep applying to other companies. A dream company is one target, not your whole plan. Keep a simple log: person, date, what you sent, response, next touch date.
locked.prompt: Build me a 90-day stay-in-touch plan for [Company]. My contacts there: [names and titles]. What I've already sent: [list with dates]. My proof project: [describe]. Give me a week-by-week calendar with specific actions, the purpose of each touch, and a short draft for each message. Keep the pace respectful: no more than one direct message per person every 3 to 4 weeks. Include a reminder to keep applying elsewhere.

guides.tip: Remote companies often publish handbooks, blogs or public docs about how they work. Read them and mention one detail in your note.
