guides.intro:
Remote roles can draw large applicant pools once they're posted. Being in a conversation before the listing goes up can make a real difference in how you're seen.

This guide gives you a calm, steady way to build those conversations by video and in writing, with a weekly routine you can keep from anywhere.

free.title: Step 1: Build a target list from hiring signals
free.body:
Before a job is posted, someone inside already knows it's coming. A manager has budget, a team is growing, or a person is leaving. Your job is to be talking to companies at that stage. Start with a list of 20 to 30 companies, then score them.

Give each company one point for each signal you can find: they recently raised money or announced growth, they launched a new product or entered a new market, a new leader joined the team you'd work on, they're posting jobs on teams next to yours, people in your kind of role are leaving or getting promoted, or a leader is posting about building the team.

Sort by score. The top 10 are where you start conversations this month. Keep the rest on the list and rescore every few weeks. Signals change.
free.prompt: I work in [field] at a [level] level and I want roles like [target titles] in [location or remote]. Help me build a target list. 1) Suggest the kinds of companies and industries where my skills are most in demand. 2) Give me a list of hiring signals to look for and where to find each one publicly (news, company pages, LinkedIn, job boards). 3) Make me a simple scoring sheet with columns for company, each signal, total score, and notes. 4) Here are companies I'm already curious about: [list]. Tell me what to check first for each one.

free.title: Step 2: Reconnect with people you already know
free.body:
Your fastest way into early conversations is people who already know you. Make a list of 30 or more: former coworkers and managers, clients and vendors, classmates and alumni, people from groups or events. Then match them against your target list. Anyone who works at, or knows someone at, a target company goes to the top.

Reconnect first, ask later. A simple script: 'Hi [Name], it's been a while. I saw [their news, new role or post] and wanted to say congrats. I'm exploring my next move in [field] and would love to hear what you're working on these days. Up for a quick call in the next couple of weeks?'

Don't open with 'Do you know of any jobs?' That puts pressure on them. Ask about them, then share what you're looking for during the call. People are usually glad to help once they know exactly how.
free.prompt: Help me reconnect with people from my past. Here's my list with how I know each one and anything I know about them now: [paste]. My target companies are: [list]. 1) Rank who I should contact first, putting anyone tied to my target companies at the top. 2) For the top 10, write a short, warm reconnect message under 70 words that mentions something real about them, says I'm exploring my next move in [field], and asks for a quick catch-up. No direct job asks. Make each one sound personal, not templated.

free.title: Step 3: Run a 20-minute conversation that leads somewhere
free.body:
When someone says yes to a call, keep it to 20 minutes and come prepared. Here's the script.

Minutes 0 to 3: thank them and say what you're exploring in one sentence. Minutes 3 to 12: ask about them. 'What's your team focused on this year?' 'What's hard right now?' 'What kind of people are doing well there?' Minutes 12 to 16: share your short pitch: the role you want, two results and the kind of problem you love solving. Minutes 16 to 20: the warm next step. 'Is there anyone else you think I should talk to?' and 'If you hear of anything where I might help, would you think of me?'

The 'who else' question is the most important one. One good conversation should lead to the next. Send a thank-you within a day that mentions one thing they said.
free.prompt: I have a 20-minute call with [Name, title] at [Company]. Here's what I know about them and their team: [notes]. My target role: [role]. My strongest results: [2 or 3]. Write me: 1) a one-sentence opener on what I'm exploring, 2) five good questions about their team and its challenges, 3) a 30-second pitch about me, 4) two natural ways to ask 'who else should I talk to', 5) a thank-you message under 70 words that I'll customize with one thing they said.

locked.title: Step 4: Make yourself easy to refer
locked.body:
People who want to help you often don't, simply because it's work to explain you to someone else. Remove that work.

Write a forwardable blurb: three or four sentences someone can paste into a message to a colleague. It should say who you are, what role you're looking for, two proof points, and how to reach you. Example structure: '[Name] is a [role] who [main outcome]. Most recently [result]. [He or she or they] is looking for [target role] at a [type of company]. Happy to make an intro.'

Send it at the end of every good conversation: 'In case it's useful, here's a short blurb you can forward if anyone comes to mind.' Also post a version on LinkedIn once, saying what you're looking for and the kind of problems you solve. Keep it confident and specific, not desperate.
locked.prompt: Write a forwardable referral blurb about me, 3 to 4 sentences, in the third person. My background: [paste summary]. Two results I'm proud of: [list]. The role I want: [role] at [type of company]. Make it easy for someone to paste into a message to a colleague. Then write a short LinkedIn post, under 120 words, that says what I'm looking for and the problems I solve, confident and specific, with no begging and no hashtag spam.

locked.title: Step 5: Let Scout start conversations at your target companies
locked.body:
If you want help keeping many conversations going at once, Scout can do this for you. Give it your target companies. It finds people there who matter for your work, like hiring managers and team leads, and reaches out with a short note and your Showcase, a personal web page built for that company.

It sends in small, paced waves, and you (or someone you authorize) approve every send. Scout follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, and gives you a prep brief on the company if they reply, so you're ready for the conversation. Each week you get a report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=get-in-before-it-s-posted&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, start conversations at my target companies

locked.title: Step 6: Set a weekly conversation routine
locked.body:
Getting in early is a habit, not a single move. Set a weekly routine you can keep for a couple of months.

Monday: rescore your target list and pick five companies for the week. Tuesday: send reconnect or outreach messages, a number you choose and can sustain. Wednesday and Thursday: hold calls and send thank-yous within a day. Friday: follow up on anything quiet for a week, send referral blurbs to anyone who offered help, and log everything.

Your log: Person, Company, How you know them, Date contacted, Call date, Who they suggested next, Promised follow-up, Next touch date. The 'who they suggested next' column is your pipeline. If it's empty most weeks, your calls need a stronger 'who else' ask.

Keep applying to posted roles too. This runs alongside your search, not instead of it.
locked.prompt: Here is my conversation log for the past [number] weeks: [paste rows]. Tell me: 1) which conversations are most likely to lead to a role and why, 2) who I owe a follow-up to and by when, 3) whether I'm getting enough referrals to new people, and how to improve my ask, 4) my five priority actions for next week. Be specific and practical.

locked.title: Step 7: Turn 'we might have something' into a real role
locked.body:
Sometimes a conversation ends with 'We might be hiring for something like that soon.' That's your moment. Handle it carefully.

Within a day, send a short note: 'Thanks again. You mentioned [team] might be adding someone for [area]. If it helps, I can send a one-page outline of how I'd approach the first 90 days.' If they say yes, send a tight, one-page plan tied to what they told you.

Ask two clear questions when the time is right: 'Who would that role report to?' and 'What's the best way for me to be considered when it opens?' Sometimes the answer is a referral, sometimes a direct intro to the manager, sometimes a formal application. Do exactly what they suggest.

Then stay close but light: one useful touch every two to three weeks until the role opens, and apply the same day it's posted.
locked.prompt: In a call, [Name, title] at [Company] said they might be hiring for [area or role] soon. Here's what they told me about the team and its goals: [notes]. My background: [summary]. Write me: 1) a follow-up note under 70 words offering a one-page 90-day outline, 2) the outline itself: three phases with two or three priorities each, tied to what they told me, 3) two polite ways to ask who the role would report to and how to be considered when it opens.

guides.tip: When you schedule calls with distributed teams, offer two or three times in their time zone. It's a small courtesy remote teams notice.

guides.intro:
Remote roles draw applicants from everywhere, so the online pile gets big. A short, direct note to the hiring manager helps you stand apart from it.

This guide walks you through the three-sentence email calmly and step by step, including how to show you write clearly, which matters a lot on remote teams.

free.title: Step 1: Learn the three sentences
free.body:
A cold email to a hiring manager has one job: get a short yes. Long emails about your journey get skimmed and saved for later, and later rarely comes. Three sentences is enough.

Sentence 1, Why them: one specific thing about their team or company and why it pulls you in. Sentence 2, Your proof: one result you have delivered that matches what they need, plus a link or attachment that shows it. Sentence 3, Easy ask: one small, low-effort request they can answer in a few seconds.

That is the whole email. No "I hope this finds you well," no life story, no list of every skill. If a line does not serve one of those three jobs, cut it. Write it, then read it on your phone. If you have to scroll, it is too long.
free.prompt:
Write a 3-sentence cold email to a hiring manager.

About them: [company name], [team or department], [the specific thing I noticed: a launch, a job post, a quote, a new market, a product feature].
The role I want: [job title].
My best matching result: [one result with a number or concrete outcome, e.g. "cut onboarding time from [X weeks] to [Y] for a [size] sales team"].
What I can link to: [portfolio, case study, one-page summary, or "attached PDF"].

Rules: Sentence 1 is about them and why their work interests me. Sentence 2 is my one result plus the link. Sentence 3 is one easy ask that takes them under a minute. Under 75 words total. No greeting filler, no "I hope this finds you well," no adjectives about myself like "passionate" or "results-driven." Give me 3 versions with different opening angles, plus a subject line for each under 6 words.

free.title: Step 2: Write a "why them" line that proves you looked
free.body:
The first sentence decides if the rest gets read. It should be impossible to send to another company. Spend ten minutes on their website, LinkedIn page, recent posts and job listings, then pick one of these angles:

1. A product or feature they just launched. 2. A new market, city or customer type they are moving into. 3. Something the manager posted or said in an interview. 4. A problem the job post hints at ("scaling," "rebuilding," "first hire"). 5. A customer story on their site. 6. A hiring spree on one team. 7. A recent funding round or partnership announcement. 8. Their product, as a real user. 9. A value or way of working they talk about publicly. 10. A competitor move that makes their next step interesting.

Write it as an observation, not flattery. "Saw you are opening a Denver office and hiring three field reps" beats "I love your company's mission."
free.prompt:
I'm writing a cold email to [hiring manager name and title] at [company]. Here's what I found about them: [paste notes: recent news, posts, job descriptions, product details].

Write 6 different opening sentences, one per angle: a recent launch, a growth move, something the manager said, a problem hinted at in the job post, my experience as a customer or user, and a team that is hiring. Each must be one sentence, under 25 words, specific to this company, and must not use the words "passionate," "love," "mission" or "excited." After each, tell me in a few words what fact I'd need to double-check before sending.

free.title: Step 3: Make one easy ask and a subject line that fits
free.body:
The ask is where most cold emails go wrong. "Can we hop on a 30-minute call?" asks a stranger for their calendar. Make it smaller.

Easy asks: "Worth a look?" "Is this on your radar for the [role] opening?" "Who is the right person to send this to?" "Would a 10-minute call next week be useful, or is email better?" "Open to me sending a short plan for [problem]?" Each can be answered in one line.

For the subject line, keep it short and plain, like a note from a coworker. Examples: "[Role] idea for [Team]", "Re: your [project] launch", "Quick question on [role]", "[Result] for [Company]". Avoid all caps, "Opportunity!", or anything that looks like marketing.

Before sending, run this checklist: under 75 words, their name spelled right, one link only, one ask only, no attachment over a couple of pages, and your phone number in the signature.
free.prompt:
Here is my cold email draft: [paste draft].

Check it against these rules and rewrite it: (1) under 75 words, (2) first sentence is about them and could not be sent to another company, (3) second sentence has one concrete result and one link, (4) third sentence is one easy ask that takes under a minute to answer, (5) no filler phrases or self-praise adjectives. Then give me 5 subject lines under 6 words that sound like a note from a colleague, not marketing. Point out anything that could come across as pushy.

locked.title: Step 4: Build the proof that goes in sentence two
locked.body:
Sentence two only works if the link behind it is worth clicking. A full resume is not proof, it is a history. Proof is one page built for this one manager.

Make a simple one-pager (a Google Doc, Notion page or PDF) with: a headline naming the role and company, the problem you think they are solving, two or three results of yours that match it, a short "how I'd approach the first 90 days" section, and your contact details. Keep it to one screen if you can.

Good proof types by role: a sales rep can show a pipeline story with numbers. A marketer can show one campaign breakdown. An operations person can show a before-and-after process. An engineer can show a project write-up or repo summary. A designer can show two case studies. A customer success person can show a churn save or renewal story.

Link it with plain words, like "here's a one-page plan," never a raw long link.
locked.prompt:
Help me build a one-page proof document for a cold email to [hiring manager title] at [company] for the [role] role.

The job post says: [paste key parts of the job description].
My relevant results: [list 3 to 5 results with numbers or outcomes].
What I know about their situation: [notes].

Give me: a headline, a 2-sentence summary of the problem I think they're solving, my 3 best-matched results rewritten as one-line proof points, a short "first 90 days" plan with 3 bullets, and a closing line. Keep it to about 250 words so it fits on one screen. Mark anything that's a guess about their situation so I can soften it.

locked.body:
If you want this done for you across many companies, Scout does the heavy lifting. It finds the people at your target company, like the hiring manager or team lead, writes a short note in the three-line style, and attaches a Showcase: a personal web page built for that one job or company, with many designs to choose from.

Nothing goes out until you, or someone you authorize, approves it. Notes go out in small, paced waves, Scout follows up, and it tells you when someone views your Showcase. When a company replies, you get a prep brief on them, and every week you get a report of everything Scout did.

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, write a 3-line note to the hiring manager

locked.title: Step 6: Steal these worked examples
locked.body:
Use these as patterns, not scripts. Swap in your facts.

Sales: "Saw [Company] is expanding into mid-market healthcare and hiring [number] AEs for it. I [opened X new accounts] in my last role, here's a one-page breakdown of how. Is this on your radar for the AE opening?"

Marketing: "Your new self-serve plan looks like a big shift from sales-led growth. I rebuilt a trial-to-paid funnel for a similar move, short case study here. Worth a look?"

Operations: "Noticed [number] warehouse roles opened in [region] this month. I set up our second site from scratch and [cut pick errors by X], plan attached. Open to a 10-minute call next week?"

Customer success: "Your post about renewals being the team's focus this year stuck with me. I ran a save program that [kept X of our largest accounts], one-pager here. Who's the right person to send this to?"

Engineering: "Read your team's write-up on moving to event-driven billing. I led a similar migration, short summary here. Open to me sending a few notes on what we'd do differently?"
locked.prompt:
Using the 3-sentence structure (why them, one proof point with a link, one easy ask), write 3 cold emails for me for these targets:
1. [Company], [manager title], [what I noticed]
2. [Company], [manager title], [what I noticed]
3. [Company], [manager title], [what I noticed]

My role: [target job title]. My results to choose from: [list results].
Match the best result to each company. Each email under 75 words, with a different easy ask each time. Add one subject line per email.

locked.title: Step 7: Track every send and plan your next move
locked.body:
Cold email is a numbers-and-notes game, so keep a simple tracker. A spreadsheet with these columns is enough: company, person, title, how you found them, date sent, subject line used, opening angle used, proof link, reply (yes/no), next step, date of next step.

Once you have sent ten or so, look at the pattern. Which opening angles got replies? Which asks? Did a certain proof type get more clicks or answers? Keep what works and drop the rest. Never email the same person twice with the same note, and never email two people at one company on the same day.

If someone says "not me," thank them and ask who is. If someone says "not now," note a date to check back in a couple of months with something new to show.
locked.prompt:
Here's my cold email tracker so far: [paste rows: company, person, opening angle, ask used, proof type, replied yes/no].

Look for patterns in what got replies and what didn't. Tell me which opening angles and asks to keep using, which to drop, and suggest 3 new angles to test on my next 10 emails. Then list who I should check back with and when, based on the dates I sent.

guides.tip: Remote teams run on written communication. Your cold email is a writing sample, so keep it tidy, clear and free of filler. Mention the time zone you work in if it matches theirs.

guides.intro:
Remote postings often draw applicants from many places, so the application pile can get large. A quiet, well-written note to the team helps you stand out without skipping steps.

This guide walks you through both tracks calmly: a tailored application, then a short direct message, plus a simple weekly rhythm.

free.title: Step 1: Understand why you need both tracks
free.body:
Going direct does not mean skipping the process. Most companies still need your application in their system before they can interview or hire you. Recruiters work from it. Legal and HR need it. So you apply, every time.

But an application alone is one file among many. A real person reading your name in their inbox, linked to that same application, is a second signal. The two tracks work together: the application makes you official, the direct note makes you noticed.

The rule for this guide: for every role you truly want, do Track A (apply properly) and Track B (reach one or two humans) on the same day. Not one or the other. Both.
free.prompt:
I'm applying for [job title] at [company]. Here's the job post: [paste it].

Help me plan a two-track approach. Track A: list exactly what I need for a strong online application (which resume points to move up, keywords from the post to include, any screening questions to prepare for). Track B: list the 2 or 3 types of people at the company I should reach out to after applying (by title, based on how this team is likely organized), and why each one. Keep it practical and short.

free.title: Step 2: Track A, apply properly in 20 minutes
free.body:
A rushed application weakens both tracks, because the person you contact may look you up in the system. Make it count.

The 20-minute tailoring routine: (1) Read the post and highlight the top five requirements. (2) Make sure each one appears in your resume in their words, where true. (3) Move your two most relevant results into the top third of the page. (4) Rewrite your summary as one or two lines aimed at this role. (5) Answer screening questions with specifics, not "yes." (6) Save the exact resume version you sent, named with the company and date.

If there is an optional cover letter box, use it for three short paragraphs: why this role, your best matching result, and what you would focus on first. Short beats long.
free.prompt:
Here's my resume: [paste resume]. Here's the job post: [paste job post].

1. List the top 5 requirements in the post.
2. For each, show where my resume already covers it, or suggest an honest rewrite of an existing bullet using their wording (don't invent experience).
3. Rewrite my summary as 2 lines aimed at this role.
4. Suggest which 2 results should move to the top third of the page.
5. Write a 3-paragraph cover note under 150 words: why this role, my best matching result, what I'd focus on first.

free.title: Step 3: Track B, reach a human the same day
free.body:
Once the application is in, find one or two people to contact. Good order: the likely hiring manager first (the person the role reports to), then a team lead or peer on that team, then the recruiter for that role if one is named.

To find them yourself, search LinkedIn for the company plus the team name, check the company's team or about page, look at who posted the job, and read recent press releases or blog posts for names.

Your note mentions that you already applied, which tells them you respect the process. Keep it short: "I just applied for the [role] opening and wanted to put a face to the application. [One matching result]. Happy to share more if useful." Send it as a LinkedIn message or email, whichever you can reach.
free.prompt:
I just applied for [job title] at [company]. I want to send a short note to [person's name and title].

What I know about them or their team: [notes].
My best matching result: [result].

Write 2 versions of a note under 70 words: one for LinkedIn (no subject), one for email (with a short subject line). Both should mention I've already applied, give one specific result, and end with a low-pressure line. Also write a shorter version for a recruiter that asks if they need anything else from me.

locked.title: Step 4: Set up a two-track tracker
locked.body:
With two tracks per role, things get lost fast. One row per role, with these columns: company, role, date applied, resume version, application status, person 1 (name, title, channel), date contacted, person 2, date contacted, any reply, next action, next action date.

Color code it simply. Gray: applied only. Yellow: applied and contacted. Green: a human replied. Red: closed or rejected.

The goal is no gray rows for roles you care about. If a role is worth applying to, it is worth one human note. If it is not worth a note, ask whether it is worth the application at all. That question alone often sharpens a search.
locked.prompt: Create a two-track job search tracker I can paste into Google Sheets. Columns: Company, Role, Date applied, Resume version, Application status, Contact 1 name, Contact 1 title, Contact 1 channel, Contact 1 date, Contact 2 name, Contact 2 title, Contact 2 channel, Contact 2 date, Reply (Y/N), Next action, Next action date. Add 3 example rows using made-up companies so I can see how to fill it in, plus a short note on simple color coding (applied only / applied and contacted / human replied / closed).

locked.title: Step 5: Let Scout run both tracks for you
locked.body:
Running two tracks on every role takes time. Scout can do both. It finds jobs that match you and applies for you, adding your Showcase link to each application. A Showcase is a personal web page built for one job or one company, with many designs to choose from.

Then Scout finds people at that company, like the hiring manager or team leads, and reaches out with a short note and your Showcase, in small paced waves. You, or someone you authorize, approve the sends. Scout follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief when a company replies, and sends you a weekly report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=apply-direct-the-two-track-job-search&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, apply and reach out for this job

locked.title: Step 6: Handle replies on either track
locked.body:
Replies can come from the system (an auto email, a screening invite) or from a person you contacted. Treat both seriously and connect them.

If the hiring manager replies first, thank them, confirm you applied, and offer times or ask what they need. If a recruiter reaches out from the application, mention that you also connected with the manager, briefly and without pressure: "I also sent [Name] a short note, glad to be talking with you." It shows initiative, not end-running.

If you get a rejection from the system but a person was warm, you can reply to that person kindly: "I saw the role moved forward without me. I'd still love to stay in touch for future openings on your team." Doors close slower than portals do.
locked.prompt:
I applied for [role] at [company] and also contacted [person and title]. Now this happened: [paste the reply or describe it: recruiter screening invite, manager reply, auto rejection, etc.].

Write a short, professional reply (under 90 words) that fits the situation, connects both tracks naturally if it helps, and suggests a clear next step. If it's a rejection, write a gracious note that keeps the door open with the person I contacted.

locked.title: Step 7: Run a weekly two-track rhythm
locked.body:
Make it a habit, not a burst. A simple week: Monday, pick five to eight roles worth both tracks. Tuesday and Wednesday, apply and send the same-day notes. Thursday, follow up once on anyone contacted a week earlier with something new (a short idea, a relevant article, a project update). Friday, update your tracker and review.

In the Friday review, ask three questions. Which roles got a human reply, and what was different about them? Are any rows still gray? Which titles or company types keep responding, and should you lean into them?

Keep the volume steady and the quality high. Fewer roles done on both tracks will usually teach you more than many roles done on one.
locked.prompt:
Here's my two-track tracker for the last [number] weeks: [paste rows].

Review it and tell me: which roles got human replies and what they had in common, which rows are still "applied only" and worth a note, who's due a follow-up this week, and 3 changes to make next week. Then draft a Monday-to-Friday plan for next week with specific tasks per day.

guides.tip: For remote roles, mention your time zone and overlap hours in your direct note. It answers a question every remote manager has before they ask it.

guides.title: When Nobody Answers: The Go-to-the-Source Plan for Silent Companies
guides.blurb: A calm, structured plan for when remote teams don't reply.
inside: Why silence is not a no, and what it usually means
A follow-up sequence with four ready-to-send messages
How to map the people at a company into waves
Fresh reasons to reach out that are not "just checking in"
When to stop, and how to close the loop kindly
A per-company plan you can reuse
guides.intro:
Remote teams work across time zones and tools, so messages can slip past easily. Silence from a remote company often just means your note landed at a bad moment.

This guide gives you a steady follow-up sequence and a wave plan for reaching the right people, without overdoing it.

free.title: Step 1: Reset how you read silence
free.body:
One unanswered email ends most job searches at that company. People assume silence means no. Usually it means busy, buried, on vacation, wrong person, or "meant to reply."

So silence is information, not a verdict. It tells you to do one of three things: follow up with the same person, go to a different person, or go to the source (the person who actually owns the problem the role solves).

Before you do anything, check your first message. Was it short? Did it have a clear ask? Was it sent to the person who owns the role, or to a general inbox? If the first message was weak, the fix is a better second message, not a louder one.
free.prompt:
I reached out to [person and title] at [company] about [role] on [date] and haven't heard back. Here's what I sent: [paste message].

Be honest: rate my message on length, clarity of the ask, and how specific it was to them. Then tell me the 3 most likely reasons for silence based on who I sent it to, and whether my next move should be a follow-up to the same person, a note to someone else, or both.

free.title: Step 2: Send a follow-up sequence, not a nudge
free.body:
"Just checking in" gives them nothing new to answer. Each follow-up should add something. Here is a simple, polite sequence for one person:

Follow-up 1 (about 4 to 5 business days later): reply on the same thread, one or two lines, with a new piece of value. "One more thought on [topic]: [short idea]."

Follow-up 2 (about a week after that): share something useful. A relevant article, a short teardown of their product, or a quick plan for one problem.

Follow-up 3 (about a week after that): the easy out. "If the timing's off or I should talk to someone else, just say so and I'll stop here." This often gets a reply because it is easy to answer.

Then stop with that person. Three follow-ups is plenty.
free.prompt:
I sent this note to [person and title] at [company] about [role]: [paste original]. No reply yet.

Write a 3-message follow-up sequence for the same thread. Message 1: under 40 words with one new idea about [topic I know they care about]. Message 2: under 60 words sharing something useful (suggest what, based on the role). Message 3: under 40 words, a polite easy-out that asks if I should talk to someone else. No "just checking in," no guilt, no pressure.

free.title: Step 3: Map the company into waves
free.body:
If one person is silent, there are others. List the people connected to the role and group them into waves.

Wave 1: the likely hiring manager (who the role reports to). Wave 2: a team lead or senior peer on that team, and the recruiter for that role. Wave 3: the manager's boss or a leader of the department, and someone in a neighboring team that works closely with it.

Find them yourself on LinkedIn (search the company plus the team name), the company's team or leadership page, conference talks, podcasts, press releases and the company blog.

Move to the next wave only after the current wave's follow-ups are done. Never message everyone on the same day. It looks like spam and makes people compare notes.
free.prompt:
I'm targeting the [role] role at [company], probably on the [team] team. Here's what I know about the company's structure: [notes, names I've found].

Help me build a 3-wave outreach map. Wave 1: likely hiring manager title. Wave 2: 2 or 3 titles of team leads, peers or the recruiter. Wave 3: 1 or 2 senior or adjacent titles. For each, explain why they'd care, what angle to take with them, and how to find them using LinkedIn search, the company website or press. Don't make up names.

locked.title: Step 4: Use a fresh reason each time
locked.body:
Every new message, to the same person or a new one, needs a reason to exist. Here are angles that give a busy person something new:

1. A news hook: they launched something, raised money, opened an office, posted a new role. 2. A short idea: "Saw your onboarding flow, here's one thing I'd test." 3. A useful share: an article, tool or benchmark relevant to their problem. 4. A referral angle: "[Name] on your team suggested I reach out" (only if true). 5. A project update: you finished a course, shipped a side project or got a result that fits the role. 6. A question about their work they'd enjoy answering. 7. A congratulations on something real.

When you move to Wave 2 or 3, say who you already tried, kindly: "I sent a note to [Name] but know things get busy, so wanted to reach you too." It shows honesty, not end-running.
locked.prompt:
I'm moving to my next wave of outreach at [company] for the [role] role. Wave 1 was [name, title], no reply after 3 follow-ups. Now I want to reach [new person's title] on [team].

Recent things I know about the company: [news, posts, launches].
What I can offer: [a result, short idea or project].

Write a first note to this new person under 80 words. Mention briefly and kindly that I'd reached out to [Wave 1 person]. Use one fresh reason to write from the list: news hook, short idea, useful share, project update, or a real question. Give me 2 versions with different angles.

locked.title: Step 5: Let Scout run your waves and follow-ups
locked.body:
Keeping track of waves, follow-up dates and fresh angles across many companies is a lot. Scout handles it. It finds people at your target company, like hiring managers and team leads, and reaches out in small, paced waves with a short note and your Showcase, a personal web page built for one job or one company.

You, or someone you authorize, approve every send. Scout follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, and gives you a prep brief on the company when they reply. Each week you get a report of everything it did, so you always know what's next for each company.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=when-nobody-answers-the-go-to-the-source-plan&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, what's next for [Company]?

locked.title: Step 6: Build a one-page plan for each silent company
locked.body:
For any company you really want, write a short plan so you never wonder what to do next. Include: the role and why you want it, the three waves of people with titles and how you found them, dates for each message and follow-up, the fresh angle for each message, and a stop date.

Also keep one alternate path: another open role at the same company, a sister team, or a future opening to watch. Silence on one role is not silence from the whole company.

And keep a few companies running in parallel. When you only have one target, every silent day feels personal. When you have eight, silence at one is just a normal Tuesday.
locked.prompt:
Build me a one-page outreach plan for [company], [role]. My start date is [date].

Include: a 1-line reason I want this role; Wave 1, 2 and 3 with titles and how to find each; a calendar of messages and follow-ups with business-day spacing (no more than one message per person per week, and waves at least a week apart); a fresh angle for each message; a stop date; and one alternate path at the same company. Format it as a simple table I can paste into a doc.

locked.title: Step 7: Know when to stop, and close the loop well
locked.body:
Persistence is good. Pestering is not. A reasonable limit: up to three follow-ups per person, up to three waves per company, then pause.

When you pause, send one short closing note to the person you most hoped to reach: "I'll stop filling your inbox. If [team] ever needs someone for [problem], I'd love to hear from you. Wishing you a great launch." Then set a reminder for a couple of months out. Check for new roles, news, or a new person on the team, and start fresh with a new reason.

If anyone tells you no or asks you to stop, stop right away and thank them. Mark it in your tracker so you never contact them again by mistake.
locked.prompt:
I've finished my outreach waves at [company] for [role] with no reply. The person I most hoped to reach is [name, title].

Write a short, gracious closing note under 50 words that leaves the door open without guilt. Then suggest 3 signals I should watch for over the next few months that would give me a good, fresh reason to reach out again.

guides.tip: Time your follow-ups for the start of their workday in their time zone. A message at the top of the inbox is more likely to be read.

guides.title: Job Search While Employed: The Quiet Plan That Fits Around Your Day
guides.blurb: A calm way to find a remote role while you're still employed.
inside: A confidentiality checklist so your current job stays safe
A 3-hours-a-week schedule that actually holds up
How to update LinkedIn without tipping anyone off
Scripts for scheduling interviews around work
What to say when asked "why are you leaving?"
How to keep your energy (and your current job) intact
guides.intro:
If you're aiming for a remote role, you can search more quietly than ever: video interviews from home, no commute excuses, and flexible hours.

This guide helps you keep your search separate from your current job, fit it into a calm weekly routine, and handle interviews without stress.

free.title: Step 1: Lock down your search before you start
free.body:
A quiet search starts with a few protections. Do these first.

Confidentiality checklist: use a personal email and phone for everything, never your work accounts. Never search or apply on a work laptop or work Wi-Fi. Don't store your resume in company drives. On LinkedIn, turn off profile update notifications to your network before you edit anything, and if you use the "open to work" setting, choose the recruiters-only option rather than the public photo frame. Don't tell coworkers, even friendly ones. Check your employment agreement for non-compete or non-solicit terms so you know your limits, and if anything is unclear, ask an employment lawyer.

Then pick your references carefully: former managers and colleagues who have left the company, not current ones. Tell employers up front that your search is confidential and that they shouldn't contact your current employer.
free.prompt:
I'm job searching while employed as a [current title] at a [type of company]. I need to keep it confidential.

Give me a confidentiality checklist tailored to me covering: email and devices, LinkedIn settings (step by step, using the current settings names as best you know them, and tell me to verify in the app), what to say if a recruiter calls during work hours, how to handle references, and what to look for in my employment agreement. Keep it practical and short.

free.title: Step 2: Use a 3-hours-a-week schedule
free.body:
Searching while employed fails when it is a vague "I'll do it this weekend." Give it a small, fixed slot instead. About three hours a week, split into short sessions, is enough to stay in motion.

A sample week: Monday evening, 30 minutes to review new postings and pick two or three roles. Wednesday morning before work, 45 minutes to tailor and apply to one or two. Thursday at lunch (off-site, on your phone), 15 minutes to send one or two direct notes to people at those companies. Saturday, 60 minutes for the bigger task of the week: a resume update, a portfolio piece, a networking coffee. Sunday, 15 minutes to update your tracker and plan next week.

Protect these slots like meetings. Short and steady beats long and occasional, especially when your day job is draining.
free.prompt:
I work [hours and schedule, e.g. 9 to 6 Monday to Friday, hybrid with office days Tue/Thu]. I have about [number] hours a week for a job search and my energy is lowest [time of day].

Build me a weekly job search schedule with short sessions that fit around my job. For each session give the time, length, exact task, and what "done" looks like. Include one weekly review. Make sure nothing happens during work hours or on work devices.

free.title: Step 3: Update your profile quietly
free.body:
Your LinkedIn and resume need to work for recruiters without looking like a flare to your boss. The trick is to make changes that look like normal professional upkeep.

Do: turn off update notifications first. Rewrite your headline to describe what you do and the value you bring, not "seeking new opportunities." Add recent results to your current role. Refresh your skills list with the keywords your target roles use. Post or comment occasionally on your industry, which looks like engagement, not a search.

Don't: announce anything, change your title to something you don't hold, or suddenly connect with every recruiter in your field in one day.

For your resume, keep a master version and make a short tailored copy for each role, saved on your personal drive.
free.prompt:
Here is my current LinkedIn headline and About section: [paste]. I'm a [current title] looking to move into [target roles], and I'm searching confidentially.

Rewrite my headline (under 220 characters) and About section (under 150 words) so they attract recruiters for [target roles] using the right keywords, but read like normal professional upkeep, not a job search. No phrases like "open to opportunities" or "seeking." Suggest 3 recent results I could add to my current role based on: [list a few accomplishments].

locked.title: Step 4: Schedule interviews without raising eyebrows
locked.body:
Interviews are where quiet searches get noticed. A few habits help.

Ask for early morning, lunch or late-day slots, and say why plainly: "I'm currently employed, so 8 a.m. or after 5 works best. I'm flexible on video." Most employers understand. Cluster interviews on the same day when you can, and take a personal day or half day for final rounds rather than many vague absences. Take video calls from home, your car or a booked room outside the office, never a work meeting room. Keep a neutral change of clothes handy if your office is casual.

You don't owe your employer a reason for using your time off, and you shouldn't invent a fake one. "I have a personal appointment" is honest and enough.
locked.prompt:
A recruiter from [company] wants to schedule a [phone screen / video interview / onsite] for [role]. I'm employed and my workday is [hours].

Write a short, friendly reply that proposes 3 time options outside my core work hours (early morning, lunch or late afternoon), mentions I'm currently employed and asks for confidentiality, and offers video as an option. Then write a second version for a final round where I'll take a half day.

locked.title: Step 5: Let Scout run your search in the background
locked.body:
When your day job takes most of your energy, a background helper is the point. Scout runs your search quietly while you work. It builds your Career ID and a career diagnosis, finds jobs that match you and applies for you, adding your Showcase link. A Showcase is a personal web page built for one job or one company.

Scout can also find people at your target companies and reach out with a short note and your Showcase, in small paced waves. Nothing sends until you, or someone you authorize, approves it, so you stay in control of what goes out and to whom. Scout follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief when a company replies, and sends one weekly report you can read on your own time.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=job-search-while-employed-the-quiet-plan&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, run my search quietly in the background

locked.title: Step 6: Answer "why are you leaving?" well
locked.body:
If your manager is the reason, don't say so. Interviewers listen for whether you will talk about them the same way one day. Speak about what you're moving toward, not what you're running from.

A simple formula: what you've done and liked in your current role, what you want more of, and why this role offers it. Example: "I've learned a lot about running campaigns end to end. I'm looking for a role with more ownership over strategy, and this team gives its marketers that."

Prepare short answers to the follow-ups too: "How does your manager describe you?" (use real feedback from reviews). "Why now?" (growth, scope, a skill you want to build). "Are you interviewing elsewhere?" (a calm yes, if true, without details).
locked.prompt:
I'm leaving my job as a [current title] partly because [honest reason, e.g. micromanagement, no growth, burnout]. I'm interviewing for [target role] at [company].

Write 3 versions of my answer to "Why are you leaving?" under 60 words each that focus on what I'm moving toward, not what I'm escaping, and never criticize my manager or company. Also write short honest answers to: "How would your manager describe you?" (using this real feedback: [paste]) and "Why now?"

locked.title: Step 7: Protect your energy and your current job
locked.body:
A quiet search is a marathon. Keep doing solid work in your current role: it protects your income, your reference and your peace of mind. Strong recent results also make better interview stories.

When work is rough, small boundaries help. Batch your replies to "quick sync?" messages, write down your wins weekly (they feed your resume), and keep searching tasks out of your work brain by using a separate tracker and phone notes.

Every two weeks, do a short check-in: How many hours did I put in? Did anything get a reply? Am I still targeting the right roles? Is the search making my days worse or better? If it's dragging you down, shrink the weekly time rather than quitting. Steady wins.

When an offer comes, resign in person, keep it short and gracious, and leave on good terms.
locked.prompt:
I've been searching quietly for [number] weeks while employed. Here's my tracker and how I'm feeling: [paste tracker rows and a few honest notes].

Give me a short two-week check-in: what's working, what to cut, whether my target roles still make sense, and a lighter or heavier plan for the next two weeks depending on my energy. Also draft a short, gracious resignation message I can adapt when the time comes.

guides.tip: If you work from home now, take interviews from a different room or background than your work calls. It keeps the two separate in your head and on screen.

guides.title: The 5-Minute Company Prep Brief: Never Freeze on "What Do You Know About Us?"
guides.blurb: A calm, quick prep brief for remote interviews, so you're ready on camera.
inside: The 5-part brief: what they do, their moat, their problem, who they help, the business
Exactly where to look in 5 minutes
A 3-sentence answer to "what do you know about us?"
Smart questions that come from your homework
A deeper 30-minute version for final rounds
A reusable brief template
guides.intro:
Remote interviews often start right on time with little small talk, so the company questions come fast. Having your notes ready makes all the difference.

This guide walks you through a quiet five-minute research routine and a simple answer format, plus questions about how the team works remotely.

free.title: Step 1: Learn the five parts of a prep brief
free.body:
"So, what do you know about us?" is not a trick. It checks whether you care enough to look. Freezing happens when you have read a lot but organized nothing. A prep brief fixes that with five short answers:

1. What they do: one plain sentence, no jargon. 2. Who they help: their main customers. 3. Their moat: why customers pick them over others (price, product, brand, network, speed, a niche). 4. Their problem right now: what they are trying to fix or grow, often visible in news and job posts. 5. The business: rough size, how they make money, recent changes like funding, new leadership or a launch.

Write each in one or two lines. That's the whole brief. If you can say these five things calmly, you'll sound prepared.
free.prompt:
Help me build a 5-part prep brief for [company]. Here's what I've gathered: [paste notes from their website, LinkedIn, recent news and the job post].

Give me, in 1 to 2 plain lines each: (1) what they do, (2) who they help, (3) their likely moat versus competitors, (4) the problem they seem focused on right now, (5) business basics (how they make money, rough stage, recent changes). Only use what's in my notes, and mark anything that's your inference with "(guess)" so I can verify it.

free.title: Step 2: Run the 5-minute research sweep
free.body:
You don't need hours. Set a timer and check these in order:

Minute 1: Their homepage and "about" page. Copy the one-line description they use for themselves. Minute 2: Their product or pricing page. Who is it for and how do they charge? Minute 3: News. Search the company name and filter to recent results. Look for launches, funding, partnerships, layoffs or new executives. Minute 4: The job post and their careers page. Which teams are hiring? Hiring patterns show priorities. Minute 5: The company and interviewer LinkedIn pages. Recent posts, the interviewer's background, and how long they've been there.

Write one line per minute as you go. Then feed your notes into the Step 1 prompt. Five minutes of focused looking beats an hour of browsing.
free.prompt: I have 5 minutes to research [company] before an interview for [role] with [interviewer name and title, if known]. Give me a checklist of exactly what to look for on: their homepage, product or pricing page, recent news, their careers page, and LinkedIn (company and interviewer). For each, give me the one question to answer and the one line I should write down. Format it as a 5-row table I can fill in.

free.title: Step 3: Turn your brief into a calm answer
free.body:
Now make your notes speakable. A strong answer to "what do you know about us?" has three sentences: what they do and for whom, something recent that caught your eye, and how it connects to the role.

Example shape: "You help [customer type] [do what] through [product], and what stands out is [moat]. I saw [recent news or hiring pattern], which suggests [problem or goal]. That's part of why this role interests me, because [your related experience]."

Say it out loud three times. Don't memorize word for word, just the three beats. End by turning it back to them: "Is that close to how you'd describe where things are now?" It invites a conversation and shows you're curious, not reciting.
free.prompt:
Here's my prep brief for [company]: [paste 5-part brief]. I'm interviewing for [role]. My most relevant experience is [1 or 2 lines].

Write 3 versions of my answer to "What do you know about us?" Each must be 3 sentences, under 70 words, sound natural when spoken, mention one specific recent detail, connect to my experience, and end with a short question back to the interviewer. Avoid sounding like I'm reading their website back to them.

locked.title: Step 4: Turn homework into smart questions
locked.body:
The best questions show you did the research and want to understand more. Each one should start from a fact you found.

Patterns to use: "I saw you [launched / hired / expanded] X. How has that changed what this team focuses on?" "Your [pricing / product / customer] seems built around Y. What do customers say makes you hard to replace?" "The job post mentions Z. What does great look like there in the first 90 days?" "What's the biggest thing standing between the team and [goal you spotted]?" "How does this role work with [team you saw hiring]?"

Prepare five. You'll use two or three. Save the one about challenges for the hiring manager, since they'll have the most honest answer, and ask the recruiter about process and timeline.
locked.prompt: Based on this prep brief for [company]: [paste brief], and this job post: [paste key parts], write 8 interview questions for me to ask. Each must reference a specific fact from my brief or the post. Label which ones are best for a recruiter, the hiring manager, or a peer interviewer. Avoid questions about salary, perks or anything I could answer by reading their website.

locked.body:
If you're reaching out to many companies, keeping up with the homework is the hard part. Scout handles it. When a company replies to your outreach, Scout gives you a prep brief on them: what they do, their moat, the problem they solve and who they help, so you walk in ready.

Scout also builds your Career ID, finds matching jobs and applies for you, builds Showcases (a personal web page for one job or one company), and reaches out to people at target companies in small paced waves, with you, or someone you authorize, approving every send. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, and sends a weekly report.

locked.prompt: Scout, prep me for [Company]

locked.title: Step 6: Go deeper for final rounds (the 30-minute version)
locked.body:
Final rounds deserve more than five minutes. Add these layers to your brief:

Competitors: name two or three and one way this company differs from each. Customers: read two or three customer stories or reviews to learn what people value and complain about. Leadership: skim recent interviews, podcasts or posts by the CEO or department head to hear their priorities in their own words. Money: if public, glance at the latest earnings summary. If private, look for funding news and what investors said it's for. Your team: look up each interviewer and note one thing in common or worth asking about.

Then write a one-paragraph "first 90 days" idea: what you'd learn, what you'd improve, and one early win. Bring it as talking points, not a lecture.
locked.prompt:
I have a final-round interview for [role] at [company] with [list interviewers and titles]. Here's my research: [paste notes on competitors, customers, leadership comments, funding or earnings, interviewer backgrounds].

Build me a deeper prep brief with: a 3-competitor comparison (one difference each), what customers value and complain about, the leadership's top 3 stated priorities, one talking point per interviewer, and a short first-90-days idea with one early win. Mark anything that's inference with "(guess)".

locked.title: Step 7: Keep a brief library and review after each interview
locked.body:
Save every brief in one folder, one doc per company. After each interview, add three lines while it's fresh: what they asked, what landed, and what surprised you.

Those notes pay off fast. Second-round interviews often repeat themes from the first, and companies in the same industry tend to ask similar questions. Over a few weeks, your library becomes a cheat sheet for your whole target market: common problems, common moats, common questions.

Before each new interview, open the closest brief you already have and update it rather than starting from scratch. And send a short thank-you note within a day that mentions one specific thing from the conversation.
locked.prompt:
I just finished an interview for [role] at [company] with [interviewer]. Here's what happened: [notes on questions asked, what went well, what didn't, anything surprising].

1. Add a short "post-interview" section to my prep brief with lessons learned.
2. Predict 3 topics likely to come up in the next round.
3. Write a thank-you note under 90 words that references one specific thing we discussed.

guides.tip: Check the company's careers page for how they describe remote work: time zones, tools, meeting habits. Asking about it shows you understand what makes remote teams work.

guides.title: Laid Off? Your First-Week Plan, Day by Day
guides.blurb: A calm first-week plan after a layoff, with remote roles in view.
inside: A day-one checklist for money, paperwork and benefits
How to take stock of your career before you apply anywhere
Scripts for telling your network, and a LinkedIn post template
How to explain the layoff in interviews, simply
A day-by-day plan for week one
A sustainable routine for the weeks after
guides.intro:
If you're laid off and hoping for remote work, the first week matters. Remote roles can draw many applicants, so a clear target and a strong story help you stand out.

This guide takes you through the first week step by step, calmly, from paperwork to your first focused remote applications.

free.title: Step 1: Handle the practical stuff first (Day 1)
free.body:
A layoff is a shock. Before you think about your next job, take care of the things with deadlines. Doing them first clears your head.

Day one checklist: Read your separation paperwork slowly and note every date. Don't sign a severance agreement on the spot. Check the paperwork for how long you have to review it, ask HR any questions, and consider having an employment lawyer look at it before you sign. Find out when your pay, any severance and unused vacation will be paid. Check your health coverage end date and ask HR or your benefits administrator about your options to continue it. Look up unemployment benefits on your state's official unemployment website and apply as soon as their rules allow. Rules and timing vary by state, so go by what the official site says. Download your pay stubs, benefits info and any performance reviews you're allowed to keep. Save personal contacts you've built, if you're allowed. Ask your manager or HR if they'll be a reference.

Then look at your monthly costs and write down how many months of runway you have.
free.prompt:
I was just laid off from my job as a [title] at a [type of company] in [state or country]. Here's what I was given: [summarize the separation paperwork: severance offered, deadlines, benefits end date, final pay date].

Make me a day-one checklist with deadlines in date order. Include questions I should ask HR before signing anything, what to look into for health coverage and unemployment benefits in my location (tell me to verify with official sources), and what records to save. Don't give legal advice, but flag anything I should have a professional review.

free.title: Step 2: Take stock before you apply (Day 2)
free.body:
The urge after a layoff is to apply to everything that day. Resist it for one day. Scattered applications lead to scattered results, and you'll spend weeks undoing a rushed start.

Instead, take stock. Write down: your last three roles and the two or three results you're proudest of in each. The parts of your job you loved and the parts you won't miss. Skills people kept coming to you for. The job titles that fit what you actually did (often more than one). Your must-haves for the next role: pay floor, location or remote, schedule, industry.

Then do an honest diagnosis. Is your target the same role at a new company, a step up, or a pivot? Each needs a different search. Knowing which one you're running is the most useful thing you can do this week.
free.prompt:
I was just laid off. Here's my background: [paste resume or summarize last 3 roles with key results]. What I loved: [list]. What I won't miss: [list]. My must-haves: [pay floor, location or remote, schedule, industries].

Give me an honest career diagnosis: (1) 3 to 5 job titles my experience genuinely supports, (2) whether I look best positioned for the same role, a step up, or a pivot, and why, (3) my 3 strongest selling points, (4) any gaps a hiring manager might notice and how to address them. Be direct, not flattering.

free.title: Step 3: Tell your network the right way (Day 3)
free.body:
Your network is your fastest path to the next role, but only if people know what you want. A vague "I'm open to opportunities" is hard to help with. A specific ask is easy.

Write one LinkedIn post: what happened in one line (no blame), what you did and are proud of, the exact roles and types of companies you want, and a simple ask. Keep it short and positive.

Then send personal messages to 15 to 20 people: former managers, colleagues, clients, friends in your field. Make each message specific: "I'm looking for [role] at [type of company]. Do you know anyone at [company A or B], or anyone I should talk to?" Personal messages often do more than the public post.

Also reach out to coworkers laid off with you. Share leads with each other.
free.prompt:
I was laid off from [company] where I was a [title] for [time]. I'm proud of [1 or 2 results]. I'm looking for [target roles] at [types of companies], [location or remote].

Write: (1) a LinkedIn post under 150 words, positive, no blame, with a clear specific ask; (2) a personal message template under 80 words for former colleagues and managers that asks for one specific thing (an intro, a name, or a 15-minute call); (3) a short version for people I haven't talked to in a while that acknowledges the gap warmly.

locked.title: Step 4: Get your story and materials ready (Day 4)
locked.body:
Layoffs are common and most interviewers understand them. What they want is a short, calm explanation and a quick turn to what you bring. The formula: what happened in one line, what you accomplished, what you're looking for next. Example: "My role was eliminated in a company-wide restructuring. In two years I [result]. I'm looking for a [role] where I can [what you want to do more of]."

No bitterness, no long backstory, no apology. Practice it until it takes under 20 seconds.

Then update your materials for the target from Step 2: rewrite your resume headline and summary for the role you want, move your best results up, and update your LinkedIn headline. Make a short list of 20 target companies that fit your must-haves.
locked.prompt:
I was laid off from my role as [title] at [company] due to [reason as given, e.g. restructuring, budget cuts, team eliminated]. Key results: [list 2 or 3]. Target role: [title].

Write: (1) 3 versions of my layoff explanation for interviews, each under 50 words, calm and forward-looking; (2) a new resume summary of 2 lines for the target role; (3) a LinkedIn headline under 220 characters. Then suggest 3 types of companies to target based on my background, with 2 neutral example companies for each that I should verify are hiring.
