locked.body:
If you'd rather not run every piece yourself, Scout is built for this moment. Start by telling it what happened. Scout builds your Career ID and a career diagnosis, so you know which roles to go after and why.

Then it builds Showcases, a personal web page for one job or one company with many designs to choose from, finds matching jobs and applies for you with your Showcase link added. It can find people at your target companies, like hiring managers and team leads, and reach out with a short note and your Showcase in small, paced waves. You, or someone you authorize, approve every send. Scout follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief when a company replies, and sends a weekly report.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=laid-off-your-first-week-plan&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, I just got laid off. Where do I start?

locked.title: Step 6: Start applying with focus (Day 5)
locked.body:
Now you're ready to apply, with a clear target and a story. Pick five roles from your target list that fit your must-haves well. For each, tailor your resume to the post, apply, and then send one short note to a person on that team, mentioning you applied. Quality over quantity this first week.

Use the layoff wisely in outreach. It's honest and it explains why you're available now: "My team was cut in last week's restructuring, so I'm available sooner than most. I [result]. I've applied for your [role] and would love to be considered."

End the day by setting up job alerts for your top titles and locations on two or three job boards, so new roles come to you instead of you hunting every morning.
locked.prompt:
Here's a job post I want to apply for: [paste]. Here's my resume: [paste]. I was recently laid off from [company] due to [reason].

(1) Tailor 4 to 5 resume bullets to this post using only my real experience. (2) Write a short note under 70 words to the likely hiring manager that mentions I've applied, briefly and positively explains I'm available due to a layoff, and gives one matching result. (3) Suggest the best 3 search terms to set up job alerts for this type of role.

locked.title: Step 7: Build a routine for the weeks ahead
locked.body:
After week one, structure matters more than intensity. Searching is a job, but it shouldn't take every hour, or you'll burn out.

A sustainable day: a fixed start time. Two focused hours on applications and outreach. One hour on networking (calls, messages, coffee). One hour on skills or a portfolio piece. Then stop. Move your body, see people, keep normal sleep.

Each Friday, review: roles applied, people contacted, replies, interviews, and how you feel. Adjust your targets if nothing is landing after a few weeks. Revisit your budget monthly so money worry doesn't drive decisions.

And be kind to yourself. A layoff is a business decision, not a verdict on your worth. Many strong careers include one.
locked.prompt:
I'm [number] weeks into my job search after a layoff. Here's my week: [roles applied, people contacted, replies, interviews, and how I'm feeling].

Give me a short Friday review: what's working, what to change, whether my target roles still make sense, and a day-by-day plan for next week that includes a fixed start time, focused application blocks, networking, one skill-building block, and real time off. Keep it realistic for someone feeling [energy level].

guides.tip: On your resume, note which past roles were remote or distributed and what tools you used to collaborate. Remote hiring managers look for proof you already work well that way.

guides.title: Track your job search like a pro: the weekly report that answers 'any luck?'
guides.blurb: A calm weekly report for your remote search, so you always know where things stand.
inside: A one-tab tracker you can set up in 15 minutes
The five numbers worth counting every Friday
Three ready-to-send replies for the group chat
How to read your numbers and know what to fix
A follow-up schedule built into your tracker
A monthly reset so the search stops feeling stuck
guides.intro:
Remote roles can draw a lot of applicants, and replies can be slow. Without a tracker it's easy to lose threads or follow up too late.

This guide gives you a quiet, steady system: one tab, a Friday report, and a follow-up rhythm. It's built to keep a remote search organized without taking over your week.

free.title: Step 1: Build a one-tab tracker
free.body:
Open a blank spreadsheet. One tab, one row per opportunity. Use these columns: Company, Role, Link or source, Date applied, Person contacted (name and title), How you reached them, Last touch date, Next follow-up date, Stage, Notes.

Use only these stages: Saved, Applied, Reached out, Replied, Talking, Interviewing, Offer, Closed. If a row doesn't fit a stage, it's probably still Saved.

The tracker is not busywork. It's what turns a fuzzy, lonely search into something you can see. When you can see it, you can explain it, and you can fix it.
free.prompt:
I'm job searching and want a simple tracker. Here is a messy list of everything I've applied to or looked at so far:

[paste your list, emails, notes, anything]

Turn it into a table with these columns: Company, Role, Source, Date applied, Person contacted, How I reached them, Last touch date, Next follow-up date, Stage, Notes. Use only these stages: Saved, Applied, Reached out, Replied, Talking, Interviewing, Offer, Closed. If a date is missing, write 'unknown'. Set Next follow-up date to 7 days after the last touch for anything in Applied or Reached out. Output it as a table I can paste into a spreadsheet.

free.title: Step 2: Count five numbers every Friday
free.body:
Every Friday, take 15 minutes and count five things for the week: 1) Applications sent. 2) People contacted directly. 3) Replies of any kind (including no thanks). 4) Real conversations (calls, screens, interviews). 5) Follow-ups due next week.

Write them in a small box at the top of your tracker, one row per week. After three or four weeks you'll see a pattern, which is far more useful than a feeling.

Add one line under the numbers: 'This week I learned...' One sentence. That line is where your next move usually comes from.
free.prompt:
Here is my job search tracker for this week:

[paste the rows you touched this week]

Write me a short weekly report with: 1) the five counts (applications sent, people contacted, replies, real conversations, follow-ups due next week), 2) the two most promising opportunities and why, 3) anything that has gone quiet for more than 10 days, 4) one thing I learned, based on the notes. Keep it under 150 words and use plain language.

free.title: Step 3: Answer the group chat without the cringe
free.body:
Friends ask because they care, but 'any luck?' can sting when the answer is no. Having a ready reply takes the pressure off. Pick the one that fits your mood.

The quick update: 'Still going. Sent 8 applications this week, had 1 good call, following up on 2. I'll tell you when there's news.'

The ask for help: 'Honestly it's slow. I'm targeting [role] at companies like [A, B, C]. If anyone knows someone there, an intro would mean a lot.'

The boundary: 'I'm giving it my all, I just don't want to talk shop tonight. I'll share when something lands.'

The ask for help version is the most useful. Friends often want to help and don't know how. A specific role and three company names gives them something to do.
free.prompt: Write me 3 short replies (under 40 words each) to a friend in a group chat asking 'any luck with the job search?'. Here is my real status: [numbers from your weekly report]. I'm targeting [role] at companies like [company 1, 2, 3]. Version 1: a calm, honest update. Version 2: a specific ask for an intro. Version 3: a friendly boundary for when I don't want to talk about it. Sound like a normal person, not a LinkedIn post.

locked.title: Step 4: Read your numbers and know what to fix
locked.body:
Your weekly numbers tell you where the search is breaking. Use this as a guide.

Lots of applications, almost no replies: the problem is usually targeting or positioning. Apply to fewer, closer-fit roles and rewrite the top third of your resume for each title. Add direct outreach to a person for your best fits.

Replies but few real conversations: your first message or follow-up may not give people a reason to talk. Make the ask smaller and clearer, like a 15-minute call.

Conversations but no next rounds: the gap is likely in how you tell your story. Practice three proof stories out loud.

Low numbers across the board: it's a time problem, not a talent problem. Block two fixed sessions a week and protect them.
locked.prompt:
Here are my weekly job search numbers for the last [number] weeks:

[paste weeks with: applications, people contacted, replies, conversations, follow-ups]

I'm targeting [role] at [level] in [location or remote]. Look at the pattern and tell me: 1) the single biggest drop-off point, 2) the most likely reason, 3) three specific changes to test next week, ranked by effort, 4) what number I should watch to know if it worked. Be direct. Don't promise outcomes.

locked.title: Step 5: Build follow-ups into the tracker
locked.body:
Most silence isn't a no. People get busy. A follow-up schedule makes sure nothing dies just because you forgot.

Use this rhythm for each row: Day 0, apply or reach out. Day 6 or 7, a short nudge with one new piece of value (a relevant idea, a link to your work, a quick result). Day 14, a polite close-the-loop note. Then mark it Closed and move on, without guilt.

In your tracker, sort by Next follow-up date every Monday. That list is your to-do list for the week. A nudge can be as short as: 'Hi [Name], following up on my note about the [role]. I put together a quick idea on [topic] that might be useful. Happy to share if helpful.'
locked.prompt: Write two follow-up messages for this opportunity. Company: [company]. Role: [role]. Person: [name, title]. What I sent first: [paste]. Something useful I can add: [an idea, a result, a piece of work]. Message 1 goes on day 7: a short nudge under 70 words that adds that useful thing. Message 2 goes on day 14: a polite close-the-loop note under 50 words that leaves the door open. No guilt trips, no 'just checking in'.

locked.title: Step 6: Let Scout write the report for you
locked.body:
If keeping the tracker is the part you never get to, Scout can do the work and send you the report. Scout builds your Career ID, finds matching jobs and applies for you with a Showcase link (a personal page built for that job), reaches out to people at your target companies in small paced waves that you approve, and follows up.

Every week it gives you a report of everything it did: applications, Showcases, outreach, follow-ups, and when your Showcase was viewed. When a company replies, you get a prep brief on them. That report is also a pretty good answer for the group chat.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=track-your-search-like-a-pro-weekly-report&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, give me my weekly report

locked.title: Step 7: Do a monthly reset
locked.body:
Once a month, put your four weekly reports side by side. Ask three questions: What should I stop? What should I keep? What should I start?

Stop: the job boards, titles or company types that produced nothing after a full month. Keep: whatever produced replies or conversations, even one. Start: one new channel or angle, like reaching out to team leads directly, or targeting a new industry where your skills transfer.

Then clean the tracker. Close anything older than 30 days with no reply. Archive it in a second tab so the main tab only shows live chances. A clean tracker makes Monday feel lighter, and it makes the next 'any luck?' easier to answer.
locked.prompt:
Here are my last 4 weekly job search reports:

[paste them]

Run a monthly reset with me. Give me: 1) three things to stop doing, with the evidence from my reports, 2) two things to keep, 3) one new thing to start next month and exactly how to do it in under 2 hours a week, 4) a one-paragraph summary of my month I could share with a friend or mentor. Be honest and specific.

guides.tip: Add a Time zone column for each company. It helps you send follow-ups at a sensible hour for the person reading them.

guides.title: The career change positioning guide: turn your old title into a new angle
guides.blurb: Position your career change for remote roles, where your resume has to do all the talking.
inside: A skill bridge map from your old field to your new one
Six strong angles career changers can lead with
A rewrite formula for the top third of your resume
A weekend proof project to show, not tell
Where to look for bridge roles and companies
A three-part answer to 'why are you switching?'
guides.intro:
In a remote search, your resume and online presence often speak for you before anyone hears your voice. For a career changer, that means the translation has to be clear on paper.

This guide helps you map your skills, choose an angle and show proof in a way a remote hiring team can see at a glance.

free.title: Step 1: Build a skill bridge map
free.body:
Your experience isn't the problem. The words are. Screening tools and busy reviewers look for the language of the new field, and your resume speaks the language of the old one.

Pull up three job posts for the role you want. Highlight every skill, tool and outcome they mention. Then make two columns. Left: what the post asks for. Right: where you've already done that, in your old job, even under a different name. A teacher 'designs curriculum' and an instructional designer 'builds learning programs'. Same work, different words.

Any row with nothing on the right is a gap. Circle those. You'll close one of them in Step 4.
free.prompt:
I'm changing careers from [old role and industry] to [new role]. Here are 3 job posts for the new role:

[paste posts]

Here is my resume:

[paste resume]

Build a skill bridge map as a table with 3 columns: 1) what the job posts ask for, using their exact words, 2) where I have done something equivalent, quoting my experience, 3) how to rephrase my experience in the new field's language. Then list the real gaps where I have no matching experience. Do not invent experience I don't have.

free.title: Step 2: Pick your angle
free.body:
A switch reads stronger when you lead with one clear angle instead of apologizing for it. Pick the one that fits you best.

1) The insider: you know the customer or industry the new team serves (a nurse moving into health tech). 2) The transferable specialist: one skill carries over at full strength (a lawyer moving into compliance). 3) The other side of the table: you used to buy, use or be served by this function (a sales rep moving into product). 4) The side builder: you've already done the new work on your own time. 5) The bridge: you connect two teams that don't speak the same language. 6) The operator: you ran the messy real-world version of what they plan on paper.

Write one sentence: 'I'm a [new role] who brings [angle] from [old field].' That's your headline.
free.prompt: Here is my background: [paste a short summary or resume]. I'm moving into [new role] in [industry or type of company]. From these 6 angles (insider, transferable specialist, other side of the table, side builder, bridge, operator), pick the 2 that fit me best and explain why using my real experience. For each, write a one-line headline in this format: 'I'm a [new role] who brings [angle] from [old field].' Then tell me which type of company would value each angle most.

free.title: Step 3: Rewrite the top third of your resume
free.body:
Reviewers often decide quickly, based on the top of the page. For a career changer, that top third has to do the translating.

Headline: your new target title plus your angle, like 'Product Operations | Former Sales Lead who knows the customer'. Summary: three lines. Line one, what you do now in new-field terms. Line two, one proof result. Line three, why your background is an advantage.

Then go through your bullets. Keep the facts, change the framing. 'Managed a team of 6 retail associates' becomes 'Led a 6-person team, trained new hires and improved weekly scheduling', if that's true. Put the most transferable bullet first under each job. Move old-field jargon to the bottom or cut it.
free.prompt:
Rewrite the top third of my resume for a move into [new role]. My angle is: [your headline from Step 2]. Here is my current resume:

[paste]

Give me: 1) a new headline, 2) a 3-line summary (new-field terms, one real result, why my background helps), 3) my top 6 bullets rewritten in the new field's language and reordered by relevance. Keep every fact true. If a bullet has no number, suggest what I could measure but mark it [confirm]. Use these keywords where they honestly fit: [paste keywords from Step 1].

locked.title: Step 4: Close one gap with a weekend proof project
locked.body:
Nothing beats proof. Pick one gap from your skill bridge map and make a small piece of real work that shows you can do it. Keep it to one weekend.

Examples: moving into marketing, write a one-page campaign plan for a brand you like. Into data, clean a public dataset and write up three findings. Into product, write a short teardown of an app's onboarding with three improvement ideas. Into UX, redesign one screen and explain your choices. Into project management, turn a messy past project into a clean plan with timeline and risks.

Put it in a simple shareable doc or page. Add it to your resume under a 'Projects' heading and mention it in outreach. It answers the question 'can they actually do this?' before anyone asks.
locked.prompt: I'm moving from [old role] into [new role]. The biggest gap in my experience is [gap]. Suggest 3 weekend-sized proof projects (under 10 hours each) that would show I can do this work. For each: what to make, the steps, what tools I need (free ones preferred), and how to present it in one page. Then write the one-line resume entry for each project and a short sentence I can use in outreach to mention it.

locked.title: Step 5: Target bridge roles and bridge companies
locked.body:
The easiest switch is often a half-step. Two kinds of targets make the jump shorter.

Bridge companies: companies that serve your old industry. A former teacher fits edtech. A former restaurant manager fits restaurant software or food delivery. Your background is a plus there, not a question mark.

Bridge roles: titles that sit between the old and new world. Sales into customer success, then into product. Accounting into finance operations, then into data. Look for words like 'operations', 'enablement', 'implementation', 'specialist' or 'analyst' in the new field.

List 15 companies that sell to or serve your old industry. Check their careers pages for bridge titles. These are your first-priority targets.
locked.prompt: I'm switching from [old role in old industry] to [new role]. 1) List 10 types of companies that sell to or serve [old industry], with 2 well-known examples each. 2) List 6 bridge job titles that sit between [old role] and [new role], and what each one does. 3) For each bridge title, say which part of my background would stand out. 4) Give me 5 search phrases I can use on job boards and LinkedIn to find these roles.

locked.title: Step 6: Let Scout position you for each switch
locked.body:
If you'd rather not rebuild your story for every application, Scout can do it with you. Tell it where you're coming from and where you're going. It builds your Career ID and a career diagnosis, then makes a Showcase for each target job: a personal page built for that one role, which tells your switch story in the new field's language.

Scout finds matching jobs and applies for you with your Showcase link, and reaches out to hiring managers and team leads at your target companies in small paced waves. You approve the sends. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, and gives you a prep brief when a company replies.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=career-change-positioning-guide&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, I'm switching from [X] to [Y]

locked.title: Step 7: Nail the 'why are you switching?' answer
locked.body:
You will get this question. Have a short answer ready in three parts. Pull: what draws you to the new work, with a real moment that sparked it. Proof: what you've already done toward it (your proof project, a course, work you took on in your old job). Payoff: how your background makes you better at it than someone who never left the field.

Keep it under 60 seconds. Don't trash the old job, and don't apologize for it. Then prepare for two follow-ups: 'Won't you miss your old field?' and 'Why should we take a chance on you?' Answer both by pointing back to your angle and your proof.

Practice out loud three times. Record yourself once. It feels awkward and it helps.
locked.prompt: Help me answer 'Why are you switching careers?' in an interview. Old field: [old role]. New field: [new role]. What drew me in: [a real moment]. What I've already done toward it: [projects, courses, tasks]. My angle: [headline]. Write a 60-second answer in 3 parts: pull, proof, payoff. Then write short answers to 'Won't you miss your old field?' and 'Why should we take a chance on you?'. Sound confident, not defensive. Then ask me 3 tough follow-up questions so I can practice.

guides.tip: Mention remote-ready skills from your old job, like written updates, async handoffs or managing work across locations. They carry over to any field.

guides.title: The internship outreach playbook: no network, no problem
guides.blurb: How students can find and stand out for remote and local internships.
inside: How to build a list of 25 places that actually take interns
Turning classes, clubs and part-time jobs into a one-page profile
Three outreach emails a student can send today
How to find the right person, and how parents can help without hovering
A 15-minute call script for alumni and team leads
A weekly follow-up rhythm for the whole season
guides.intro:
Remote internships widen the options for students who don't live in a big city, but they can also draw applicants from everywhere.

This guide helps students build a focused target list, reach people directly and present themselves clearly, whether the internship is remote or down the road.

free.title: Step 1: Build a list of 25 real targets
free.body:
Mass applying to big-name programs is the most crowded path there is. Mix in places where a student can actually get noticed.

Aim for a list of 25 split like this: 5 well-known companies you'd love, 10 small or mid-size companies in your city or field, 5 places where alumni from your school work, and 5 nonprofits, labs, local agencies or family businesses. Smaller places often don't post internships at all, but many will say yes to a good, specific ask.

Where to look: your school's career center and job board, the alumni tool on LinkedIn (search your school, then filter by company and city), local business news, startup lists for your city, and professors who have industry contacts. Put each one in a spreadsheet with a column for why you picked it.
free.prompt: I'm a [year, e.g. sophomore] studying [major] at [school]. I want a summer internship in [city or remote] doing [type of work, or 'not sure yet, I like X and Y']. Help me build a target list of 25: 5 well-known companies, 10 small or mid-size companies in [city] in relevant fields, 5 types of nonprofits or local organizations, and 5 types of companies where graduates of my major often work. For each, say what an intern could realistically help with. Then give me 5 LinkedIn search ideas to find more.

free.title: Step 2: Make a one-page student profile
free.body:
Students often think they have nothing to show. Usually that's not true. Class projects, part-time jobs, clubs, sports, babysitting, a small online shop, volunteering: all of it shows skills like reliability, teamwork, writing or handling customers.

Write each one as a result, not a duty. 'Worked at an ice cream shop' becomes 'Served 100+ customers on weekend shifts and trained two new hires', if that's accurate. 'Group project' becomes 'Led a 4-person team that built a marketing plan for a local business, presented to the class'.

Top of the page: your name, school, major, graduation year, city, and one line on what you want, like 'Looking for a summer internship in marketing or operations'. Keep it to one page.
free.prompt:
Help me write a one-page internship resume. I'm [year] studying [major] at [school], graduating [year]. Here is everything I've done, messy is fine:

[list jobs, classes, projects, clubs, sports, volunteering, side projects]

Turn each into 1 to 2 bullets that start with an action verb and show a result. Don't invent numbers; where a number would help, mark it [add number]. Write a one-line goal at the top for an internship in [field]. Suggest which items to cut if it runs over one page.

free.title: Step 3: Send three kinds of outreach emails
free.body:
The shift that changes things: write to a person, not just a portal. Short, specific and polite wins. Here are three to adapt.

To an alum: 'Hi [Name], I'm a [year] at [school] studying [major]. I saw you work on [team] at [company]. I'm exploring [field] and would love 15 minutes to hear how you got started. Would a quick call in the next couple of weeks work?'

To a small company: 'Hi [Name], I'm a [major] student in [city]. I admire what [company] does with [specific thing]. I'm looking for a summer internship and could help with [2 concrete tasks]. Would you be open to a short chat?'

To a team lead at a bigger company: 'Hi [Name], I applied for the [program] and wanted to say hello directly. I'm especially interested in [team] because [reason]. Any advice for a student hoping to join?'
free.prompt: Write a short outreach email (under 100 words) from a student to [person's name, title] at [company]. Who they are to me: [alum of my school / no connection / met at an event]. About me: [year, major, school, one relevant thing I've done]. Why this company: [specific reason]. What I'm asking for: [15-minute call / advice / to be considered for a summer internship]. Two tasks I could help with: [task 1, task 2]. Tone: polite, confident, not stiff. Give me a subject line too.

locked.title: Step 4: Find the right person, and let parents open doors
locked.body:
Who to write to: at small companies, the founder or the head of the team you'd join. At bigger ones, a team lead, a recent hire from your school, or the campus recruiter. Find them on the company's team or about page, on LinkedIn (search company name plus your school), in press releases, or in event speaker lists.

Parents: your best move is intros, not writing the emails. Think about your own coworkers, clients, neighbors and friends. Send a short note: 'My [son/daughter] [Name] is a [major] student looking for a summer internship in [field]. Would you be open to a 15-minute call with her? [He/She] will reach out directly.' Then hand it to your kid to follow up.

The student should always send their own messages. Hiring teams want to hear from the person they'd hire.
locked.prompt: I'm a parent helping my [son/daughter], a [year] studying [major], find a summer internship in [field] in [city]. Help me: 1) brainstorm 10 types of people in my own network who might know someone in [field] (based on my job as [your job] and community [groups, clubs]), 2) write a short intro request under 60 words that I can send, 3) write the follow-up message my kid sends after I make the intro. Keep it respectful of everyone's time.

locked.title: Step 5: Run a 15-minute call like a pro
locked.body:
When someone says yes, be ready. Show up a minute early, have questions written down and keep it to the time you asked for.

A simple flow: 1) Thank them and say why you reached out (one sentence). 2) Ask two or three questions about their path and their team. 3) Ask what a summer intern could realistically help with there. 4) The ask: 'If your team ever takes interns, I'd love to be considered. Is there someone I should talk to or a way to apply?' 5) Thank them and end on time.

Good questions: What does a normal week look like on your team? What do you wish you'd known as a student? What skill should I build this year? Within 24 hours, send a thank-you email that mentions one thing you learned.
locked.prompt: I have a 15-minute call with [name, title] at [company]. I'm a [year] studying [major] looking for a summer internship in [field]. Here's what I know about them and the company: [paste anything from LinkedIn or the website]. Write me: 1) a one-sentence opener, 2) 6 smart questions (pick the 3 best), 3) a polite way to ask about internships near the end, 4) a thank-you email under 80 words that I can customize after the call.

locked.title: Step 6: Let Scout run the internship search with you
locked.body:
If juggling classes and outreach is too much, Scout can carry the workload. Tell it the city and the kind of internship. It builds a Career ID from the student's background, finds matching internships and applies for them, and builds a Showcase for a target role: a personal page that shows a student's projects and strengths better than a one-page resume can.

Scout also finds people at target companies, like team leads and hiring managers, and reaches out with a short note and the Showcase in small paced waves. Nothing goes out until you approve it. It follows up, tells you when someone views the Showcase, and sends a weekly report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=the-internship-outreach-playbook&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, help me land a summer internship in [City]

locked.title: Step 7: Keep a weekly rhythm all season
locked.body:
Internship timing varies a lot. Some larger programs recruit many months ahead, while smaller companies often decide closer to summer. So keep going steadily instead of stopping after one burst.

A simple weekly rhythm: Monday, add 5 new targets to the list. Tuesday and Wednesday, send 5 to 8 personal emails. Thursday, follow up on anything older than a week with a short, friendly note. Friday, update the spreadsheet and write down one thing that worked.

Track each row with: name, company, date sent, reply (yes, no, none), next step. After two silent follow-ups, mark it closed and move on. One good yes is all it takes, and it often comes from a place that wasn't on the first list.
locked.prompt: Make me a weekly internship search plan for the next [number] weeks. I'm a [year] studying [major], aiming for a summer internship in [field] in [city]. I have about [hours] hours a week. Give me: a day-by-day weekly rhythm, a spreadsheet layout with columns, a short follow-up email under 50 words for people who haven't replied after a week, and a checklist of what to prepare before any call or interview.

guides.tip: For remote internships, mention a time you worked on something independently and stayed on schedule. It answers the biggest remote-intern worry up front.

guides.blurb: A calmer, time-boxed system for running a remote job search.
inside: A quick time audit that shows where your search hours go
A 10-minute search kit you build once and reuse everywhere
A weekly batching plan that caps the hours
Four ways to create feedback when nobody gives you any
The small automations that save time every week
A 15-minute weekly check-in so you stay the boss
guides.intro:
A remote search can quietly spread across your whole day, because the job boards are always one tab away. That makes it tiring and hard to switch off.

This guide helps you set limits: a reusable kit, a batched week, simple automations and a short Friday check-in. A steady system for a remote search.

free.title: Step 1: Audit where your hours actually go
free.body:
Job searching feels like a full-time job partly because the hours leak. Scrolling boards, rewriting the same cover letter, checking email, starting applications you never finish.

For three days, keep a rough log. Every time you work on your search, write the activity and the minutes: browsing, applying, tailoring, outreach, follow-ups, interview prep, worrying. No judgment, just data.

Then sort it into two piles. Pile A: things that put you in front of a person (tailored applications, outreach, follow-ups, interviews). Pile B: everything else. Don't be surprised if Pile B is bigger. Your goal is to shrink it, so the same effort produces more contact with real people.
free.prompt:
Here is a rough log of my job search time over the last [number] days:

[paste activities and minutes]

Sort each activity into Pile A (puts me in front of a real person: tailored applications, outreach, follow-ups, interviews) or Pile B (everything else). Total the minutes in each. Then suggest 5 specific ways to cut Pile B time in half next week, and how to move that time to Pile A. Be practical.

free.title: Step 2: Build your search kit once, in 10 minutes
free.body:
A lot of wasted time comes from rebuilding the basics for every application. Build them once.

Your kit is one doc with six parts: 1) Target titles, two or three max. 2) Must-haves: location or remote, salary floor, level. 3) Deal-breakers. 4) Ten target companies. 5) Three proof stories, each one a problem, what you did and the result. 6) A 3-line summary you can paste anywhere.

Keep the kit open whenever you search. When a job doesn't match your must-haves, skip it in seconds. When you need to tailor, pull a proof story instead of writing from scratch. This one doc is also exactly what you'd hand to anyone helping you, human or AI.
free.prompt:
Help me build a job search kit in one page. My resume:

[paste]

What I want: [titles, location or remote, salary floor, level]. What I won't take: [deal-breakers]. Companies I like: [any you have].

Give me: 1) 2 to 3 target titles that fit my background, 2) must-haves and deal-breakers as a checklist, 3) 10 target companies that fit, with one line on why, 4) my 3 strongest proof stories from my resume in problem, action, result format, 5) a 3-line summary I can paste into applications and messages. Mark anything you're unsure of with [confirm].

free.title: Step 3: Batch the week and cap the hours
free.body:
Doing a little of everything every day is exhausting. Batching makes each task faster because you stay in one mode.

Try this weekly plan with a fixed cap, like 8 to 10 hours: Monday (90 minutes): find and shortlist 10 roles that pass your kit's checklist. Tuesday (2 hours): apply to the best 5, tailoring only the summary and top 3 bullets. Wednesday (90 minutes): reach out to one person at each of those 5 companies. Thursday (60 minutes): follow-ups and replies. Friday (30 minutes): update your tracker and plan next week.

When the time block ends, stop. Close the tabs. The cap protects your energy, and a rested you interviews better than a burned-out you.
free.prompt: I can spend [number] hours a week on my job search. My target role is [role]. Build me a weekly batching plan: which day for finding roles, applying, outreach, follow-ups and review, with time limits for each. Include a short checklist for each day so I know when I'm done. Add one rule for what to do when I feel like doing 'just one more' application after the block ends.

locked.title: Step 4: Create your own feedback
locked.body:
The worst part of a search is silence. You can't fix what nobody tells you. So build feedback in.

1) Version your resume. Name each version (A, B) and log which one you sent. After a few weeks, see which gets more replies. 2) Ask after a rejection: 'Thanks for letting me know. If you have a moment, is there one thing that would have made my application stronger?' Some people answer, and one answer can be gold. 3) Swap with a peer: trade resumes with another job seeker and give each other three honest notes. 4) Run a 6-second test: show your resume to a friend for six seconds, then ask what job you want. If they can't say, the top needs work.

Feedback won't come to you. You have to go get it.
locked.prompt:
Act as a tough but fair hiring manager for a [target role] at a company like [example company]. Here is my resume:

[paste]

Give me feedback as if you were screening 100 resumes: 1) what you notice in the first 6 seconds, 2) the top 3 reasons you might pass, 3) the top 3 things that make you want to keep reading, 4) the single change that would help most. Be honest. Don't rewrite it, just tell me.

locked.title: Step 5: Automate the small stuff
locked.body:
Little tasks eat the day. Set these up once.

Saved searches: on each job board you use, save a search with your exact titles and location and turn on daily alerts. Stop browsing from scratch. Email templates: save your outreach, follow-up and thank-you messages as templates or drafts in your email so you only change names and details. Text snippets: store your 3-line summary, your proof stories and common application answers somewhere you can paste them in seconds. Calendar blocks: put the batching plan from Step 3 on your calendar as recurring events.

An AI assistant can draft first versions of tailored lines in a minute. Always read and edit before you send. You're the one whose name is on it.
locked.prompt: Write me a set of reusable job search templates with [brackets] for the parts I change each time: 1) a short outreach message to a hiring manager, 2) a day 7 follow-up, 3) a thank-you after an interview, 4) answers to 'Why do you want to work here?' and 'Tell me about yourself' for a [target role]. My 3-line summary is: [paste]. My best proof story is: [paste]. Keep each under 100 words.

locked.title: Step 6: Hand the search to Scout
locked.body:
If you want the hours back, you can hand the grind to Scout. Setup is simple, and you already have what it needs from Step 2: your resume, your target titles, where you want to work, your LinkedIn and your biggest challenge.

From there Scout builds your Career ID and a career diagnosis, finds matching jobs and applies for you with a Showcase (a personal web page built for that job or company), and reaches out to hiring managers and team leads in small paced waves. You approve the sends, or someone you authorize does. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief when a company replies, and sends a weekly report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=hand-off-the-job-search-setup-in-10-minutes&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, take over my job search

locked.title: Step 7: Stay the boss with a 15-minute weekly check-in
locked.body:
Whether you do the work yourself or have help, one short weekly check-in keeps you in control.

Every Friday, set a 15-minute timer and answer five questions: 1) What went out this week (applications, messages, follow-ups)? 2) Who replied, and what do I need to do next? 3) What do I need to approve or decide? 4) Is anything off-target, like the wrong titles or companies? 5) What one change do I make next week?

Write the answers in three lines at the top of your tracker. Then close it and do something that has nothing to do with job searching. The search is important. It shouldn't be your whole week.
locked.prompt:
Here's what happened in my job search this week:

[paste your tracker updates, replies and notes]

Run my 15-minute Friday check-in. Answer: 1) what went out, 2) who replied and my next step for each, 3) what I need to decide or approve, 4) anything that looks off-target compared with my goals of [titles, location, salary floor], 5) the one change to make next week. Keep it to a short list.

guides.tip: Add the word 'remote' plus your country or time zone to every saved search. It cuts out roles that say remote but only hire in certain locations.

guides.intro:
Remote searches often happen entirely online, which makes them easy to automate and easy to lose track of. It helps to know what a good week actually involves.

This guide walks through each day steadily, from diagnosis to follow-up, and offers a simple scorecard for judging any tool you might use.

free.title: Step 1: Monday, run a 20-minute career diagnosis
free.body:
Before doing more, figure out what's actually wrong. A diagnosis looks at three things: what you're aiming at, how you're presented, and how you're reaching people.

Aim: are your target titles a realistic match for your last two roles, or a big stretch? Presentation: if someone read only your resume's top third, would they know exactly what you do and what you've achieved? Reach: are you only applying through portals, or also reaching real people?

Write one line for each, then pick the weakest. That's the focus for your week. Every good search, done by hand or with help, starts here, and you can do a solid version yourself with the prompt below.
free.prompt:
Act as a career coach running a diagnosis. Here is my resume:

[paste]

Target roles: [titles]. Location: [city or remote]. What's happened so far: [e.g. 40 applications, 2 replies, 1 interview]. How I've been applying: [portals only / some outreach / referrals].

Give me: 1) a rating of my aim, presentation and reach from 1 to 5 with one sentence of reasoning each, 2) the weakest of the three, 3) three specific actions for this week that target the weakest area. Be honest and specific.

free.title: Step 2: Tuesday, build a Showcase page for one job
free.body:
A resume is the same for every company. A Showcase is a short page built for one job or one company. It shows a hiring manager you get their world before they've even met you.

Pick your top target role. Build a one-page doc or simple web page with five parts: 1) A headline written for them: 'How I'd help [company] with [their goal].' 2) A short intro: who you are in two lines. 3) Three proof points that match the job post, each with a real result. 4) A first-90-days idea list: three things you'd look at or do first. 5) How to reach you.

Keep it skimmable. A hiring manager should get the point in under a minute. Then share it as a link in your application and outreach.
free.prompt:
Help me build a one-page Showcase for this job. Job post:

[paste]

Company: [name]. What I know about their goals: [from their website, news, or the post]. My resume:

[paste]

Write: 1) a headline in the format 'How I'd help [company] with [their goal]', 2) a 2-line intro, 3) three proof points that match the post's top requirements, each with a real result from my resume (mark missing numbers [add]), 4) a first-90-days list with 3 specific ideas, 5) a short closing line inviting them to talk. Keep it under 300 words.

free.title: Step 3: Wednesday, score jobs for fit and apply with your page
free.body:
Applying to everything wastes the week. Score first, then apply only to strong fits.

For each job, give 0 to 2 points on five things: title matches your target, level matches your experience, you meet most must-have requirements, location or remote works, and the company is one you'd genuinely want. Apply to 8s, 9s and 10s. Save the 6s and 7s for a slow week. Skip the rest.

When you apply, put your Showcase link where it will be seen: in the cover letter's first line, in a 'website' or 'portfolio' field, or in the 'anything else?' box. Tailor only the summary and top three bullets. Then log it in your tracker with the date and the version you sent.
free.prompt:
Score these jobs for fit. My target: [titles], [level], [location or remote]. My top skills and experience: [summary]. Score each job 0 to 2 on: title match, level match, must-have requirements met, location fit, company appeal. Give a total out of 10 and one sentence on the biggest risk. Then rank them and tell me which to apply to this week.

Jobs:
[paste 3 to 10 job posts or summaries]

locked.title: Step 4: Thursday, reach the people behind one role
locked.body:
For your top-scored job, find two or three people connected to it: the likely hiring manager (often the head of that team), a team lead, and maybe someone who recently joined the team. Look on LinkedIn (search the company plus the team name), the company's team or about page, press releases and conference speaker lists.

Send each a short note. Not a cover letter. Three sentences: who you are, why this role at this company, and your Showcase. Example: 'Hi [Name], I applied for the [role] on your team and put together a short page on how I'd approach [their goal]: [your page]. If it's useful, I'd welcome 15 minutes to talk.'

Send a few at a time, not dozens in one day. Personal and paced beats bulk.
locked.prompt: Write 3 short outreach notes (under 70 words each) about the [role] at [company]. Note 1 to the likely hiring manager, [name, title]. Note 2 to a team lead, [name, title]. Note 3 to a recent team member, [name, title], asking for a quick perspective rather than a job. Each should mention one specific thing about the team or company: [detail]. Each should include my Showcase as [my page link]. No flattery, no pressure.

locked.title: Step 5: Friday, follow up and write an honest weekly report
locked.body:
Friday is for closing loops. Follow up on anything from last week with no reply. Respond to every reply within a day, even a no, with a short thank-you. Then write your own weekly report so you can see the whole week at once.

Your report has four sections: Built (Showcases, resume versions). Sent (applications, outreach notes, follow-ups, with counts). Heard back (every reply, and what it said). Next (the three most important moves for next week).

This is the same shape as the report Scout sends each week. Writing it by hand once shows you what a useful report looks like, so you can judge any tool's version against it.
locked.prompt:
Write my weekly job search report from these notes:

[paste what you did each day this week]

Use four sections: Built, Sent (with counts), Heard back (every reply with a one-line summary), Next (3 most important moves for next week). Then flag any follow-ups that are overdue. Keep it under 200 words and don't exaggerate anything.

locked.title: Step 6: Try Scout and check its week against yours
locked.body:
If you're skeptical, good. Test it. Scout does the week you just read: it builds your Career ID and diagnosis, makes Showcases for target jobs (with many designs to choose from), finds matching jobs and applies with your Showcase link, finds hiring managers and team leads at target companies and reaches out in small paced waves, and follows up. You, or someone you authorize, approve the outreach before it goes. It alerts you when someone views your Showcase and gives you a prep brief when a company replies.

At the end of the week, ask it what it did and compare the report with the work you'd have done by hand. Judge it on what you can see.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=what-scout-does-in-a-week-walkthrough&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, what did you do for me this week?

locked.title: Step 7: Judge any AI job tool with a skeptic's scorecard
locked.body:
Whatever you use, Scout or anything else, hold it to a clear standard. Score it after one week, yes or no on each:

1) Did it show me everything it did, item by item? 2) Did it only apply to jobs that match my targets and must-haves? 3) Was the writing something I'd be proud to sign? 4) Did I approve outreach before it went out? 5) Did it follow up without me reminding it? 6) Did I learn something about my search I didn't know before? 7) Did it save me real hours compared with doing it by hand?

Five or more yes answers: keep going and check again next week. Fewer: change the targets or settings, or stop. A tool should earn its place every week, the same way you would at a new job.
locked.prompt:
I've been using [tool or method] for my job search for one week. Here is what it reported doing:

[paste report]

My targets are: [titles, location, must-haves]. Act as a skeptical reviewer. For each of these 7 questions, answer yes, no or unclear with evidence from the report: shows all work, matches my targets, writing quality, I approved outreach, follows up on its own, taught me something, saved me time. Then tell me whether to keep, adjust or stop, and what to adjust.

guides.tip: In your Showcase, add a short line on how you work remotely, like your usual hours and how you share updates. It answers a common remote question before it's asked.

A remote search needs clear focus, because the options seem endless and the competition can come from anywhere.

This guide helps you set firm targets, position yourself clearly, apply with care, reach real people and prepare well. A calm system for every stage of a remote search.

free.title: Step 1: Fill out your target card
free.body:
The job search feels broken partly because it has no edges. Every job looks possible, so nothing gets done well. Start by drawing the edges.

Make a one-page target card: 1) Two or three job titles, written the way companies post them. 2) Level (individual contributor, manager, director). 3) Location: city, hybrid or remote. 4) Salary floor, the number below which you'd say no. 5) Industries you prefer, and any you'd avoid. 6) Fifteen target companies, written out by name.

Keep the card where you can see it. Every job, message and hour gets checked against it. If something doesn't fit, it's a no, and you move on without guilt.
free.prompt:
Help me fill out a one-page job search target card. My resume:

[paste]

What I think I want: [roles, location, salary, industries]. Based on my background, suggest: 1) 2 to 3 job titles as companies usually post them, 2) the level I'm most competitive for, and why, 3) 3 industries where my experience is a clear plus, 4) 15 target companies across those industries, with one line each on why I fit. Point out anything in my wish list that looks unrealistic, kindly and honestly.

free.title: Step 2: Write your positioning and three proof stories
free.body:
Hiring managers need to answer one question fast: what is this person great at? Give them the answer.

Write a positioning statement in one sentence: 'I help [type of team or company] [achieve a result] by [how you do it].' For example: 'I help growing software companies cut support costs by building self-serve help systems.'

Then write three proof stories that back it up. Use this shape: the situation, what you did, the result, and what it shows about you. Use real numbers where you have them. These three stories go everywhere: your resume summary, your outreach, your Showcase and your interviews. Write them once, use them all season.
free.prompt:
Help me write a positioning statement and 3 proof stories. My resume:

[paste]

Target role: [title]. Target companies: [examples].

1) Write 3 versions of a one-sentence positioning statement in the format 'I help [who] [achieve what] by [how].' 2) Pick my 3 strongest accomplishments and write each as a proof story: situation, what I did, result, what it shows. Keep each under 80 words. Use only facts from my resume and mark any missing numbers [add]. 3) Tell me which positioning version fits my target role best.

free.title: Step 3: Apply smarter, not more
free.body:
Volume without fit is what makes the process feel broken. Use a quick filter before every application.

Apply only if all three are true: 1) The title and level are on your target card. 2) You meet most of the must-have requirements (not every nice-to-have). 3) You can name one specific reason you'd want this company.

For each job that passes, spend 15 minutes tailoring: rewrite your summary to echo the post's top priority, move your most relevant proof story to the top bullet, and add the post's key terms where they honestly fit. Apply within a few days of the post going up when you can. Then log it with the date and the next follow-up date.
free.prompt:
Here is a job post:

[paste]

And my resume summary and top bullets:

[paste]

My target card: [titles, level, location, salary floor]. First, tell me if this job passes these 3 checks: on my target card, I meet most must-haves, there's a clear reason to want this company. If it passes, rewrite my summary to echo the post's top priority and reorder my bullets so the most relevant one is first. Show me only what changed.

locked.title: Step 4: Pair a Showcase with outreach for your top 5 companies
locked.body:
For your five favorite companies on the target card, go beyond applying. Make a Showcase for each: a short page built for that company, with a headline about their goal, your positioning, your three proof stories and a few first ideas for the role.

Then find one or two people on the relevant team, like the team lead or the hiring manager, using LinkedIn, the company website or recent news. Send a short note with the Showcase. Wait a week. If there's no reply, send one follow-up that adds something new, like a quick idea related to their latest announcement.

Five companies done this way can teach you more than fifty generic applications, because you'll actually learn what each one cares about.
locked.prompt:
I'm targeting [company] for a [role]. Here's what I know about them: [recent news, product, goals from their site]. My positioning: [statement]. My proof stories: [paste].

Write: 1) a Showcase headline and 3 first ideas for the role, specific to this company, 2) a short note under 80 words to [name, title] that introduces me and links to my Showcase as [link], 3) one follow-up under 60 words for a week later that adds a new idea tied to [recent news].

locked.title: Step 5: Or let Scout run all five stages with you
locked.body:
If you're done doing this alone, Scout can take on the whole flow: apply, Showcase, reach out, follow up, and get you ready to interview. Say the word, and it starts by building your Career ID and a career diagnosis from your resume, target titles, location, LinkedIn and biggest challenge.

Then it finds matching jobs and applies for you with your Showcase link, builds Showcases for target jobs and companies (with many designs to choose from), and reaches out to hiring managers and team leads in small paced waves. You, or someone you authorize, approve sends before they go. It follows up, alerts you when someone views your Showcase, gives you a prep brief on a company when it replies, and sends you a weekly report of everything it did.

Start Scout here: https://scoutjob.ai/start?ref=remotejobreport-hub&utm_source=remotejobreport&utm_medium=creator-hub&utm_campaign=start-here-your-scout-setup-guide&utm_content=emma

Honest note: Scout has a 7-day free trial with a card, and plans start at $97/month. Everything else in this guide is free either way.
locked.prompt: Scout, let's get me hired

locked.title: Step 6: Prepare for the interview with a brief and a story bank
locked.body:
When a company replies, prep like you already work there. Build a one-page brief: what they do, who their customers are, what problem they solve, what makes them hard to compete with, recent news, and the likely priorities for your role. Find this on their website, recent press, product pages, and the LinkedIn profiles of people you'll meet.

Then build a story bank: your three proof stories plus five more covering common themes (a conflict, a failure and what you learned, leading without authority, a tight deadline, a time you changed someone's mind). Match each story to a likely question.

Finish with three questions of your own that show you read the brief. Practice out loud once the day before.
locked.prompt:
I have an interview for [role] at [company] with [names and titles if known]. Here's what I found about the company: [paste notes from their site, news, LinkedIn].

1) Turn this into a one-page prep brief: what they do, customers, the problem they solve, what makes them hard to compete with, recent news, likely priorities for my role. 2) List the 8 interview questions I'm most likely to get. 3) Match each to one of my stories: [paste your story bank]. 4) Suggest 3 sharp questions for me to ask that show I did my homework.

guides.intro: Many people apply to everything because nothing feels like a clear fit. The result is a scattered search. Recruiters read scattered as unfocused. A short list of adjacent roles gives your search a direction, and that makes your applications easier to write and easier to read.

free.title: Step 1: Gather your raw material (5 minutes)
free.body:
You can do this with any AI chat, ChatGPT or Claude. You don't need Scout for this part.

Open your current resume or LinkedIn profile. Copy the text. If you have performance reviews, project notes, or a list of things you're proud of, grab those too.

free.title: Step 2: Describe your experience in plain words
free.body:
Open a new chat and paste this, filling in the brackets:

Read the summary. Fix anything that's off.
free.prompt:
I want to find roles that fit my experience that I may not have considered. Here is my background:

[Paste your resume or LinkedIn text here]

Before you suggest anything, summarize in 5 bullet points what I seem to be good at, based only on what I wrote. Do not guess beyond the text. Then ask me up to 3 questions if something is unclear.

free.title: Step 3: Ask for adjacent roles
free.prompt:
Based on my background and my answers, suggest 2 to 3 roles that are adjacent to what I've done and that I may not have considered. I'm looking for remote work. For each role, give me:
1. The role title
2. The evidence from my background that supports it (quote or point to specific items I shared)
3. The gap: what's missing or weak for this role
Do not include salary figures. Do not tell me what my "perfect" career is. Be plain about where my fit is weak.

free.title: Step 4: Pressure-test each role
free.prompt:
For each role you suggested, tell me:
- What a hiring manager would likely question about my background
- One small, specific thing I could do in the next 30 days to reduce that gap
- Whether this role is commonly offered remotely, and what to check in a job post to confirm it

locked.title: Step 5: Pick one direction
locked.body: Choose the role with the strongest evidence and a gap you can actually close. Write it down. Use that title as your search term for the next two weeks.

locked.title: Step 6: Tune your resume to match
locked.body: Check every line for accuracy before you use it.
locked.prompt: I've chosen [role title] as my focus. Rewrite my resume summary in 3 sentences for this role. Use only facts from my background. Flag anything you'd need me to confirm.

guides.tip: Treat the gap as your to-do list, not a verdict. When a role shows a gap, search for 5 remote postings with that title and note which requirement shows up most often. If the same one appears again and again, that's the gap worth closing first. If it only appears once, skip it. This keeps your search calm and focused, and it keeps you from chasing every requirement you see.
